name: Anthropic
desc: Anthropic — LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #1. Maker of Claude, Claude Code, and Claude Science. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Anthropic is a San Francisco AI company founded in January 2021 by former OpenAI researchers, including siblings Dario Amodei, its chief executive, and Daniela Amodei, its president. It builds Claude, a family of large language models, and sells it three ways: as a chat assistant people use directly, as a coding and office tool for teams, and as an API developers build on. The chat assistant lives at claude.ai and on web, desktop, and mobile apps. Claude Code is its agentic coding tool, working inside a terminal or editor to read code, edit files, and run commands. Claude Cowork, which folded into Claude itself, handles longer office tasks across files. Claude Science is a workbench for researchers, built to produce auditable artifacts from tools and packages scientists already use. Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation, a legal form that lets its directors weigh a stated public benefit purpose against shareholder returns, and its governance includes a Long-Term Benefit Trust that elects a growing share of the board. It ranked number one on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States.
Anthropic makes money from subscriptions and from API usage. Claude is free at a basic tier. Pro costs $20 a month, or $17 a month billed annually at $200 up front, and adds more usage, Claude Code, Claude Science, and task scheduling. Max starts at $100 a month, with a $200 tier, and adds five or twenty times Pro's usage plus $100 or $200 a month in API credits. Team plans run $20 per seat a month billed annually with a 20-seat minimum. The API is priced per million tokens: Haiku 5.5 at $0.10 input and $0.50 output for prompts up to 100,000 tokens ($0.50 and $2.50 above that), Sonnet 5.5 at $2 and $10, Opus 5.5 at $4 and $20, and Fable 5.1 at $10 and $50. The Batch API halves those rates, and prompt caching cuts repeat input to a fraction of the base rate. Buyers range from individual subscribers to engineering teams, large companies, and government agencies. Its direct rivals are OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, and its pitch against both is safety research, careful behavior, and strength in coding and long, multi-step work.
Claude's traction is concentrated where the work is hardest to fake. Engineering teams run Claude Code against real codebases all day, and the API business grows with every agent a customer deploys, because agents consume far more tokens than a person chatting. Claude is also available through Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud, the two cloud platforms whose owners are also Anthropic investors, which puts Claude inside enterprise procurement channels Anthropic could not reach alone. Government agencies buy it for the same reason firms do: a model with published system cards, a written constitution, and a public benefit charter is easier to defend in procurement than a black box. Anthropic bets this trust premium survives a price war, and that coding agents, not mere chat, are where the money in AI models will settle.

## Claude Code and the developer surface
Claude Code is the product that turned Anthropic from a chatbot company into a developer tool company. It runs in the terminal, in editors, and in the browser, and it is built for agentic work: given a task, it explores a codebase, makes edits, runs tests, and reports back, rather than answering one question at a time. Around it sit Claude Cowork for file-based office work, Claude in Chrome for browser tasks, and integrations with Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, so Claude can work inside the documents and inboxes teams already use. The Claude Platform, formerly the developer console, is where API keys, usage, and managed agents live. Claude Academy publishes courses and tutorials for building on the API. The developer surface matters because it is where Anthropic's usage revenue concentrates: a single engineering team running agents all day spends far more than a single chat subscriber.

## The 5.5 model ladder and API rates
The current lineup, announced across September and October 2026, is Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1. Haiku 5.5 is the fast, cheap model for high-volume work such as summarization, classification, subagents, and browser use, and it is the only current model whose price steps up once a prompt passes 100,000 tokens. Sonnet 5.5 is the balanced default, which Anthropic says runs 30 percent faster and costs up to 30 percent less for most work than Sonnet 5. Opus 5.5 is the strongest model for agentic coding and knowledge work, and Anthropic says it costs 40 percent less to run than Opus 5 on typical workloads. Fable 5.1 sits above Opus for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work, at $10 input and $50 output per million tokens. Every current model offers a context window up to 1 million tokens, varying by model. Older models such as Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5 remain available as legacy options, and some earlier models are retired except on Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud.

## Constitutional AI, the PBC charter, and the Trust
Anthropic's public identity rests on safety research. Its models are trained with Constitutional AI, an approach in which the model is guided by a written constitution of principles rather than only by human ratings of individual answers. The company publishes system cards for each model, a Responsible Scaling Policy that sets out its voluntary framework for managing catastrophic risk from advanced systems, and a 2026 Public Benefit Report on how it is serving its charter. The charter itself is the responsible development of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. The Long-Term Benefit Trust is the unusual part: a separate body that elects a growing share of the board, designed to keep the mission from being traded away in a sale or a shift in ownership. Amazon and Google are both investors and cloud partners, but neither holds voting control under this structure, according to company accounts of the arrangement.

## ChatGPT and Gemini: where Claude wins and loses
Against OpenAI, Claude's edge is coding and sustained agentic work: Claude Code is widely used inside engineering teams, and Opus 5.5 is positioned as the leader in agentic coding. Against Google, Claude's edge is independence from a search and advertising business, which appeals to companies that do not want their data inside a rival's stack. Claude loses on distribution: ChatGPT and Gemini ship inside operating systems, browsers, and office suites with hundreds of millions of users, while Claude must win each user and each enterprise deal on its own. It also loses on breadth: OpenAI and Google sell video, image, and consumer hardware stories that Anthropic does not try to match. Anthropic's answer is depth in one place, the model and the developer tools around it, rather than a consumer platform spanning everything.

## What Anthropic keeps private
Anthropic does not publish a single headline user count for Claude, and it does not publish enterprise pricing beyond the Team tier; larger deals are negotiated directly. Press reports of its private valuation have moved sharply through 2025 and 2026 and disagree with each other, so no valuation figure is stated here. What is public and checkable is the price list: the subscription tiers and the per-million-token API rates above, all taken from Anthropic's own pricing page on 2026-10-30. The company's exposure is concentration: its models run on cloud infrastructure owned by its largest investors, its revenue depends on developers and enterprises continuing to pay per token while rivals bundle AI free into products they already sell, and its safety positioning is a claim that competitors dispute by publishing their own safety work.

Sources: anthropic.com homepage, pricing page, company page; claude.ai product pages as linked from anthropic.com; third-party API pricing guides cross-checked against Anthropic's pricing documentation, accessed 2026-10-30.

name: Mercor
desc: Mercor — LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #2. AI data company organizing human expertise for frontier models. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Mercor is a San Francisco expert marketplace founded in 2023 by Brendan Foody, Adarsh Hiremath, and Surya Midha, three former high-school debate teammates. It finds credentialed professionals, vets them with an AI interview, and matches them to work training and evaluating AI systems. The experts are doctors, lawyers, engineers, bankers, scientists, writers, and other specialists, and the buyers are the labs building frontier AI models and, increasingly, large companies deploying AI inside their own operations. The core mechanism is a roughly 20-minute AI video interview, role-specific and transcript-based, which a candidate takes once per role type and can retake up to three times. Mercor's software reads resumes and profiles, scores the interview, and matches people to listings, replacing the recruiter screen with a machine screen. Experts work remotely, on their own schedules, and are paid weekly by the hour. Mercor ranked number two on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States.
Mercor makes money as the intermediary between buyers who need expert judgment and experts who sell it by the hour. Its homepage reports an average contracted rate of $93 an hour, 677,000 roles created, and more than $4 million paid out to experts each day. Listed rates show the spread: oncologists at $350 to $450 an hour, general physicians around $150 an hour, legal experts around $90 an hour, and sales and marketing experts at $60 to $70 an hour. Client pricing is not published; enterprise engagements are negotiated directly, and the company does not disclose what margin it keeps between what a client pays and what an expert receives. That margin is the business: Mercor keeps the spread between the hourly rate a lab or enterprise pays and the hourly rate the expert takes home, plus fees on larger managed engagements. Its company timeline reports a $350 million Series C at a $10 billion valuation.
Mercor started by connecting freelance programmers in India with companies in the United States, then shifted as the AI boom changed what buyers wanted: not cheap coding hands, but credentialed experts who could write hard problems, solve them, and grade a model's answers. Today its network spans 300-plus professional fields, and its customer story is the frontier labs themselves: Mercor says it partners with the labs and enterprises building the most advanced AI systems, and third-party market coverage names OpenAI and Anthropic among the labs buying expert data. Reported revenue figures have climbed steeply, with market analyses putting Mercor at about $2 billion in gross annualized revenue by mid-2026, up from a business barely existing three years earlier. In 2026 it acquired Deeptune, a specialist in work-software sandboxes, to build the simulated environments where agents are now trained and tested. That acquisition shows where the market is heading: from labeling answers to building whole workplaces where an agent can practice a job and be graded on it.

## The AI interview as the product
The interview is what separates Mercor from a job board. A candidate creates a profile, takes a role-specific AI interview of about 20 minutes, and is scored on the transcript rather than on a resume keyword match. A free practice interview lets candidates try the format without affecting future applications. Once vetted, an expert is matched to listings, and hiring can be close to instant: Mercor advertises one-click hiring and automated contract generation for employers. For experts, the pitch is high hourly pay for remote work that uses their actual training, from a chemist red-teaming chemical safety to a lawyer grading a model's legal reasoning. For buyers, the pitch is speed: a vetted specialist in days, not the months a traditional recruiting process takes. The weakness is the same mechanism: an interview conducted and graded by AI can be gamed, can misread accents and communication styles, and can reject strong candidates for reasons no human ever reviews.

## APEX benchmarks and the move into evaluation
Mercor's second business is measuring AI, not just staffing it. Its APEX benchmark family tests whether models can do economically valuable professional work, and it publishes leaderboards by field. The legal benchmark, built in partnership with Harvey, grades models on 1,749 real legal tasks across 24 practice areas, judging finished work products such as memos and redlines rather than multiple-choice answers. The software benchmark, built with Cognition, tests real engineering work from bug fixes to feature builds. Accounting tests long-horizon tasks across spreadsheets, PDFs, and accounting software, and a banking benchmark built with Sierra tests customer-support agents against more than 700 policy documents. Benchmarks serve two purposes: they are marketing, showing buyers that Mercor understands the work, and they are product, because the same expert-graded tasks become the training and evaluation data the labs buy.

## Mercor Enterprise and the agent deployment pitch
Mercor Enterprise takes the same expert network into large companies that are not AI labs. The pitch is threefold: find where AI creates value in a specific business, deploy agents built and benchmarked on the company's own data, and keep improving them in production with expert grading. Published case studies claim a 50 percent-plus reduction in median incident-mitigation time for a technology customer's support agent, $7 to $9 million in run-rate savings identified for a private equity target, and roughly 12,000 support requests handled each week by a deployed customer-success system. These figures are Mercor's own case-study claims, not independently audited results. The enterprise business matters because lab demand for training data is cyclical: it surges when a new model generation is trained and falls between cycles, while enterprise deployments, if they stick, pay over years.

## Surge AI, Scale AI, and the neutrality pitch
Mercor's named rivals are Surge AI and Scale AI. Surge AI vets credentialed experts and sells managed expert work to frontier labs, and it positions itself, like Mercor, as independent of any single lab. Scale AI built the largest contributor platform in the labeling business, but Meta bought 49 percent of it in June 2025, and several labs cut or reduced their Scale contracts afterward rather than route proprietary training data through a vendor half-owned by a competitor. Mercor's pitch is that it is the neutral alternative: independent, fast, and expert-only, with AI vetting instead of a crowd. The risks cut the other way. In late March 2026, Mercor was reportedly hit by a supply-chain attack involving the LiteLLM package that potentially exposed up to 4 terabytes of internal data and contractor personal information; that incident is reported, not confirmed in Mercor's own public statements fetched here, and its full scope remains unclear. Mercor also faces the structural risk of its own customers: labs are building synthetic data and in-house evaluation teams that could shrink the expert market, and experts themselves have no employment protections as contractors.

Sources: mercor.com homepage, mission page, enterprise page, and experts page; talent.docs.mercor.com AI interview documentation; public coverage of Mercor's founding, funding, and the reported March 2026 LiteLLM incident, accessed 2026-10-30.

name: Perplexity
desc: Perplexity — LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #3. AI answer engine with real-time web search and cited answers. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Perplexity is a San Francisco answer engine founded in 2022 by Aravind Srinivas, Denis Yarats, Johnny Ho, and Andy Konwinski, and launched publicly in December 2022. Instead of returning a list of links, it searches the live web for each question and writes a direct answer with numbered inline citations to the sources it used, so the reader can check every claim against the page it came from. That citation-first design is the whole product idea: a general chatbot answers from what it memorized in training, while Perplexity re-queries the web each time, which keeps answers current and makes the sourcing visible. It runs its own crawler and index, and its default models are its own Sonar models, tuned for search. Paying users can also pick frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, and others for a given thread, and Max subscribers get Model Council, which sends one question to several frontier models at once and synthesizes where they agree and differ. Perplexity ranked number three on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States.
Perplexity makes money from subscriptions and from enterprise and developer sales. A free tier covers everyday searching. Pro is reported at $20 a month, or $200 a year, and adds higher Pro Search limits, Deep Research runs, file uploads, image and video generation, and the frontier model picker. Max is reported at $200 a month, or $2,000 a year, and adds the highest limits, the frontier models held back from Pro such as Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, and 10,000 Computer credits a month. Enterprise Pro is reported at $40 per seat a month and Enterprise Max at $325 per seat a month, with admin controls, single sign-on, and internal-file search. Perplexity's own pricing page returned only a script shell when fetched on 2026-10-30, so the prices in this dossier are as reported by pricing guides reading that page in October 2026, not figures taken from a rendered Perplexity page. Its buyers are consumers who research for a living, students, professionals, and companies that want cited answers over their own documents as well as the web.
Perplexity's scale is reported, not audited: its chief executive said the service handled about 780 million queries in May 2025, and third-party profiles put it past 100 million monthly active users in 2025. Press reports put its private valuation at $20 billion in September 2025, and later coverage discussed a higher figure in 2026 talks. The company has never published audited user numbers, so those figures are best read as direction, not fact: rapid growth from a small base, with monetization still catching up to usage. Its commercial answer to publishers has been partnership rather than confrontation, with revenue-sharing and premium publisher content inside Comet Plus, and content deals that give paying users access to reporting they could not otherwise read in full. Whether publishers accept that bargain will decide how much of the web Perplexity is allowed to cite.

## Deep Research, Labs, and Computer
Beyond the search box, Perplexity sells three deeper modes. Deep Research runs a long, multi-step investigation and returns a report with citations, aimed at market research, literature review, and due diligence. Labs builds spreadsheets, reports, and simple apps from a prompt. Computer is the agentic tier: it breaks a complex project into subtasks, routes each to the model best suited to it, and delivers a combined result, metering the work in Computer credits. Max includes 10,000 Computer credits a month plus a one-time bonus, while Pro gets a smaller one-time signup bonus and no monthly allocation, according to October 2026 pricing guides. These modes are where Perplexity stops being a search replacement and becomes a research assistant: the user states a project, and the system does the gathering, the synthesis, and the drafting.

## Comet, the browser that does the errands
Comet is Perplexity's browser, built on Chromium, and it has been free worldwide since October 2025 after launching behind the Max paywall and a waitlist. Inside Comet, the assistant can answer questions about the page open, respond to email, and carry out routine web tasks without switching apps. Comet Plus, reported at $5 a month and bundled into Pro and Max, adds premium content from partner publishers inside the browser. The browser matters strategically: if the assistant lives where the user already browses, Perplexity does not have to win a search query first, and it can see the task, not just the question. The risk is the same as for any AI browser: users must trust it with their inboxes, logins, and purchases, and a browser that acts on a user's behalf can also be tricked by a malicious page.

## Perplexity Enterprise and the internal knowledge pitch
Perplexity Enterprise, which the company says is trusted by more than 50,000 organizations, is its pitch to companies that already pay for chatbots but cannot cite them. It connects to the tools a company already uses, surfaces answers from internal files alongside web research, and promises enterprise security: SOC 2 Type II certification, GDPR and HIPAA compliance, and a commitment not to train its models on enterprise customer data. The internal search is the differentiator against consumer search: an analyst can ask one question and get an answer drawn from both a company memo and a public filing, with citations for each. Enterprise pricing is per seat, and the Max enterprise tier adds the highest Computer credit allocation, audit logs, and data-retention controls. Perplexity does not publish a breakdown of enterprise versus consumer revenue, so the split between the two businesses is not public.

## Google, ChatGPT, and the publisher problem
Perplexity's rivals are Google, whose AI-generated answers now appear directly on the results page, and OpenAI's ChatGPT, whose search features answer from the web with citations of their own. Google's advantage is default placement: it is the search box most people already use. ChatGPT's advantage is the chat habit: hundreds of millions of people already open it for everything, and search is one feature among many. Perplexity's advantage is that citations are the product, not an add-on: every answer shows its sources by design, and its index is built for retrieval rather than for advertising. Its structural problem is publishers. News and reference sites argue that cited summaries let readers skip the original article, and Perplexity's answer has been commercial: revenue-sharing and premium publisher content through Comet Plus, and content partnerships, rather than a legal settlement. How much traffic Perplexity sends back to publishers, and whether that satisfies them, is still contested, and the company does not publish referral figures.

Sources: perplexity.ai enterprise page; perplexity.ai pricing page (returned a script shell only, so prices are as reported by October 2026 pricing guides reading that page); public company coverage of Perplexity's founding, Comet launch, and Model Council, accessed 2026-10-30.

name: EPIA NEURO
desc: EPIA NEURO — a San Francisco neurotechnology startup building intent-driven brain-computer interfaces, listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #4.
distilled:
EPIA NEURO is a San Francisco neurotechnology company that launched on April 2, 2026, with a single first job: restoring hand function for people after a stroke. Its system reads a person's intent to move from the brain and turns that intent into a physical grip, so a stroke survivor who still knows what they want their hand to do can pick up, hold, and release everyday objects again. The company was founded by Michel Maharbiz, a former UC Berkeley professor of electrical engineering and bioengineering who previously founded iota Biosciences, a bioelectronics company later acquired by Astellas. Epia's pitch is that stroke leaves many people with intent intact but the pathway from intent to movement damaged, and its product is built to bridge exactly that gap rather than to let someone type or move a cursor with their thoughts. The system has three parts that work together. A proprietary implant sits in the skull, under the skin, placed in under an hour with standard neurosurgical tools; it does not pierce the dura, the membrane that protects the brain, and it is charged wirelessly through a headset worn outside the head. The implant both senses neural signals and delivers stimulation, a read-write design, and it is built to be swapped for a newer version in a short, simple procedure rather than being a one-time, permanent device. Adaptive software models read the decoded intent together with context from external sensors — what is in front of the person, what object they are reaching for — and choose the right movement. A lightweight soft-robotics glove, the grip-assist exoskeleton, then carries that movement out, grasping and releasing on command. The company says the glove is deliberately simple and replaceable, designed for daily life at home rather than only for sessions in a clinic. Epia is not selling a product yet. It has published no price, and it has announced no regulatory approval; its first-in-human system demonstrations were planned for later in 2026 at the Department of Neurosurgery at Lenox Hill Hospital in New York, and no human results have been published as of this writing. The company estimates that about 60,000 of the 690,000 people who have a new stroke in the United States each year could be candidates for its products, which it describes as a market opportunity above $5 billion; that figure is the company's own estimate, not an independent market sizing. It has not disclosed how much funding it has raised or who its investors are. Stroke is the proving ground, not the end of the plan: Epia says the same platform could later address cognitive decline, Parkinson's disease, and epilepsy, but it has given no timelines for any of those conditions. Epia ranked fourth on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States, a striking position for a pre-revenue company. Its story is a launch announcement, a product description, and a hospital partnership — enough to explain the plan, not yet enough to judge whether it works.

## The skull implant and the grip-assist glove

The implant is the part Epia talks about most precisely, because its design choices are the company's main technical bet. It learns intent from the brain and how each individual expresses it, rather than assuming every brain signals a movement the same way. Nothing penetrates the brain itself or the dura, which Epia presents as the reason the procedure can be short, use standard neurosurgical tools, and stay scalable beyond a handful of specialist centers. The read-write architecture matters because the device does not only listen: it can deliver targeted electrical feedback, and the company's longer-term platform description includes adaptive stimulation driven by real-time feedback instead of fixed stimulation settings programmed once and left alone. Continuous recording from the brain, paired with a model that learns what a person is trying to do, is how Epia describes extending assistance from movement into everyday tasks. The glove is the other half of the bet. It is a soft-robotics exoskeleton, light and affordable by the company's description, shaped with input from stroke survivors, advocates, and clinicians. Its job is deliberately narrow — grasp, hold, release — because Epia's first product is about restoring skilled, context-aware hand action, not about building a general-purpose robotic limb. The whole system is designed for years of everyday use, with a rechargeable implant and a replaceable glove, so a person is not tied to a clinic or to hardware that cannot be upgraded.

## Stroke first, neurology later

Epia chose stroke deliberately, and the choice shapes everything about its early story. Stroke is a leading cause of serious long-term disability, and hand and arm impairment is one of its most common and most stubborn consequences: many survivors recover some walking but never regain useful hand function, which is what makes dressing, eating, and holding a phone hard. Epia targets survivors who retain neural intent to move but have lost the ability to translate that intent into action, a narrower group than all stroke survivors and the reason its candidate estimate is 60,000 a year rather than the full 690,000. The company's own framing is that stroke therapy proves the platform, and the platform then treats across neurology. That sequence — one hard, well-defined indication first, then cognitive decline, Parkinson's, and epilepsy — is also a regulatory and commercial sequence: a single indication with a measurable outcome (can the hand grasp and release?) is easier to demonstrate than a general brain interface. The risk in that sequence is concentration. If the stroke system stalls in first-in-human demonstrations, or if the benefit turns out to be small compared with intensive rehabilitation alone, there is no second product to fall back on, and the later indications are only plans.

## Neuralink, Synchron, and the rest of the brain-interface field

Epia enters a brain-computer interface field that is crowded and moving fast, and its differences from the best-known names are specific. Neuralink, the highest-profile company in the field, implants electrodes that penetrate brain tissue and has focused on letting paralyzed people control computers and devices directly with their thoughts; Epia's implant penetrates neither brain nor dura and is aimed at physical rehabilitation through a glove rather than digital control. Synchron takes yet another route, delivering its interface through blood vessels in a stent-like device, and has focused on communication for people with severe paralysis. Shanghai-based Neuracle received what was reported as a world-first commercial approval in China in 2026 for a system aimed at restoring some hand movement after spinal cord injury, which shows regulators are beginning to clear this category outside the United States even as Epia remains pre-human-demonstration. Epia's bet against all of these is that the winning product is not the most invasive or the most general, but the one a neurosurgeon can place in under an hour, a patient can wear and recharge at home, and a rehabilitation team can swap for an upgrade without a major operation. That bet is untested in humans, and the field's history is full of interfaces that decoded signals well in a lab and struggled with reliability, durability, and daily use in real life.

## People, advisors, and what is still unproven

The leadership team is small and academic. Michel Maharbiz is chief executive officer; Gil Mandelbaum, a neuroscientist with more than 15 years building hardware and software for neuroscience research and clinical use, is chief technology and science officer; Michelle Patruno, an operations executive with more than 15 years scaling organizations from early stage through IPO, is chief operating officer. The advisory bench is unusually senior for a company at this stage: David J. Lin, director of the NeuroRecovery Clinic at Massachusetts General Hospital; Mark Richardson, director of functional neurosurgery at Massachusetts General; Netanel Ben-Shalom, director of the neuroplastic and reconstructive surgery program at Lenox Hill Hospital, where the first demonstrations are planned; Bernardo Sabatini of Harvard; Marc Slutzky of Northwestern, president of the Brain Computer Interface Society; and Joshua Aronson of Beth Israel Deaconess. That roster gives Epia clinical credibility and a direct line to the hospital where it plans to start, but advisors are not results. What remains unproven is everything that matters to a patient: whether the implant decodes intent reliably over months and years, whether the glove restores function that rehabilitation alone does not, what the surgical and long-term safety profile looks like, what the device will cost, and who will pay for it. Neural data is also among the most sensitive data a device can collect, so privacy protections and who controls the recordings will matter as much as the engineering. Until first-in-human demonstrations produce published results, Epia is a well-specified plan with a strong team, not a proven treatment.

Sources: epianeuro.com homepage; Inside BCI launch report (April 2026); Fierce Biotech launch report (April 2026); FirstWord HealthTech launch report (April 2026). Accessed 2026-10-30.

desc: Harvey — LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #5. Enterprise legal AI for research, drafting, and document analysis. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Harvey is a San Francisco legal AI platform founded in 2022 by Winston Weinberg, a former securities and antitrust litigator at O'Melveny & Myers, and Gabriel Pereyra, a former AI researcher at Google DeepMind and Meta. It is named for Harvey Specter, the lead character of the television legal drama Suits. Harvey sells software to law firms, in-house legal teams, and professional services firms, and it does one job: take the document-heavy work that fills a lawyer's day and do the first pass with AI, leaving judgment to the lawyer. That work includes legal research, first-pass document review, due diligence, drafting, and contract review, all inside a platform built for legal documents rather than a general chatbot with a legal prompt. Its products are Agents, which run multi-step legal work end to end; Vault, which stores, organizes, and bulk-analyzes legal documents; Knowledge, which researches legal, regulatory, and tax questions across more than 1,000 global sources; Spaces, for secure collaboration with outside counsel and business partners; and Command Center, for analytics and benchmarking of a firm's AI use. Around those sit Contract Intelligence, Horizon Scanning for regulatory change, Intake for routing legal requests from the business, a Connector Library, and Legal Work Orchestration. Harvey works inside Microsoft Word and Outlook, so lawyers use it without leaving the tools they already bill in. Harvey ranked number five on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States.
Harvey does not publish its prices. It sells annual enterprise contracts, negotiated per firm, with cost depending on seats, products, and term. Third-party estimates consistently put pricing around $1,000 to $1,200 per lawyer per month with seat minimums in the range of 20 to 50 lawyers, which implies a minimum annual commitment in the low six figures before implementation and content integrations; those estimates are reported, not Harvey's published rates, and Harvey itself publishes no per-seat price. Its traction is public in other forms: in September 2026 Harvey announced it had raised $550 million at a $15.5 billion valuation, and its earliest landmark deal was Allen & Overy, now A&O Shearman, which in February 2023 rolled Harvey out across the firm after a trial involving about 3,500 lawyers. Public customer references also include PwC's legal business and Reed Smith. Harvey's own site says more than 2,300 mid-sized and small firms use the platform, a claim that sits alongside its BigLaw reputation. Security is part of the sale: Harvey holds SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, and GDPR and CCPA compliance, and it reports FedRAMP Class D, the highest tier for sensitive unclassified federal data, for government legal teams.
Harvey also sells the change around it all: Harvey Academy offers training and workflows for lawyers new to the platform, and ROI calculators for firms and in-house teams estimate the savings from shifting first pass work to agents.

## Vault, Agents, and the daily work of a matter
A matter on Harvey typically starts in Vault: the deal documents, diligence files, or litigation records are loaded in bulk, and the lawyer asks questions across the whole set, builds review tables that pull the same clause from every agreement, or runs a playbook review that checks each agreement rule by rule and suggests edits as tracked changes in Word. Agents take the repeatable multi-step jobs: a workflow agent that runs the same research and review steps on every new agreement, a diligence agent that works a data room, a chronology agent that builds a cited timeline from incident reports, emails, and claims correspondence. Knowledge answers research questions with citations to source text, across the firm's own documents and external legal sources. The point of the design is that the lawyer never copies text between tools: the document, the research, and the draft live in one platform, and the audit trail shows which source supported which answer. That audit trail is what makes the product defensible inside a firm: a partner can check the citation before signing the advice.

## Who buys Harvey, and who cannot
Harvey's buyers are Am Law 100 and Magic Circle firms, Fortune 500 legal departments, and professional services networks, plus government legal teams at national, state, and local level. For those buyers, the math is simple: a lawyer billing several hundred dollars an hour who saves even a few hours a week pays for the seat many times over. The same math excludes everyone else. A boutique firm of 15 lawyers faces a minimum commitment designed for organizations ten times its size, and Harvey's own mid-sized-firm pages acknowledge the gap by pitching prebuilt workflow agents and Harvey-handled onboarding for firms with little or no knowledge-management staff. In-house teams use it differently from firms: they bring routine review in-house, cut outside-counsel spend on first-pass work, and use Intake to capture and route requests from across the business instead of answering them by email. Harvey is software, not a law firm: it gives no legal advice to the public, and the lawyers using it remain responsible for the work it produces.

## Legora, CoCounsel, and Lexis+ AI
Harvey's named rivals are Legora, Thomson Reuters' CoCounsel, and LexisNexis' Lexis+ AI. Legora is the closest direct rival, a legal AI platform built the same way, for the same large-firm buyers. CoCounsel and Lexis+ AI come from the incumbents that already own the legal research market: Thomson Reuters and LexisNexis sell AI inside the research databases lawyers already pay for, which makes them the default purchase for firms that want one vendor. Harvey's relationship with LexisNexis is both rivalry and partnership: Harvey uses LexisNexis content in its research, so a firm buying Harvey may also be paying LexisNexis for the underlying sources. Harvey's edge against the incumbents is that it was built as an AI platform from the start, with agents and workflows rather than a search box with a chat panel. Its exposure is the reverse: it does not build its own frontier models, it builds on models from others, so its advantage is workflow, data, and distribution inside firms, not a model no one else can buy. If the model layer commoditizes, Harvey must win on the legal workflow alone.

## The risks a buyer should weigh
The first risk is price opacity: with no published rates, a buyer cannot benchmark Harvey against a rival without running a full sales process, and reported per-seat figures vary widely. The second is accuracy: Harvey's answers carry citations, but a citation is not a guarantee, and a lawyer who files unchecked AI work faces professional consequences that no vendor warranty removes. The third is concentration: Harvey's early growth came from a small number of very large firms, and its valuation assumes it can repeat that sale across in-house teams and governments, markets with lower per-seat budgets and longer procurement cycles. None of this has slowed its fundraising so far, but it is the difference between a tool firms pilot and a platform firms standardize on, and Harvey's next phase depends on the second outcome.

name: OpenEvidence
desc: OpenEvidence — LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #6. Clinical decision support with cited peer-reviewed evidence for doctors. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
OpenEvidence is a medical information platform founded in 2022 by Daniel Nadler and Zachary Ziegler, and headquartered in Miami, Florida. It is an AI copilot for doctors: a clinician types a clinical question in plain language, and OpenEvidence returns a synthesized answer drawn from licensed, peer-reviewed medical literature, with citations the clinician can open and check. It is built for the point of care, the moment a doctor must decide between treatments, doses, or tests, when reading the primary literature directly would take hours. The content comes from signed agreements with the New England Journal of Medicine, the JAMA Network, Nature Portfolio, the National Comprehensive Cancer Network, and Cochrane Systematic Reviews, so answers can quote figures, tables, and full-text findings from journals that are normally paywalled. OpenEvidence describes itself as the most widely used medical AI among verified United States clinicians, and says it has supported more than 200 million AI-powered clinical consultations. Those usage figures are company-reported, not independently audited. OpenEvidence ranked number six on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States.
OpenEvidence is free for verified clinicians, and advertising pays for it. Access requires proof of professional status: a United States National Provider Identifier for physicians, nurse practitioners, and physician associates, a medical school enrollment credential for students, and, since September 2026, a Medical Identification Number for Canada for Canadian physicians. The company says pharmaceutical and medical device advertising shown beside answers funds the service, and it does not charge verified clinicians for search. That model is the pitch and the tension at once: a doctor gets a free tool, and the companies selling the drugs the doctor prescribes pay for the page the doctor reads. OpenEvidence's terms of use, updated in September 2026, exclude the European Union, the European Economic Area, and the United Kingdom, so the service is effectively a United States and Canada product. Its terms also say it is not intended for patients and does not replace a clinician's judgment, a line that matters because the tool's answers inform treatment decisions.
OpenEvidence's adoption figures are company-reported and striking. In July 2025 the company reported 430,000 registered physicians in the United States, about 40 percent of American physicians, and later coverage repeated the claim that more than 40 percent of United States physicians use it daily, across more than 10,000 hospitals and medical centers. The product launched in 2023 after development with support from the Mayo Clinic Platform Accelerate program, and its deal with the JAMA Network gives it access to JAMA and eleven specialty journals that a general chatbot cannot reproduce. OpenEvidence says it is HIPAA compliant, and users who are covered providers can earn continuing education credit through the platform.

## Quick Consult, DeepConsult, and Visits
OpenEvidence has grown from a single search box into a small suite. Quick Consult is the rapid lookup: one question, one cited answer, in seconds. DeepConsult, released in July 2025, is the agentic research mode: it cross-references hundreds of studies in parallel and returns a full research report, at roughly one hundred times the compute of a standard search, and it is free to verified United States clinicians. Visits, released in August 2025, is an ambient scribe: it transcribes a patient encounter and drafts the clinical note with evidence attached. Around those sit more than 50 clinical calculators, drug monograph modules, and guideline-based modules, plus iOS and Android apps and a built-in dialer for calling patients and pharmacies. In September 2026 the company announced a model family named Osler, Sackett, and Snow, trading speed for search depth, with a fourth model, Darwin, available only by application as a research preview. The suite's direction is clear: from answering questions to documenting the visit and drafting the note, which puts OpenEvidence deeper inside the clinical record.

## The content licenses and the CME platform
The licenses are OpenEvidence's moat. A general chatbot can summarize a medical abstract, but it cannot legally reproduce full-text NEJM or JAMA findings, and OpenEvidence's agreements let it show figures, tables, and multimedia from those journals inside an answer. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network agreement adds NCCN Guidelines treatment algorithms, the standard oncology pathways, directly into answers. In 2026 the company added an education platform offering accredited continuing education and Maintenance of Certification credit to NPI-verified physicians, nurse practitioners, and physician associates at no cost, with transcripts trackable through the ACCME's CME Passport system. Verified users could already earn AMA PRA Category 1 credit by reviewing a previous question and completing a brief assessment. The education business converts a search tool into a credentialing habit: the same clinician who asks a question on Monday earns credit for studying it on Friday.

## Cedars-Sinai, EHR integration, and the hospital sale
In May 2026 OpenEvidence partnered with Cedars-Sinai to integrate its platform into the hospital's electronic health record infrastructure, as reported in public coverage. That integration is the next sale: from a tool a doctor opens in a browser to a tool embedded where the doctor already works, with patient context available and answers filed back into the record. Earlier, OpenEvidence was developed with support from the Mayo Clinic Platform Accelerate program, and it has partnered with Elsevier's ClinicalKey AI on a paid offering. The hospital sale brings a different buyer: not the individual doctor, who pays nothing, but the health system, which pays for integration, governance, and controls. It also brings a different risk: once answers feed the record, an error is no longer a bad web page but a permanent note, and the company positions itself as support rather than diagnosis or treatment recommendation precisely to keep that line intact.

## Medscape, Vera Health, and the limits of a free tool
Clinicians comparing OpenEvidence usually weigh it against Medscape, which pairs a drug reference, interaction checker, calculators, and free continuing education with advertising, and against newer entrants such as Vera Health and ChatGPT for Clinicians, which offers deep research and continuing education inside ChatGPT with an optional business associate agreement. OpenEvidence's edge is depth of licensed content and citation discipline: a 2026 audit of 4,979 citations in npj Health Systems found no fabricated reference, though it did not test whether each reference actually supported its answer. Its limits are structural. It is free only to verified professionals, so patients and the public cannot use it as a medical search engine. It is unavailable in Europe under its current terms. Its advertising model means the companies whose products appear in answers also fund the platform, and OpenEvidence does not publish a breakdown of advertising revenue by sponsor. And its most quoted figures, daily use by more than 40 percent of United States physicians and use in more than 10,000 hospitals, are company claims, repeated in press coverage but not verified by an independent count.

name: Function Health
desc: Function Health — a membership-based health platform with comprehensive lab testing and longitudinal tracking, listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #7.
distilled:
Function Health is an Austin health company that sells one thing on a yearly subscription: far more lab testing than a standard annual physical, with the results explained back to you in plain language. Membership costs $365 a year, charged annually — Function cut the price from $499 in November 2025 — and it buys 160+ lab tests a year across two blood draws: 100+ biomarkers at the first visit and 60+ at a mid-year retest three to six months later. The tests run at more than 2,000 Quest Diagnostics locations across the United States, or by an at-home blood draw with a licensed specialist in select areas, and no insurance is involved; the membership is HSA/FSA eligible. A licensed clinician reviews the results, writes notes flagging what stands out, and the member gets a personalized action plan covering food, supplements, and lifestyle, plus a biological-age estimate and a dashboard that tracks results over time. The panel spans heart health, thyroid, hormones, metabolic health, nutrients, inflammation, and markers tied to cancer and fertility, including ApoB, Lp(a), advanced LDL particles, thyroid hormones and antibodies, sex hormones, vitamin D, iron studies, omega fatty acids, and lead and mercury. Function was founded in 2021 by chief executive Jonathan Swerdlin, with physician and author Mark Hyman as chief medical officer, and it describes itself as a healthcare technology company, not a laboratory or a medical provider: it arranges testing and explains results, and it says plainly it is not a replacement for a doctor. Membership is open to adults 18 and older who are not pregnant, in 48 states — not yet Rhode Island or Hawaii — and people testing in New York and New Jersey pay extra lab fees of up to $248 a year because of state rules. Function says it has delivered more than 75 million results to members, and third-party reviews report more than 100,000 members; both figures are company-stated or reported, not independently audited. Reported funding includes a $298 million Series B at a reported $2.5 billion valuation, and Function was named to TIME's Most Influential Companies list in 2025; treat those as reported figures, not Function's own published financials. The comparison Function itself invites is with a standard checkup, which covers roughly 26 markers against Function's 160+ across the year, and with executive physicals that cost thousands for a single day of testing. Its bet is that people will pay a flat yearly fee for measurement and explanation rather than for a doctor's visit, and that tracking numbers over years matters more than any single result. Function ranked seventh on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States. The dashboard is what members live with day to day: results explained for non-doctors, trends across draws, a protocol for what to do next, and past lab results uploaded into the same view. Function also sells to employers through Function for Work, a second channel beyond direct subscriptions.

## The twice-yearly blood draw

Function's product is a cadence, not a single test. Step one is personalizing: members share health history so insights can be tailored, then book a first appointment that covers 100+ biomarkers in one short visit. Step two is the clinician review, where clinicians look at the results alongside the member's history, surface what matters, and write it up with food and supplement guidance; results can be downloaded and shared with the member's own doctor, which is how Function is meant to sit alongside existing care rather than replace it. Step three is the retest: 60+ tests midway through the year, so a member sees what changed rather than getting a single snapshot. Step four is monitoring over years, watching for patterns and early signs across thousands of conditions, with the option to add back any test that was out of range and to order additional tests on demand at a member price. Results are typically ready about two weeks after an appointment, and at-home draws run on a two-hour scheduling window in select areas through a phlebotomy partner. The membership renews automatically at the then-current price, and unused mid-year tests expire at renewal, so the value of the membership depends on actually using both draws. Function's own framing for the price is blunt: testing that would cost far more ordered test by test is $365 flat, about $1 a day, with no per-test fees inside the base panel.

## MRI, CT, and the add-on panels

Beyond the base blood panel, Function sells depth in three directions. Advanced MRI and CT scans, added after Function's acquisition of Ezra, scan for signs of cancer and hundreds of other conditions; they are priced separately as member add-ons, and third-party reviews report the full-body MRI at about $899 for members, though Function's own pages describe the add-on without a single headline price, so confirm the current price before buying. Add-on blood panels go deeper into specific worries: heart health, cancer screening including multi-cancer early detection tests such as Galleri, Alzheimer's risk, Lyme disease, autoimmunity, and extended heavy metals. Two newer software features arrived with the membership in beta: Private AI Chat, for asking questions about your own results, and Protocols, personalized plans built from them. Function also runs a SuppCo Buying Club, where members shop supplements and earn credits back, and a Function for Work program for employers, priced at $349 per membership for teams of 1–9 and $325 for 10–499. The add-on strategy is also the main way the bill grows: a member who starts at $365 and adds Lyme, autoimmunity, and imaging can pass $1,000 quickly, which is worth knowing before treating the headline price as the total cost.

## Superpower, InsideTracker, and Mito Health

Function did not invent consumer lab testing, but it set the template its rivals now copy or undercut. Superpower is the closest like-for-like rival: about $349 a year for 150+ biomarkers across two draws with clinician review, and as of late October 2026 it listed a $199 annual option for 100+ biomarkers from one draw. InsideTracker is the older name in the category, built around blood analysis plus wearable data and personalized recommendations, with a narrower panel and a different emphasis on athletic performance. Mito Health undercuts on entry price, selling one-time panels from about $90 at member price with no annual commitment, built around past-lab uploads and a biological-age readout, plus an optional $9-a-month membership. Function's edge against all three is panel breadth at a flat yearly price plus the Quest network's scale — 2,000+ locations — and the clinician-written notes that reviewers consistently praise. Its weakness is the mirror image: it is a membership, not a one-time purchase, so a member who only wants one panel pays for a year; it offers written review rather than a routine one-to-one doctor visit; and its member chat does not give medical advice. Function also does not describe prescribing, so anyone whose results point to a problem still needs their own clinician to act on them.

## The argument against testing this broadly

The sharpest criticism of Function is not about its price or its labs but about the idea itself, and it comes from physicians and academics rather than competitors. Testing healthy people across 160+ markers will surface incidental findings — numbers slightly out of range that would never have caused illness — and those findings can drive anxiety, repeat testing, imaging, and specialist visits of uncertain value. Function's answer, built into the product, is the clinician review and the action plan: results arrive with context and next steps rather than as a raw list of numbers, and the retest cadence is meant to separate a one-off blip from a real trend. But the criticism has a second edge that the product cannot fully answer: a broad panel is only as useful as the follow-up it triggers, and Function is explicit that it does not provide ongoing medical care. Members who lack a good primary-care doctor may get a detailed map of their body with nobody to walk the route with them. The honest version of Function's value is narrower than its marketing: it is a thorough, well-explained set of measurements, tracked over time, for people who already have — or will find — a clinician to act on what it finds. For that person, $365 for two deep draws is cheap. For someone expecting a diagnosis or a treatment plan, it is the wrong purchase.

Sources: functionhealth.com homepage and how-it-works page; functionhealth.com Function for Work page; Agewell Function Health review (2026); Blood Test Comparison Function review (October 2026); Yespress Function Health company profile. Accessed 2026-10-30.

name: ElevenLabs
desc: ElevenLabs — an AI audio platform for realistic speech, voice cloning, dubbing, and sound effects, listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #8.
distilled:
ElevenLabs is a voice AI company founded in 2022 in London by Mati Staniszewski, a former Palantir deployment strategist, and Piotr Dąbkowski, a former Google machine learning engineer. The two childhood friends from Poland started from a specific frustration — the flat, single-narrator dubbing of foreign films they grew up watching — and built a company whose mission is to make content accessible in any language and any voice. Today ElevenLabs turns written text into speech that carries pacing, emotion, and emphasis rather than sounding like a flat robot read, and it sells that capability to three kinds of buyer: creators making videos, podcasts, and audiobooks; developers building voice into apps; and enterprises running customer-facing voice agents. Its flagship models are Eleven v3, the expressive text-to-speech model with multi-speaker dialogue in 70+ languages and a 5,000-character request limit, and Eleven v4, released in September 2026, covering 90+ languages at up to 10,000 characters per request, alongside faster Turbo and Flash variants for low-latency work. Around the models sits a full audio shop: Instant Voice Cloning from a short sample and Professional Voice Cloning on higher tiers; a Voice Library of more than 10,000 community-shared voices; Dubbing Studio, which translates speech into other languages while keeping the original speaker's voice; Scribe for speech-to-text; Eleven Music and sound effects; Studio for long-form projects like audiobooks; and ElevenReader, an app that reads PDFs, ebooks, and articles aloud. Conversational AI, sold as ElevenAgents, lets companies deploy voice agents on phone, chat, email, and WhatsApp. ElevenLabs says its tools are used by employees at more than 72% of the Fortune 500, a company claim from 2025, and third-party reporting put its valuation at $6.6 billion in October 2025; that valuation is reported, not a figure ElevenLabs publishes on its pricing page. The company ranked eighth on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States. Its customers range from individual YouTubers narrating videos to publishers producing audiobooks at scale and enterprises running phone agents, and its revenue comes from all three at once: subscriptions from creators, usage from developers, and custom enterprise deals for agents. That mix is why ElevenLabs looks like a creator tool, a developer API, and an enterprise platform at the same time — because it is all three, sharing one set of models. For publishers, Studio is the long-form workspace where an audiobook keeps one narrator's voice and tone steady across tens of thousands of words, and ElevenReader turns PDFs, ebooks, and articles into audio for individual listeners. For enterprises, Agents puts a voice on the phone that takes down order numbers and hands off to a human at its limit. The company's growth came from getting the voice right first — pacing, breath, and emphasis — and then building every adjacent audio product on top of that voice.

## Eleven v3, v4, and the model shelf

Choosing an ElevenLabs model is a real decision with audible consequences, and the shelf is organized by what the audio is for. Eleven v3 is the dramatic one: built to perform text rather than just read it, with audio tags that let a script direct laughter, pauses, and emphasis, and multi-speaker dialogue so a single generation can carry a conversation between characters. Eleven v4 is the newer general model, broader in languages and request size, and the default choice for plain narration at scale. Multilingual v2 remains the stable long-form workhorse at 29 languages and 10,000 characters, while Flash and Turbo variants trade some expressiveness for speed — Flash v2.5 at around 75 milliseconds latency — which is what conversational agents need to avoid talking over a caller. A lower-latency v3 Conversational variant, at about 280 milliseconds, sits between the two. The practical rule creators use is simple: v3 when the performance matters, v4 or Multilingual v2 when the volume matters, Flash or Turbo when a human is on the other end waiting for a reply. Speech-to-text runs on Scribe v2, priced separately, and dubbing, music, and sound effects each consume the shared credit pool at their own rates, so a project that mixes narration with dubbing burns budget faster than the headline text-to-speech rate suggests.

## Voice Library, cloning, and Dubbing Studio

The Voice Library is ElevenLabs' marketplace idea applied to voices: thousands of voices shared by the community, searchable by language and style, that any user can pick up and use, with voice owners earning when their voice is used. Cloning is the personal version of the same idea. Instant Voice Cloning, available from the Starter plan up, builds a usable clone from a short sample; Professional Voice Cloning, from Creator up, trains a higher-fidelity clone that captures more nuance and is the tier serious audiobook narrators and studios use. Voice Design generates an entirely new voice from a text description, returning three previews to choose from. Dubbing Studio is where the founding idea lives most directly: upload a video or audio file, and ElevenLabs transcribes it, translates it, and re-synthesizes it in the target language in the original speaker's voice, with timing matched to the source. Studio, formerly Projects, is the long-form workspace: chapters, consistent voices across a whole book, and context-aware delivery that keeps a narrator's tone steady across tens of thousands of words. One dated fact matters for anyone building a catalog on ElevenLabs: the company has said its default voices expire on December 31, 2026, and will no longer be accessible after that date, replaced by voices users can keep in perpetuity — so projects built on default voices need a migration plan before year-end.

## The credit pool: Creative, Agents, and API pricing

ElevenLabs does not sell minutes. It sells credits, and one shared monthly pool covers nearly everything, which is both the simplicity and the trap of its pricing. The Creative subscription tiers, monthly billing, are: Free at $0 with 10,000 credits (about 10 minutes of speech), no commercial license, and attribution required; Starter at $6 with 30,000 credits, a commercial license, and Instant Voice Cloning; Creator at $22 with 121,000 credits, Professional Voice Cloning, and 192 kbps audio; Pro at $99 with 600,000 credits and 44.1 kHz PCM output via API; Scale at $299 with 1.8 million credits and 3 workspace seats; and Business at $990 with 6 million credits and 10 seats. Enterprise is custom, with SSO and HIPAA business associate agreements. Annual billing costs ten months for twelve, so the effective monthly equivalents are $5, $18.33, $82.50, $249.17, and $825. Text-to-speech costs about one credit per character, so 1,000 credits is roughly a minute of audio; speech-to-text runs about 330 credits per minute, sound effects 200 per generation, music 900 per minute, and automatic dubbing 2,000–3,000 per minute. Developers can skip the subscription and pay as they go through the API: $0.08 per 1,000 characters for Eleven v4, v3, and Multilingual v2, and $0.04 for v4 Turbo, v3 Conversational, and Flash/Turbo, with speech-to-text at $0.22 per hour and dubbing at $0.33 per minute with a watermark or $0.50 without. Agents are priced separately again, with voice-agent minutes around $0.08 per call minute plus language-model and telephony charges. Paid credits on higher tiers can roll over for a limited period and usage-based billing can top up a plan mid-month, but Free credits do not roll over and the Free tier is non-commercial — the two mistakes new users make most often.

## Deepfakes, robocalls, and the no-go list

No honest account of ElevenLabs can skip the misuse problem, because the company's own history is shaped by it. In the lead-up to the January 2024 New Hampshire Democratic primary, AI-generated robocalls purporting to be Joe Biden urged voters to skip voting; the state attorney general investigated, and audio experts concluded the calls were made using ElevenLabs. Early in the platform's life, users also generated fake celebrity voices and impersonations, and audiobook narrators sued, alleging their voices had been cloned from copyrighted audiobooks; that case was settled out of court. ElevenLabs responded with the safeguards that now define its trust posture: a no-go list of high-risk voices that cannot be cloned, voice-captcha verification to confirm a user is cloning their own voice, consent requirements for professional clones, automated and manual content moderation, and a free AI Speech Classifier that detects whether audio was made with ElevenLabs. The tension has not gone away. The same fidelity that makes ElevenLabs the default choice for audiobooks and dubbing makes it a tool for convincing impersonation, and the company's defenses are procedural — lists, checks, and classifiers — against an adversary that only needs one convincing minute. That is why enterprise buyers ask about ElevenLabs' safeguards before its model quality, and why the company's reputation now rests as much on what it refuses to generate as on what it can.

name: Fora Travel
desc: Fora Travel — a platform powering travel advisors to build their own travel businesses, listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #9.
distilled:
Fora Travel is a New York-based modern travel agency founded in 2021 by Henley Vazquez, Evan Frank, and Jake Peters, and it works as a host agency: independent travel advisors run their own businesses under Fora's accreditation, booking travel for clients through Fora's supplier relationships and splitting the commission with Fora. The traveler-facing side is simple — a client works with a named advisor who plans the trip, and that advisor can unlock hotel perks the client could not get booking direct: room upgrades, resort credits, late checkout, and preferred rates at more than 5,000 partner properties. The advisor-facing side is the real business. Fora charges advisors $299 a year or $99 a quarter, which buys the Advisor Portal, training, community, Fora's IATA number, and errors-and-omissions insurance. Advisors keep 70% of each commission to start, rising to 80% once they pass $300,000 in calendar-year bookings and 90% at $2 million, re-qualifying each year. Commissions are tracked automatically and paid by direct deposit as supplier payments arrive. Fora says its advisors have booked more than $3 billion in travel since 2021 across 180+ countries, that 97% of its advisors had never sold travel before joining, and that advisors now work from 140 countries. The company is a Virtuoso member and a CLIA Premier Agency Member, and its backers include Forerunner, Thrive Capital, Insight Partners, and Heartcore Capital. Henley Vazquez, the travel-industry founder, was on the founding teams of two Virtuoso agencies before Fora; Evan Frank previously co-founded onefinestay, the luxury home-sharing platform acquired by Accor; Jake Peters, chief technology and product officer, previously co-founded PayPerks. Fora ranked ninth on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States. Its model only works if both sides of the marketplace show up: travelers who want a human expert rather than a booking site, and advisors willing to build a business on commission with no salary underneath it. The company's growth since 2021 suggests both sides have, in large numbers — thousands of advisors, more than $3 billion booked — but the model's honesty about year-one earnings is the part a prospective advisor should weigh most heavily, since the subscription is cheap and the work of finding clients is not. Advisors tend to specialize — honeymoons, safaris, cruises, group travel, family trips — and Fora supports that with dedicated leadership for tours, groups, flights, cruises, and hotel partnerships, plus destination training every week. The community is a working part of the product, not a perk: Fora's own account of its third year describes the Forum app with 1,500+ daily active users, 100 new posts and roughly 18,000 comments a month, and local Chapters where advisors share supplier knowledge and mentor newcomers. That peer layer is what a solo advisor cannot build alone, and it is the reason many advisors stay after the novelty of the Portal wears off.

## The Advisor Portal and Fora Reserve

The Portal is Fora's answer to the way traditional travel advising actually worked: spreadsheets, a dozen browser tabs for rate comparison, and chasing suppliers for commission payments. In the Portal, an advisor can book from 170,000+ commissionable hotels worldwide — from IHG, Hyatt, Belmond, and Rosewood down to boutique properties — plus cruises, villas, all-inclusives, tours, transportation, vacation packages, and travel insurance, and can book any hotel that accepts Fora's IATA number even if it is not listed in the Portal. Around the booking engine sit the tools that make the business run: a CRM, an itinerary builder, automated supplier invoicing, rate comparison, AI-powered research assistance, and commission tracking. Fora Reserve is the preferred-partner layer on top: more than 5,000 hotel, cruise, and tour partners where advisors get exclusive rates and client perks, and where Fora says advisors earn higher base commissions, averaging about 12% against an industry standard of 5–10%. There is also a flights tool and group booking support, though Fora does not currently offer Sabre access, which matters to advisors with GDS experience. Training is included in the subscription rather than sold separately: a digital certification program for new advisors, live hands-on labs led by Fora headquarters staff including the founders, weekly partner and destination trainings, office hours, and a community app called Forum, plus local Chapters across North America and a growing international presence. Fora's pitch to suppliers completes the triangle: advisors bring them their best customers at lower cost than other channels, which is why the preferred partnerships exist at all.

## Commission tiers and the $299 subscription

Fora's economics are transparent in a way the travel industry rarely is, and that transparency is a selling point. Worked example from Fora's own join page: a $1,200 booking at an 11% commission produces $132 in commission, of which the advisor at the 70% base split takes home $92.40. The split improves only with volume, not with a pricier subscription tier — unlike some host agencies that sell higher splits as plan upgrades — so the way to earn more at Fora is to book more travel. The subscription itself is flat: $299 a year or $99 a quarter, the same for every advisor, covering technology, training, support, community, the IATA number, and insurance. That flat fee plus volume-based splits is the whole compensation design, and it has a blunt consequence Fora states openly: there is no salary, no guaranteed monthly income, and especially in year one there may be very little income at all. Most advisors build toward full-time earnings over multiple years, and they generate their own leads — Fora does not hand them clients. Agent rates and familiarization trips, the discounted travel that draws many people to the industry, are reserved for advisors with well-established books of business, not new joiners. Fora is also explicit that it is not for people seeking passive income or discounted personal travel: advisors are meant to advise other travelers, not to self-book their own trips.

## WorldVia, Outside Agents, and the host-agency field

Fora competes with a long-established host-agency field, and the differences are in pricing structure more than in product. WorldVia Travel Network, founded in 1998, charges $9 to $299 a month across four subscription tiers plus a one-time activation fee, and gates higher commission splits and training behind the pricier tiers; its Individual plan starts at the same 70/30 split as Fora but caps there, while its Growth and Team plans reach 90/10. Outside Agents starts at a higher base split, 80/20, rising to 90/10 at $10,000 in prior-12-month commission earnings and 95/5 at $40,000, on a $26- or $46-a-month plan — but it reserves its luxury preferred partnerships for a separate luxury division with its own enrollment fee and sales minimums, while every Fora advisor gets preferred-partner access from day one. Fora is also an exclusive host agency: an advisor cannot be affiliated with Fora and another host agency at the same time, so switching requires a clean cutover date. Against both rivals, Fora's case is that it bundles everything — training, platform, and luxury partnerships — into one flat fee from the start, aimed at newcomers, where the older agencies were built for experienced agents and price their extras separately. The counter-case is just as clear: an experienced advisor who already has clients and wants the highest starting split, or Sabre access, or a cheaper first year, may find a better deal elsewhere, and Fora's own comparison pages concede WorldVia's first year can be cheaper.

## Who should not join Fora

Fora's own materials are unusually direct about fit, and that directness is useful. It fits people who want training, technology, and supplier relationships while building a client base from scratch — the wedding planner already fielding travel questions, the career changer who loves planning trips, the 25-year American Express Travel veteran weighing a switch. It does not fit people looking for passive income, a discount on their own holidays, or a quick side income: advisors earn commission only on travel they book for clients, leads are self-generated, and the first year is typically lean. Advisors who live in Ontario need Travel Industry Council of Ontario certification before selling travel to the public, and advisors everywhere work under Fora's accreditation rather than their own, which is the point of a host agency but also a constraint. The $3 billion booked since 2021 and the 97%-newcomer figure cut both ways: they prove the model can take a complete beginner and turn them into a booking advisor, and they also mean the community is dominated by people still learning, which is why Fora invests so heavily in training, mentorship, and Chapters. A prospective advisor should judge Fora on that trade — a low flat fee and a full toolkit in exchange for building the business themselves — rather than on the romance of travel.

Sources: foratravel.com about-us page; foratravel.com join pages and host-agency comparison pages (Fora vs. WorldVia, Fora vs. Outside Agents, Is Fora Right for Me); PhocusWire Fora launch report. Accessed 2026-10-30.
