name: Sierra
desc: Sierra — an enterprise AI agent platform for customer experience, listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #10.
distilled:
Sierra is a San Francisco company founded in 2023 by Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor that builds AI agents for customer service at large companies. Taylor is the former co-CEO of Salesforce and the current chair of OpenAI's board; Bavor spent 18 years at Google, where he ran Google Labs. Sierra's product is a platform it calls Agent OS: a company builds one AI agent, and that agent serves customers across chat, voice, SMS, WhatsApp, email, and ChatGPT, with the same knowledge, tone, and guardrails on every channel. The agent does not just answer questions. It connects to the company's own systems — order management, CRM, knowledge bases, payment processing — and takes real actions: processing a return, updating a subscription, refinancing a mortgage application, routing an insurance claim, saving a cancellation. Sierra says it builds agents from 15+ frontier, open-weight, and proprietary models, with routing and orchestration handled by the platform, so the customer is not buying a single model's chatbot but an agent that can reason, use tools, and escalate to a human when it should. The business model is the part Sierra talks about most, because it is a deliberate break from how enterprise software is usually sold: Sierra charges by outcome, not by seat. When its agent resolves a case on its own, the customer pays a fee for that resolution; when the agent has to transfer to a human, in most cases there is no charge. Sierra publishes no price list, no self-serve plan, and no per-resolution rate — contracts are custom enterprise deals — and third-party estimates of roughly $1.50 per resolution and typical annual contracts above $150,000 are unverified analyst figures, not Sierra's published rates. Reported traction is large and fast: a $950 million Series E in May 2026 led by Tiger Global and GV at a reported $15.8 billion valuation, reported annual recurring revenue above $150 million in February 2026 and about $200 million by May 2026, and a company claim of serving more than 40% of the Fortune 50. Treat the valuation and revenue figures as reported, not as audited financials. Sierra ranked tenth on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2026 list for the United States. Its bet is that customer service is the right first market for agents that act rather than chat, because a resolved case is countable where a helpful conversation is not, and a large brand's support volume turns countable resolutions into large contracts. If that bet is right, outcome pricing becomes the standard way agents are sold; if customers find outcomes hard to define or agents hard to supervise, the custom-contract model that makes Sierra lucrative also makes it slow to adopt. Before launch Sierra simulates an agent against thousands of past tickets, so a CX team sees how it handles cases before trusting it with one. Its customers lean toward regulated industries — mortgages, banking, healthcare, telecom, retail — where a supervised agent following enforced workflows beats a clever chatbot.

## Agent OS, Studio, SDK, and Ghostwriter

Agent OS is the layer everything else sits on: the runtime where an agent is built, deployed, supervised, and improved. It has three ways in. Agent Studio is the no-code path, where customer-experience teams describe goals in plain language and build journeys — the multi-step workflows an agent follows for a return, a cancellation save, or a subscription change — with version control in GitHub-style workspaces and a simulation environment that runs the agent against thousands of past tickets before it touches a live customer. The Agent SDK is the developer path, with declarative goals, composable skills, full API control, and deep system integrations for teams that want to build the agent in code. Ghostwriter, launched in March 2026, is the newest path and the most distinctive: an agent that builds agents, drafting workflows, integrations, guardrails, and tone from standard operating procedures, call transcripts, whiteboard sketches, or plain-English descriptions. Around those builders sit Insights and Explorer analytics for watching what agents do, and Agent Memory, which gives the agent persistent context across interactions — a customer who called last week about a delayed shipment and chats today about the same order does not have to start over. Agents work in 59 languages according to Sierra's product pages, and the platform carries compliance badges its enterprise buyers require: SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, and CCPA, plus ISO 42001, the AI management-system standard. Sierra also says it is the first Level 1 PCI-compliant conversational AI platform, listed on the Visa Global Service Provider Registry, with card data captured and routed to the merchant's existing payment processor without ever entering the conversational model — which is why its agents can take a payment in the same conversation that resolved the problem.

## Paying only for resolved outcomes

Outcome-based pricing is Sierra's core commercial argument, and it is worth stating exactly because it is easy to overstate. The customer and Sierra agree, per contract, what counts as a qualifying outcome — a resolved support conversation, a saved cancellation, an upsell or cross-sell — and Sierra is paid when the agent achieves it. When a conversation is unresolved or escalated to a human, in most cases there is no outcome fee. Routing or greeter-style interactions, where the agent's job is just to point the customer in the right direction rather than resolve anything, may instead be billed by conversation count. The per-outcome rate and the definition of an outcome are negotiated per contract and not disclosed, so two Sierra customers may pay different rates for the same kind of resolution. Taylor's argument for the model is about incentives: if Sierra is paid per resolution rather than per seat, per conversation, or per token, its revenue grows by getting better at solving problems, not by generating more billable chatter. The model's weakness is the mirror image of its strength: it requires a customer whose problems have clean, countable outcomes and enough volume to make a custom enterprise contract worthwhile. A company with a few thousand support tickets a month, or with problems that are mostly judgment calls rather than resolvable cases, cannot use Sierra the way a high-volume consumer brand can. There is no free tier, no trial a team can start on its own, and implementation is services-led over multiple quarters — third-party reviews report three to seven months — so Sierra is a buying decision for a CX leadership team, not a tool an individual support agent adopts.

## Decagon, Zendesk AI, and Salesforce Agentforce

Sierra's competitors divide into two camps, and Sierra positions against both. Decagon, the closest direct rival, also builds AI agents for enterprise customer service and also sells through demos with no published price; Decagon charges a fixed rate per conversation or a higher rate per resolution and says most customers choose per conversation, while Sierra charges per outcome. Decagon frames its product as an AI concierge built around Agent Operating Procedures; Sierra frames its as an operating system for agents. The other camp is the incumbents: Zendesk AI and Salesforce Agentforce, which sell AI as an extension of the support platform the customer already runs. Salesforce has cycled through three pricing models in eighteen months — $2 per conversation, then Flex Credits at $0.10 per agent action, then per-user seat licenses and pay-per-resolution for its Help Agent — which Sierra presents as evidence that seat and usage pricing misalign incentives for agentic software. Sierra's answer to both camps is the same: a purpose-built agent platform, not a chatbot bolted onto a ticketing system, paid for only when it does the job. Its disadvantages are also visible in third-party reviews: context loss in longer conversations, a steep learning curve during setup, and limited ability for customers to self-edit live agents without involving Sierra's team. The platform's reach into ChatGPT itself — Sierra agents deployable inside ChatGPT — is a distribution advantage no rival can copy directly, and it is inseparable from Taylor's position as OpenAI's board chair, a relationship that is both an asset and a concentration risk.

## StoreEase's Amber and the supervised-agent bet

The clearest public picture of a Sierra agent at work comes from StoreEase, a self-storage operator whose agent, Amber, serves customers across phone, web, and the facility lobby. On the phone Amber answers 24 hours a day with no voicemail; on the web an Ease Web Assistant handles customers who prefer to self-serve; on site, an Ease Virtual Console brings the same agent into the lobby so a walk-in never faces a locked door and a QR code. StoreEase's chief technology officer describes the design rule as "constrained beats improvising": every journey is an enforced workflow the agent cannot wander outside of, access and account information are gated behind real authentication and good standing, and the team keeps a running list of questions the agent will not answer, each one added after a real hallucination surfaced in testing. The result, according to StoreEase, is that the agent now contains 65 to 70 percent of service calls end to end without escalation to a person. That number is the supervised-agent bet in miniature: Sierra's value is not that its agents are clever, but that they are constrained, authenticated, tested against real tickets before launch, and measured on outcomes a business can count. Sierra's named customers span the same pattern across industries: SiriusXM, Sonos, ADT, Rocket Mortgage, Vanguard, Wayfair, WeightWatchers, Chime, Nubank, Ramp, Rivian, Sutter Health, Gap, Hyatt, Uber, and Santander, among others. The risk for Sierra is that this bet requires deep, expensive, multi-quarter implementations for each customer, which is why its growth depends on landing a relatively small number of very large deals — and why a slowdown in enterprise AI spending, or a rival that makes supervised agents cheaper to deploy, would hit it harder than a company selling a self-serve tool.

Sources: sierra.ai product and customer pages; Sierra Agent OS 2.0 announcement (November 2025); CNBC Series E reporting (May 2026); Sierra vs. Decagon comparisons checked October 2026; StoreEase customer story on sierra.ai. Accessed 2026-10-30.

name: Thinking Machines Lab
desc: Thinking Machines Lab — an AI research lab founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #11.
distilled:
Thinking Machines Lab is an artificial intelligence research and product company founded in February 2025 by Mira Murati, formerly chief technology officer of OpenAI. Its team includes people who built ChatGPT and Character.ai, open-weight models like Mistral, and open-source projects including PyTorch, OpenAI Gym, Fairseq, and Segment Anything. The lab's stated aim is AI that is more widely understood, customizable, and generally capable, with an emphasis on systems that collaborate with people rather than fully autonomous systems alone. It works on frontier model intelligence, multimodal systems spanning text, image, and audio, and the infrastructure needed to customize models. It makes money through Tinker, its post-training platform, which charges for usage: training, sampling, and prefill priced per million tokens at rates that vary by model and context length, plus checkpoint storage at $0.10 per gigabyte per month. Its open-weight models, Inkling and Inkling-Small, are free to download from Hugging Face, and the paid step is fine-tuning and running them through Tinker. Thinking Machines matters because post-training used to require hiring an infrastructure team, sourcing GPUs, and debugging failed runs; Tinker turns that into an API call, and its customers report custom models beating frontier models on narrow jobs. Bridgewater trained Qwen3-235B on Tinker to filter financial information and reported 84.66% accuracy across six held-out tasks against GPT-5.5's 78.2%, at roughly one-fourteenth the inference cost. That result is the lab's pitch in one line: a smaller model, trained on your own expertise, outperforming a general frontier model on your task, for less money. The lab also publishes its research openly, with technical blog posts, papers, and code under its Connectionism banner, arguing that scientific progress on AI is a collective effort and that sharing work improves its own research culture as well as public understanding. Its stated research directions are model intelligence as the cornerstone, infrastructure quality as a top priority, and advanced multimodal capability, so that systems can adapt to the full spectrum of human expertise rather than excelling only at programming and mathematics. For a prospective customer, the buying decision is therefore two-part: the open weights cost nothing to download, and the question is whether managed post-training on Tinker beats building the same capability in-house or fine-tuning a closed model through another lab's API. The lab's answer rests on its first year of Tinker results, where enterprise users report custom models beating frontier models at their own tasks, and on the claim that its team has already built this kind of infrastructure inside frontier labs. What remains unproven is breadth: the public results cover a handful of domains, and the lab must show the same uplift for the next hundred customers, not just the first few it chose to highlight.

## Tinker: fine-tuning as an API

Tinker is a managed post-training platform. A user keeps their own data and training loop; four API functions connect their code to Tinker's managed infrastructure, which handles GPUs for sampling and training and stores checkpoints. The platform supports open-weight models from 4 billion to 1 trillion parameters, dense and mixture-of-experts, and charges only for tokens actually used rather than idle time, with automatic retries and kernel-level optimizations including LoRA-specific kernels. Tinker publishes cookbook recipes for common jobs, such as SDFT for continual learning and forecaster training, drawn from its research grantees and early customers. Publicly disclosed customer work spans classification, forecasting, search agents, continual learning, and content and code generation. Lightning Rod Labs trained gpt-oss-120b to predict clinical events from raw patient notes and reported 27% lower prediction error and 69% lower calibration error than the prompted base model on 500 held-out retrospective questions, a research evaluation the lab notes does not establish clinical deployment performance. Monoid Labs trained DeepSeek V3.1 to research questions and predict real-world outcomes, and Krea and Architect Labs are named as Tinker users in design and architecture work. Tinker's first users were AI researchers avoiding GPU management; by its first anniversary in October 2026, the lab said enterprise customers training custom models had shifted its focus toward speed, security, and production inference.

## Inkling and Inkling-Small: the open models

Inkling is Thinking Machines' most capable open model, with native reasoning over text, images, and audio. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 975 billion total parameters and 41 billion active, a 1 million token context window (64K or 256K on Tinker), and controllable effort that trades thinking time against speed and performance. Inkling-Small matches its larger sibling on many benchmarks at a quarter of the size, the lab says, with 276 billion total parameters and 12 billion active, the same 1 million token context, and lower cost and latency. Both are positioned as generalist models: knowledge, math, and science; agentic coding and tool use; speech at the open-source frontier on input; instruction following across detailed multi-step instructions; and forecasting with calibrated confidence. The lab publishes model cards for both and invites rightsholders to contact it about the models. Inkling is designed to be grabbed two ways: download the open weights from Hugging Face, or fine-tune them for a domain on Tinker. That pairing is the business model in miniature: the weights are free, the managed training and inference around them are not.

## Who builds with it, and who it is up against

Tinker's users are AI researchers, research labs, and enterprises with a domain where a general model is not good enough: finance, clinical forecasting, hardware design, search, specialized coding, and audio analysis are all named by the lab. Its competition comes from three directions. Frontier labs sell their own fine-tuning APIs for their closed models, trading openness for convenience. The open-weight ecosystem, including Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, and Mistral, offers weights anyone can run, but leaves the training infrastructure to the user. And training and inference platforms sell managed GPU capacity without the post-training tooling. Thinking Machines' difference is combining the two halves: open weights plus a managed post-training API built by a team that ran frontier post-training internally. The risk is concentration: the lab is young, its reputation rests on a small number of public customer results, and its open models are judged against frontier closed models that improve every few months. Funding, valuation, and headcount are not stated as company facts here; public reporting on those figures changed through 2025 and 2026, and the lab's own site does not publish them.

Sources: thinkingmachines.ai homepage, thinkingmachines.ai/tinker, thinkingmachines.ai/inkling, thinkingmachines.ai/news/one-year-of-tinker, accessed 2026-10-30.

name: Feastables
desc: Feastables — a chocolate and snack brand created by Jimmy Donaldson (MrBeast), listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #12.
distilled:
Feastables is a chocolate and snack brand launched in January 2022 by Jimmy Donaldson, the YouTuber known as MrBeast. It began with chocolate bars and has grown into a consumer packaged goods company selling chocolate bars, peanut butter cups, and gummies, plus limited-time collaborations and branded apparel. It makes money the way a packaged food company does: wholesale sales to retailers, plus direct online sales. Its retail footprint is the core of the business, with shelf space at Walmart, Target, 7-Eleven, Costco, Kroger, Albertsons, and Sam's Club, all named on its own store locator. As of 2026-10-30, feastables.com carries a banner saying online sales have moved to mrbeast.store, so the brand's own website now routes shoppers to that storefront rather than selling direct itself. Feastables matters because it is the clearest test of creator-led packaged goods: a YouTube audience converted into national retail distribution in under two years, without the television advertising budgets that legacy candy brands rely on. Feastables is a private company and does not publish audited sales figures; third-party revenue estimates vary so widely that they are omitted here rather than presented as fact. The brand's growth path runs through Donaldson's audience first and retail second. He built one of the largest YouTube audiences in the world with large-scale stunt and philanthropy videos, then launched a food product that audience would actually buy in a store, rather than merchandise that only fans would wear. Chocolate was a deliberate choice: it is a repeat purchase, it sits in every grocery and convenience store, and it turns a viewer into a shopper without asking them to learn a new product category. From bars, the line expanded into peanut butter cups, then gummies, then limited-time collaborations that keep the brand in the news between videos. For a shopper, the practical facts are simple: bars and share bags are on shelves at the major chains named above, the brand's own site now sends online buyers to mrbeast.store, and a store locator on feastables.com covers the United States plus the United Kingdom, Ireland, Germany, Austria, France, Spain, and Australia. For a retailer, the pitch is foot traffic: stocking Feastables brings in shoppers who arrived looking for it by name, which is a rarer asset in the candy aisle than another chocolate bar. What to watch next is whether the brand can hold its shelf space as a food company rather than a creator novelty, and whether moving online sales to mrbeast.store helps or hurts: it consolidates Donaldson's brands under one storefront, but a shopper who lands on feastables.com can no longer check out there and must follow the banner to a different store. The brand's answer so far is more drops, more collaborations, and more countries on the store selector, betting that novelty plus distribution keeps it ahead of the next creator brand that tries the same playbook.

## Chocolate bars, cups, and gummies on the shelf

The catalog starts with chocolate bars: Milk Chocolate, Milk Crunch, Peanut Butter, Peanut Butter Crunch, and Cookies & Creme, sold as single bars, share bags, pantry packs, and bulk boxes. A Milk Chocolate Share Bag lists at $6.99, a Milk Chocolate Pantry Pack at $14.99, and a Chocolate Variety Bulk Box at $45.00 on the brand's catalog. Peanut Butter Cups come as a $6.99 share bag and larger packs, and the brand sells a Feastables x Liquid Death Peanut Butter Cup Bundle at $49.98. Gummies arrived later under the Sour Strikes line, with Raspberry and Assorted varieties at $39.99. Limited-time lines rotate through the catalog, including Mario Sour Boosts at $27.99, Mario Galaxy Cocoa Crunch at $23.99, Yoshi Eggs at $29.99, and a Beast Games Box at $14.99 tying the snacks to Donaldson's Amazon show. Branded apparel sits alongside the food: Retro Hoodies at $59.99, Wavy Tees at $29.99, and hats at $19.99. Prices are list prices from the catalog on 2026-10-30 and change with promotions; free shipping on feastables.com orders over $50 was advertised on the homepage the same day.

## From a YouTube audience to retail shelf space

Feastables' distribution model reverses the usual packaged-goods playbook. A legacy candy brand buys attention with advertising; Feastables launched to an existing audience of tens of millions of YouTube subscribers, and retailers took the product because shoppers would come looking for it. That is why Walmart and Target carried it from the early days, and why the brand expanded into convenience and grocery chains across the United States, Canada, and Mexico, with listings in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Germany, Austria, France, Spain, and Australia on its own store selector. The marketing engine is Donaldson's content itself, plus collaborations that borrow other audiences: the Liquid Death bundle, the Mario line, and the Beast Games tie-in all put Feastables in front of buyers who did not arrive through a MrBeast video. The risk in this model is concentration. The brand's trial and attention still run substantially through one creator, so a controversy around Donaldson or a shift in his audience lands directly on a food company that now has to hold shelf space on its own merits, against competitors that do not depend on any single person.

## Cocoa sourcing and the child-labor pledge

Feastables' site carries the line "On A Mission To End Child Labor" and an Ethical Sourcing section in its navigation, positioning its cocoa sourcing as a deliberate break from an industry with a long record of child labor in West African cocoa farming. The brand's pitch is that a chocolate company built in public, by a creator whose audience watches every claim, has to source differently to keep its story straight. What the site does not do, on the pages fetched for this dossier, is publish a certification, a supplier list, or an audited sourcing report; the dedicated ethical-sourcing page did not load on 2026-10-30, so the specifics of its sourcing program beyond the stated mission are not verified here. Shoppers who care about this should check the current ethical-sourcing page and any certification marks on the packaging itself rather than taking the mission statement as proof.

## Feastables against Hershey, Mars, and the candy aisle

On the shelf, Feastables competes with Hershey, Mars, and Nestle, plus store brands and premium chocolate makers, for the same impulse purchase at the checkout and the same planned purchase in the candy aisle. Its difference is not price: at $6.99 for a share bag it sits in the normal range for branded chocolate, not at a discount. Its difference is how trial happens. A legacy brand pays for a television spot or an endcap display; Feastables gets trial from videos, creator collaborations, and limited-time drops that create a reason to look for it this week rather than next month. name: Solace
desc: Solace — a digital platform connecting patients with dedicated healthcare advocates, listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #13.
distilled:
Solace is a digital health platform founded in 2022 by Jeremy Gurewitz and Sara Sargent that pairs patients with dedicated healthcare advocates who navigate the American healthcare system on the patient's behalf. Advocates are experienced healthcare professionals, primarily registered nurses plus licensed practical and vocational nurses, with an average of 16 years in the field, according to Solace. They schedule appointments, coordinate between doctors, manage medical records, research conditions and local resources, attend appointments, organize documents, keep family members updated, and fight insurance denials, including prior authorizations and appeals. The patient journey starts with an eligibility check that takes under a minute, followed by a roughly 20-minute call with a Solace physician who listens to the patient's goals and history, after which the patient is matched with a dedicated advocate and works with that same advocate for as long as help is needed. Solace makes money from insurers, not from patients: advocacy is covered by Medicare and most major commercial plans, including UnitedHealthcare and Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield, so eligible patients pay little or nothing out of pocket, though eligibility varies by plan and must be checked. Solace matters because the system's complexity is itself a health problem: patients miss care, lose appeals, and give up on referrals not for medical reasons but because no one owns the paperwork, the phone calls, and the follow-up, and Solace sells someone who does. The patients who use it most are people with complex, ongoing care: a new diagnosis that needs several specialists, a chronic condition with medications and appointments to track, a parent or spouse whose care a family caregiver is trying to coordinate, or an insurance denial that needs an appeal letter and a phone campaign. Solace's site lets visitors browse advocates by specialty and by state, and it runs a dedicated path for caregivers and for patients' families, since the person doing the navigating is often not the patient. Scale claims on the site run into the tens of thousands of patients helped, with a 4.7 star rating across 8,332 reviews on its outcomes page, and the company says advocates are covered by Medicare and most major commercial plans nationwide. What the site does not publish on the pages fetched here is a self-pay price for patients whose plan does not cover advocacy; those visitors are directed to the eligibility check rather than a price list, so anyone without coverage should ask what, if anything, they will owe before starting. The open question for Solace is whether payer-funded advocacy stays generous as it scales: the model works for patients precisely because someone else pays, and that someone else will keep measuring whether the advocacy saves more than it costs. The test is simple: patients who would otherwise give up on an appeal get someone who does not give up for them.

## What an advocate actually does, day to day

Solace's own list of advocate tasks is practical rather than medical: scheduling appointments, communicating with doctors, clarifying instructions, attending appointments, reducing medical bills, coaching and support, locating local resources, organizing medical documents, keeping family updated, managing insurance appeals, managing transitions of care, and researching conditions and solutions. Solace says that for every hour an advocate spends communicating directly with a patient, about three additional hours go to behind-the-scenes work on that patient's care: insurance calls, scheduling, records, and follow-up. Advocates do not provide medical or legal advice or services, Solace states plainly, and patients must be 18 or older. The model has a clinical backstop: Solace Health Medical Group, a clinician-led provider group, delivers clinical services through licensed physicians board-certified in family medicine, internal medicine, or geriatric medicine, and behavioral health services through licensed clinical psychologists, with medical services in all 50 states and Washington, D.C. Solace's physicians oversee the advocate work and handle the intake conversation, so the advocate is not freelancing on clinical judgment.

## How Solace gets paid: Medicare and payer contracts

Solace operates a three-sided arrangement: patients get advocacy at little or no out-of-pocket cost, advocates get flexible work, and payers get patients who stay engaged with care and avoid duplicated or delayed treatment. The payer side runs through CMS-recognized care management programs: chronic care management with personalized plans for patients with two or more chronic conditions, ongoing check-ins, medication reconciliation, remote support, screening for health-related social needs such as housing, food access, and transportation, and connection to community and payer-supported resources. Preventive care, transitional care after a hospital stay, advance care planning, and behavioral health support and coordination are also part of the clinical model. Medicare coverage of advocacy services for chronic and complex conditions, which expanded in 2024, is the reimbursement foundation that made the model work at scale; Solace's payer pages pitch insurers on fewer avoidable costs and better continuity rather than on patient fees. That payer dependence is also the business risk: if Medicare or a major plan narrows what it reimburses, Solace's free-to-the-patient offer narrows with it, and eligibility already varies by plan today.

## Solace against hospital, insurer, and independent advocates

Solace's central claim against its alternatives is independence plus continuity. An advocate employed by a hospital or an insurer answers to that organization; an independent advocate hired privately is paid by the patient, which puts the service out of reach for many. Solace argues its advocates stay focused on the patient across the whole system, for as long as help is needed, because the payer funds the work rather than the patient or a single provider. Against other navigation services, its differentiators are the insurance-covered price point, the dedicated single advocate rather than a rotating call center, and the physician oversight behind the advocate. The counter-evidence to weigh is public: Solace's outcomes page shows a 4.7 star rating across 8,332 reviews, and company announcements claim 98% of patients feel more in control and 92% experience measurably better outcomes, both company-reported figures rather than independent studies. At least one public complaint has alleged Medicare was billed $4,600 for work amounting to obtaining one set of medical records, a third-party report that Solace has not publicly answered in the material reviewed here. Prospective patients should check their own plan's eligibility and ask what will be billed before starting.

Sources: solace.health homepage, solace.health/what-can-patient-advocates-do, solace.health/payers, solace.health/outcomes, BusinessWire coverage of Solace's expanded insurance coverage, accessed 2026-10-30.

desc: Decagon — an enterprise AI platform for conversational customer-service agents, listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #14.
distilled:
Decagon is a San Francisco conversational AI company founded in August 2023 by Jesse Zhang and Ashwin Sreenivas that builds AI agents for customer service. Its agents handle conversations across voice, chat, email, and SMS, and they do not just answer questions: under guardrails the business controls, they take action, pulling data from a CRM, processing a refund, rebooking a reservation, or changing an account, and handing the hardest cases to a human. Decagon sells to large enterprises through demo-led sales; pricing is not published, and deals are enterprise contracts rather than self-serve subscriptions. Its named customers include Chime, Avis Budget Group, Duolingo, Notion, Oura Health, 1-800-FLOWERS.COM, Hunter Douglas, Hertz, Mercado Libre, Rippling, and Perplexity. Decagon's own site claims more than 10 million customers served, an 80% deflection rate, a 65% decrease in support operations costs, and a 93% agent quality score, all company-reported figures. Decagon matters because customer service is where AI agents first have to be trusted with real money and real customer relationships: a wrong refund or a broken rebooking is visible immediately, so the company that can prove its agents act safely at scale owns the most demanding enterprise AI market there is. The founders' path to the product is part of the story: per investor accounts, Zhang and Sreenivas spent their earliest weeks interviewing hundreds of customer service executives and studying how support organizations actually function before deciding what to build, settling on the repetitive, high-volume work human agents handled one call or chat at a time. Zhang had previously founded Lowkey, a social gaming clip-sharing app acquired by Niantic in 2021; Sreenivas had founded Helia, a real-time video AI startup acquired by Scale AI in 2020, and worked as a deployment strategist at Palantir. Decagon came out of stealth in June 2024, disclosing $35 million across its seed and Series A rounds and early customers including Eventbrite, Bilt, and Substack. The enterprise buyer's calculation is straightforward: support tickets arrive faster than human teams can close them, hiring more agents raises cost without shortening waits, and an agent that resolves 70 to 80 percent of conversations without a human touch changes the cost structure of the whole operation. The counterweight is trust: every deployment puts Decagon's agent between a brand and its customers, so a single bad wave of refunds, rebookings, or tone-deaf replies can cost more than the savings, which is why the company's traceability, guardrails, and testing tools are sold as hard as its resolution rates. The newest direction is personal agents: Decagon now detects when a customer's own AI agent contacts a business and serves it through a dedicated channel with permissions the business controls, a bet that agent-to-agent service becomes a real channel rather than a curiosity.

## Agent Operating Procedures: the product core

Decagon's core framework is Agent Operating Procedures, or AOPs, which let a business define agent behavior in natural language the way it trains human agents with standard operating procedures, combined with the precision of code for integrations, guardrails, and versioning. A CX team can change how an agent behaves without filing an engineering ticket, while engineers keep control of integrations and track changes with Git-based versioning. AOPs carry guardrails across every channel for brand voice, escalations, and hallucinations, and every agent decision is traceable: teams can see explanations of an agent's reasoning at any point in a conversation, with runtime and latency numbers, instead of debugging a black box. The pitch against traditional approaches is speed of iteration: a workflow change that used to require a technical team or outside professional services becomes an edit to a procedure, testable and shippable the same day. That ownership argument is Decagon's main wedge against both legacy contact-center software and rival AI agent vendors whose customers cannot easily inspect or change agent behavior.

## Voice, chat, email, and Duet

Decagon's channels are voice, with human-like conversation; chat, with safe on-brand replies; email, with contextual resolutions; and SMS, alongside a newer feature for detecting customers' personal AI agents and serving them through a dedicated channel with permissions the business controls. Around the channels sit the tools for running agents at scale. Duet is the AI partner for building self-improving agents: it manages the agent lifecycle, finds improvement opportunities, and maintains quality as complexity grows. Experiments runs live A/B tests on agent behavior. Testing and QA runs simulations at scale before changes ship. Watchtower is always-on quality assurance over live conversations. Insights and reporting covers voice of the customer, and Suggestions offers AI-powered knowledge improvements. Integrations are pre-built connectors to the business's existing support stack, so agents pull live data and trigger workflows in the systems the company already uses. Recent launches highlighted by Decagon include Voice 3, Modules, and Duet Apprentice, announced at its Dialogues event.

## Chime, Hertz, and the enterprise customer list

Decagon's case studies are its proof points. Chime runs Decagon Voice with cross-channel memory, and its chief operating officer Janelle Sallenave credits the combination of performance, brand customization, and connected interactions; Decagon reports a 70% chat and voice resolution rate for Chime, and third-party reporting puts Chime's Decagon call volume above 1 million calls a month. One operations manager quoted by Decagon reports an 80% deflection rate and says maintaining the previous vendor consumed at least half his week. A CX operations director reports 10 times higher deflection at launch than anticipated and a 95% cost reduction. A global customer experience director reports more than $1 million in revenue from fully AI-handled conversations. The customer list spans financial services (Chime, Bilt), travel and hospitality (Avis Budget Group, Hertz, 1-800-FLOWERS.COM), health and wellness (Oura Health, Noom), technology (Notion, Duolingo, Perplexity, Rippling), retail (Hunter Douglas, Rituals, Curology), and telecommunications (Deutsche Telekom). That breadth is the point: the same agent framework is sold as working for a bank's compliance-heavy calls, a retailer's order questions, and a travel company's rebookings.

## Decagon against Sierra and the incumbent helpdesks

Decagon's most direct rival is Sierra, founded the same year by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor and former Google executive Clay Bavor, which sells AI customer service agents to many of the same enterprises. Third-party estimates from 2026 put Sierra ahead on revenue, roughly $200 million in annual recurring revenue in May 2026 against roughly $100 million annualized for Decagon in July 2026, and ahead on funding, about $1.6 billion against about $481 million, though both figures are reported estimates, not audited results. Salesforce is also in the frame after agreeing to buy Fin, formerly Intercom, in June 2026. Decagon's answer to better-funded rivals is the AOP ownership story: customers who can inspect, version, and change agent behavior themselves, plus voice quality and cross-channel memory, rather than a managed black box. Its funding, as reported, totals about $481 million, including a $131 million Series C in June 2025 at a reported $1.5 billion valuation and a $250 million Series D in January 2026 at a reported $4.5 billion valuation, backed by a16z, Accel, Bain Capital Ventures, Coatue, and Index Ventures. Business Insider reported in 2026 that Decagon held early acquisition discussions with ServiceNow and hired an investment bank to evaluate interest, and that those talks are no longer ongoing; that reporting is unconfirmed by the company in the material reviewed here, and Decagon remains private with no audited profit figures published.

Sources: decagon.ai homepage, decagon.ai/product/aop, decagon.ai/about, decagon.ai/case-studies, public reporting on Decagon funding and the Sierra comparison, accessed 2026-10-30.

Comfrt is a loungewear and home goods brand founded in 2022 by Hudson Leogrande that sells slightly weighted clothing and blankets under the tagline "Wear The Feeling." Its core products are oversized hoodies, sweatpants, loungewear sets, and blankets designed to give the wearer a feeling of gentle pressure and comfort, extended into athleisure, outerwear, kids' clothing, pet items, travel gear, and accessories. It sells direct to consumers through comfrt.com and through TikTok Shop, where founder accounts describe it as the most purchased hoodie brand on the platform, and it is self-funded, with no outside investors, according to founder interviews. It makes money from direct retail sales with heavy promotional pricing: list prices are shown against much higher "comp. value" anchor prices, and the homepage on 2026-10-30 advertised up to 70% off Black Friday early access with free shipping on orders over $99. Comfrt matters because it turned a simple product idea, a hoodie that feels like a hug, into one of the largest creator-era apparel brands without venture funding or traditional retail, riding short-form video and a membership program instead of department stores. Leogrande started Comfrt from his own experience with anxiety, wanting a hoodie that gave the feeling of being supported at any time, and funded the launch from an earlier teeth-whitening kit business he ran from his mother's basement, according to founder interviews; the company remains self-owned with no outside investors on those same accounts. The product line grew the way a comfort brand grows: hoodies first, then sweatpants and loungewear, then blankets and home goods, then kids, pets, travel, and athleisure, each extension staying inside the same promise of soft, slightly weighted, oversized comfort. For a shopper, the practical facts are the price ladder and the discounting: most hoodies list at $39 to $59, the Dreamer Blanket at $99, and nearly everything carries a much higher comp. value anchor plus rotating sale codes, so the price on any given week depends on the current promotion. For the business, the membership layer is the retention play: ComfrtClub is free, gives credit back on every order and first access to drops, and offers a $9-per-year VIP tier, converting impulse TikTok purchases into repeat orders without paying a retailer a wholesale margin. What to watch is whether discount-led growth holds up as the catalog widens: every new category, from heated blankets to pet items, competes with specialists who do only that product, and a brand built on impulse-priced hoodies must prove shoppers return for robes, pillows, and loungewear rather than only during a sale. The homepage on 2026-10-30 leaned fully into that event logic, with Black Friday early access banners, a gift guide, and an extra 20% off code stacked on sale prices, which moves units and trains customers to wait for the next event.

## Dreamer Blanket, CalmTouch, and the hoodie lineup

The Dreamer Blanket is the brand's flagship home product, listed from $99 against a $349 comp. value, and Comfrt calls it "America's #1 Sold Blanket," a brand claim that has not been independently verified. The hoodie lineup is built around oversized "Mega" fits with dropped shoulders and tapered silhouettes: the CalmTouch Hoodie, described as designed to ease busy minds through touch, lists at $59 against a $150 comp. value; the Minimalist Hoodie in Mega and the Signature Hoodie list from $39 against $120 comp. values; the Camo Hoodie lists at $39 against $130; and the Airplane Mode Travel Hoodie and Snak Hoodie list at $59 against $140. Newer drops on the homepage include the Sweater Knit Hoodie at $39 against $90, the Dreamer Robe at $75 against $120, the LunaCurve Pillow at $65 against $189, and the Ember Heated Blanket from $105 against $249. Beyond hoodies and blankets, the catalog covers sweatpants and joggers, lounge sets, pajamas and robes, bedding and pillows, athleisure tops and bottoms, kids' tops and bottoms, and accessories including hats, socks, and underwear. Prices are homepage list prices on 2026-10-30 and move with promotions; the brand also runs ComfrtClub, free to join with credit back on every order, first access to drops, and members-only pieces and prices, plus a VIP tier at $9 per year.

## Slightly weighted: the design idea

Comfrt's design idea is pressure as comfort. Its own disclaimer describes its hoodies as "slightly weighted," and the brand's framing is that gentle, even pressure across the body gives a grounded, settled feeling, the same logic behind weighted blankets, applied to clothing you wear out of the house. The Dreamer Blanket spreads weight across the body for what the brand calls steady sensory input, and its clinician endorsements cite research on firm, even pressure and pulse rate, plus a randomized controlled trial in which weighted-blanket users reported less anxiety and better sleep over four weeks. The fit is part of the idea too: oversized Mega sizing with extra room through the chest, shoulders, and arms, meant for lounging, layering, and travel rather than a tailored look. The brand's hoodies carry embroidered affirmations in some lines, tying the product to its mental-wellbeing positioning rather than to performance or streetwear. Comfrt's own footer is candid about the limits: its hoodies are not a substitute for professional medical advice or treatment, and claims about managing anxiety rest on personal belief and customer experience.

## TikTok Shop, discounting, and ComfrtClub

Comfrt's sales model is built for short-form video. Discovery happens on TikTok, where the brand, its founder, and its ambassador program post the product in everyday use, and purchase happens on TikTok Shop or comfrt.com, with email signup offers and a gift guide funnel on the homepage. The pricing model is promotional by design: most products carry a struck-through comp. value far above the selling price, frequent sale events, extra percentage-off codes such as the EARLYACCESS code worth an extra 20% off orders over $95 on 2026-10-30, and shop-with-credit offers like a $20 e-credit on home orders over $99. ComfrtClub turns one-time buyers into repeat buyers with order credit, early drop access, and a $9-per-year VIP tier. The model works because the product is visual, the price point is impulse-friendly at $39 to $99 for most items, and the purchase decision is emotional rather than technical. The risk is margin: permanent discounting trains customers to wait for the next sale, and a brand that lives on one social platform's algorithm and shop is exposed if that platform's rules, fees, or audience shift.

## Comfrt against weighted-blanket and loungewear brands

Comfrt sits between two markets. In weighted products it competes with weighted-blanket specialists such as Bearaby and Gravity, plus the weighted offerings of large home brands, and its difference is wearing the weight: a hoodie and blanket wardrobe rather than a single bedroom product, sold on feeling rather than sleep science. In loungewear it competes with every major apparel label and with direct-to-consumer comfort brands, and its difference is the wellbeing story and the oversized, slightly weighted fit rather than fabric technology or athletic performance. Its advantage over both sets of rivals is distribution through TikTok Shop, where it reaches buyers at the moment of discovery instead of waiting for them to search for a blanket or hoodie. Its disadvantage is the same as any comfort brand's: low barriers to entry, easy imitation of an oversized fleece hoodie, and claims that invite scrutiny. The "America's #1 Sold Blanket" line is the brand's own claim, its clinician endorsements are collected through FrontrowMD, an independent clinical review platform, and the clinicians themselves note that larger-scale research supporting the product claims is still developing and that their statements have not been reviewed by the FDA and are not medical advice. Buyers should read those endorsements as marketing with a research footnote, not as clinical proof.

# Corgi — AI-native insurance carrier for startups

Corgi sells business insurance to venture-backed technology companies, and it does so as the carrier itself rather than as a broker shopping your application to someone else's underwriters. You apply online, answer questions about stage, revenue, headcount, and product type, and Corgi quotes in under 10 minutes and can bind a policy the same day, with a certificate of insurance in hand. That speed is the whole pitch: the traditional route runs 2 to 4 weeks through broker review and manual underwriting, and Corgi replaces it with AI underwriting, modular coverage packages, and claims handled in-house. Corgi is listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #16. It was founded in 2024 by Nico Laqua and Emily Yuan, came through Y Combinator's Summer 2024 batch, and launched its platform in July 2025 after regulatory approval to operate as a licensed carrier. It sells direct, so its money comes from premiums paid by the startups it covers, not from brokerage commissions.

Corgi's mechanics are deliberately boring in the best sense: an online application asking about stage, revenue, headcount, and product type; an AI underwriting pass that returns a quote in under 10 minutes; a same-day bind with a certificate of insurance. The packages are pre-configured by stage so a founder does not have to assemble coverage line by line — Pre-Seed and Seed covers the basics a landlord or first hire requires, Series A adds the lines a board and enterprise customers demand (D&O, media, EPLI), and Growth adds fiduciary coverage at higher limits for companies approaching IPO scale. The underwriting entity behind the policy matters as much as the speed: Technology Risk Retention Group, a federally chartered risk retention group, carries most of the risk, is not AM Best rated, and is not backed by state guaranty funds, while admitted paper through A- or better rated carriers is available where a state or contract requires it. Corgi's founders, Nico Laqua and Emily Yuan, built the company through Y Combinator's Summer 2024 batch and launched the platform in July 2025 after regulatory approval to operate as a licensed carrier. For a venture-backed startup, the value proposition is time: coverage in place before a funding round closes, before a board seat is filled, and before an enterprise contract's insurance clause becomes a blocker.

## D&O, Tech E&O, and the stage packages

Corgi's catalog is organized by funding stage, and the package grows as the company does. Pre-Seed and Seed gets commercial general liability (CGL), directors and officers (D&O), Tech errors and omissions (E&O), and cyber. Series A adds media liability and employment practices liability (EPLI), aimed at companies signing enterprise contracts and completing SOC 2. Growth stage adds fiduciary liability at higher limits, aimed at late-stage companies with large teams and IPO plans. A custom package covers specialized lines, including AI liability, for fintech, AI, and health-tech companies with unusual risk profiles. Corgi's Tech E&O is written to cover AI-specific exposures that standard policies often exclude: model hallucinations and false outputs, algorithmic bias claims, and training-data disputes, including IP defense for training data.

## The TRRG structure, and what it means for a buyer

The entity you contract with is Corgi Insurance Services, Inc., a licensed producer (CA license #6012791) that Corgi's own disclosures describe as the program administrator, not the insurer. Coverage is underwritten primarily by Technology Risk Retention Group, Inc. (TRRG), a federally chartered risk retention group regulated under the Liability Risk Retention Act of 1986. TRRG is not rated by AM Best, and state insurance insolvency guaranty funds are not available for policies it issues — Corgi discloses both points itself. Where a state or a contract requires admitted paper, Corgi places coverage through affiliated or partner carriers, including its own admitted property and casualty carrier, Corgi Insurance Company, Inc. (NAIC #17989), and unaffiliated partner carriers rated A- (Excellent) or better by AM Best. A founder buying here should understand that tradeoff plainly: the speed and modularity come with a carrier structure that is not the same as buying from a rated admitted carrier, and enterprise customers with strict vendor requirements may need the admitted-paper route.

## Corgi's own price guidance

Corgi publishes planning estimates rather than a rate card: $2,000 to $4,000 a year for eligible pre-revenue or early-revenue startups with $1M limits for general liability, Tech E&O, and cyber, and $10,000 to $25,000 or more at Series A as limits rise and D&O and EPLI are added. Final price depends on the business and coverage. Against Embroker and Vouch, which operate as digital brokerages routing applications to third-party carriers, Corgi's argument is that owning underwriting, policy design, and claims lets it quote and bind faster and let founders toggle modules like EPLI and fiduciary as they grow, without rebrokering. Reported funding figures for Corgi conflict across sources, so no funding total or valuation is stated here.

## AI liability, written for companies whose product is a model

Corgi's most distinctive coverage line is AI liability, and it deserves a closer look because it is where standard Tech E&O most often leaves an AI company exposed. Corgi names three categories: model performance and hallucination risk, covering liability when a language model provides false, defamatory, or harmful information that causes a third-party loss; algorithmic bias, covering claims of discriminatory outcomes in hiring, lending, or healthcare AI; and training-data disputes, including IP defense for training data. For a company selling an AI product into enterprise customers, these are not hypothetical: enterprise buyers increasingly require proof of AI risk management and cyber coverage before integrating an API, which Corgi calls the AI safety audit trigger. The practical consequence is that a startup whose product is a model cannot treat Tech E&O as a checkbox — it needs to check whether its policy's definitions actually reach model outputs, and Corgi writes its Tech E&O to reach them. Claims handling is in-house, which Corgi presents as part of the full-stack advantage: the same organization that underwrote the risk handles the claim, rather than handing it to a third-party administrator.

## Who should not buy Corgi

Corgi is not the right carrier for every startup. Coverage is not yet available in all 50 states, and international coverage beyond the US market requires separate arrangements, according to third-party review coverage. Companies with contractual requirements for admitted paper in every state, or with complex multinational footprints, may need the admitted-carrier placement route or a different carrier altogether, and should confirm availability before relying on a same-day bind. The TRRG structure also deserves a second thought for companies whose board or investors require rated paper: the absence of an AM Best rating is not, by Corgi's own FAQ, a measure of financial condition, and TRRG operates under federal prudential oversight with dedicated reserves — but a risk-averse board may still prefer a rated admitted carrier and accept the slower timeline. Corgi's sweet spot is the venture-backed US technology startup that needs D&O before a funding round closes, Tech E&O and cyber to satisfy enterprise vendor contracts and SOC 2, and a policy that scales from Pre-Seed to Growth without rebrokering at each stage.

Sources: corgi.insure startup insurance page and FAQ; corgi.insure blog on modular coverage and on binding D&O and Tech E&O; QuoteSweep Corgi profile; Dealroom Corgi profile. Accessed 2026-10-30.

# Profound — tracking how brands show up inside AI answers

Profound sells enterprise software that measures how a brand appears when people ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot, DeepSeek, and Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode — and then turns that measurement into marketing work. The buyer is a marketing or SEO team at a large company that can no longer tell from Google rankings alone whether customers ever see its name, because the answer a chatbot gives has replaced the list of links. Profound's homepage names Plaid, MongoDB, Ramp, and Zoom as customers. It is listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #17. Money comes from enterprise subscriptions; the live pricing page shows only a free trial and a custom-quoted Enterprise plan, and there is no ongoing free plan and no published self-serve price.

The measurement itself is what Profound sells, and its specifics matter. Answer Engine Insights tracks a brand across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, DeepSeek, Google AI Overviews, and Google AI Mode, reporting six metrics: visibility score, share of voice, mention position, citation share, co-citation share, and co-mention share. Prompt Volumes, built on more than 1.5 billion real user prompts, tells a team what people actually ask in its category, segmented by intent and demographics, rather than what a strategist guesses they ask. Agent Analytics ties AI crawler visits and referral traffic back to the customer's own domains, so a team can see whether AI visibility turns into visits. The Profound Index extends the same measurement into public view: 50-plus industries, prompt sets built from real prompts retrieved over six months and filtered toward brand-agnostic questions, run weekly across all major models. The commercial terms are narrow: a free trial of 50 prompts tracked daily for 7 days on three engines, then custom-quoted Enterprise, with an Agency Growth plan whose price is not shown. Named customers on Profound's homepage include Plaid, MongoDB, Ramp, and Zoom, and the company says a third of the Fortune 100 uses its enterprise features — a homepage claim, not independently verified here.

## Answer Engine Insights, Prompt Volumes, and Agent Analytics

Answer Engine Insights is the core tracker. It runs a brand's prompt set daily across the answer engines and reports visibility (how often the brand appears), share of voice (its percentage of total category visibility), mention position (where in the answer it lands), citation share (how often its domain is cited as a source), co-citation share (which domains are cited alongside it), and co-mention share (which competitors appear with it). Prompt Volumes estimates what users actually ask about a category, built on a dataset Profound describes as 1.5 billion-plus real user prompts, segmented by intent and demographics — the point being that the prompt list reflects observed questions rather than a strategist's guesses. Agent Analytics tracks AI crawler visits and AI referral traffic to the customer's own domains. Shopping tracks product visibility inside AI shopping answers. Enterprise plans cover up to 9 engines, with unlimited seats and all-time data history.

## The Profound Index and the agent layer

The Profound Index, announced in 2026, is a public leaderboard for AI search: for each of 50-plus industries, Profound builds a prompt set from real user prompts retrieved over the last six months, filters it toward open-ended, brand-agnostic questions, clusters it by topic, and runs it weekly across all major LLMs through Answer Engine Insights. The stated contrast is with benchmarks built on synthetic prompts written by analysts. On top of the measurement sits an agent layer: an AI Marketer agent called Aim, launched in July 2026, plus credit-metered content agents and a Context Manager, which draft or update content and sharpen recommendations as that content gets cited. Profound says every account gets a dedicated AI strategist and engagement manager, and it holds SOC 2 Type II certification and HIPAA compliance, with SSO and role-based access.

The free trial covers 50 prompts tracked daily for 7 days on three engines (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews). Enterprise is custom-quoted, and an Agency Growth self-serve plan exists but its price is not shown; earlier Starter ($99) and Growth ($399) tiers no longer appear on the pricing page, so they should not be quoted as current. Reported funding — a $180M Series D at a reported $1.8B valuation, with more than $335M raised in total — is third-party reporting, not a company-confirmed figure stated here as fact. Profound's named rivals in answer-engine optimization include the SEO platforms adding AI visibility features and smaller pure-play trackers; its argument against both is depth of real-prompt data plus attribution and an agent layer in one platform. Teams that only want a lightweight visibility score, or a clear self-serve price, are not its buyer.

## Who buys Profound, and what the engagement looks like

Profound's buyer is an enterprise or growth-stage marketing and SEO team managing a global brand across many prompts, several engines, and multiple regions — the kind of team that reports AI visibility trends over time and needs exports, API access, and SSO to do it. Enterprise plans carry unlimited seats and all-time data history, which matters for trend reporting, and every account comes with a dedicated AI strategist and engagement manager rather than a ticket queue. Tracking runs daily across all major engines through front-end browsers, capturing the response a real user sees rather than the thinner version an API returns, and coverage extends across 50-plus countries. The agent layer is credit-metered: each agent run consumes credits based on complexity and shows an estimate first, so content work is budgeted rather than open-ended. Profound's own AEO guide claims it ranks number one on G2 for AEO with more than 300 reviews at 4.6 out of 5, the largest verified review base of any pure-play AEO platform — a company-guide claim, not an independent audit, but a useful signal of where its users concentrate.

## Profound against the SEO platforms and the lightweight trackers

Profound's competitive argument has two halves. Against the SEO platforms adding AI visibility features, it says it was built for answer-engine optimization from the start rather than retrofitted from keyword rank tracking, and that its architecture — real-prompt data, front-end browser capture, attribution — reflects that origin. Against lightweight visibility trackers, it says a single score is not enough: a team needs to know which competitors appear alongside it, which domains get cited as sources, and where in the answer its brand lands, because each of those has a different fix. The Profound Index extends the same argument into public view: a category leaderboard measured the same way for every brand, updated weekly, that lets a company see what good looks like without buying anything. The weakness in Profound's position is the same as its strength: depth costs money and attention, and a team that only needs to know whether it appears in ChatGPT answers at all will find the Enterprise-only pricing and the strategist-led engagement to be more than it wants.

# Wispr Flow — dictation that rewrites your speech into clean text

Wispr Flow is a dictation app from Wispr AI that turns spoken words into cleaned-up, punctuated text inside whatever application you are already typing in — Slack, Gmail, Notion, VS Code, WhatsApp, and more than 50 others — on Mac, Windows, iPhone, and Android. You hold a hotkey or tap the Flow button, speak naturally with ums and restarts, and Flow pastes back text adjusted for the context, so a Slack message does not read like an email. It is listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #18. Wispr AI was founded by Tanay Kothari and Sahaj Garg. Money comes from subscriptions: a free tier, a Pro plan, team Growth plans, and custom Enterprise, with no lifetime purchase option.

The product mechanics are simple enough to describe in one paragraph: hold a hotkey on Mac or Windows, or tap the Flow button on iPhone or Android, speak naturally, and Flow pastes cleaned-up text into the focused field — email, Slack, Notion, Google Docs, ChatGPT, or a code editor like Cursor — adjusting tone for the destination. Wispr claims speech input at roughly 220 words per minute against about 45 for typing, and the app works in more than 100 languages. The free plan's weekly word cap, reported as 2,000 words on desktop and 1,000 on iPhone, is enough to test whether voice typing fits; Pro at $15 a month (or $144 a year) removes the dictation cap and raises Notetaker limits; Growth at $23 or $33 a month adds team administration, SAML single sign-on, usage reports, and organization-wide privacy and HIPAA controls; Enterprise is custom-priced with advanced security. Students get roughly half off Pro, and non-profits can ask for a discount. The tradeoff that defines the product is architectural: transcription always happens in Wispr's cloud, so there is no offline mode and no on-device option, and model-training and cloud storage of dictations start switched on unless a plan or organization restricts them.

## Dictation, Notetaker, and the word allowances

Dictation is the core: cloud transcription in more than 100 languages, with an AI cleanup pass, a shared dictionary, and snippets for repeated text. Notetaker is a separate product inside the same app: it records meetings on Mac and Windows and produces transcripts and summaries, and it has its own allowance — paying for unlimited dictation does not mean unlimited Notetaker. The free plan carries a weekly word cap, reported as 2,000 words a week on desktop and 1,000 a week on iPhone. Pro removes the dictation cap and raises Notetaker limits. Growth adds SAML single sign-on, individual usage reports, and organization-wide privacy and HIPAA controls; Enterprise adds advanced security. Wispr says transcription always happens on its servers, so the app needs an internet connection, and model-training and cloud storage of dictations start switched on unless a plan or organization restricts them — the privacy tradeoff that matters most for anyone dictating sensitive work.

## Wispr Flow's published prices

Published US list prices, checked against Wispr's pricing page in October 2026: Free at $0; Pro at $15 per user per month, or $144 per user per year ($12 a month equivalent); Growth dictation-only at $23 per user per month ($216 a year); Growth with Notetaker at $33 per user per month ($312 a year); Enterprise at a custom price through sales. Students and educators with an education email get roughly 50% off Pro, and non-profits can ask for a discount. Prices are fixed per currency rather than converted at live exchange rates, so checkout totals outside the US differ. Against Apple and Microsoft's built-in dictation, Wispr's argument is the cleanup layer and cross-app behavior; against one-time-purchase rivals such as Voibe ($199 lifetime) and Superwhisper ($249.99), its argument is polish and cross-platform coverage, while its weakness is the subscription-only model and the cloud-only architecture — there is no on-device mode, and third-party review scores reflect real reliability complaints, including a 2.7 out of 5 Trustpilot rating reported in October 2026.

## Command Mode, dictionary, and context-aware formatting

Beyond raw dictation, Wispr Flow's differentiating layer is how it shapes text for where it lands. Command Mode lets users control applications by voice, and the shared dictionary and snippets handle names, jargon, and repeated blocks so the transcript does not mangle them every time. The formatting adapts to the destination: the same spoken ramble becomes a tight Slack message, a properly punctuated email, or code-editor-friendly text, which is why the product positions itself as a replacement for typing rather than a transcription utility. Wispr claims speech input at roughly 220 words per minute against about 45 words per minute for typing, and works inside more than 50 applications. The free plan's weekly word cap is the on-ramp: enough to learn whether voice typing fits a workflow, with Pro removing the dictation cap for anyone who dictates more than about 2,000 words a week on desktop. Notetaker's meeting notes are the second habit: recorded conversations become transcripts and summaries on Mac and Windows, with its own allowance that paid plans raise but do not always make unlimited.

## Wispr Flow's privacy controls, in detail

Wispr Flow's cloud architecture is the thing a careful buyer must weigh. Transcription always happens on Wispr's servers, so the app needs an internet connection, and two data settings — model training and cloud storage of dictations — start switched on unless a plan or organization restricts them. Growth plans add organization-wide privacy and HIPAA controls, and Enterprise adds SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, enforced HIPAA, zero data retention options, SSO and SAML, and admin usage dashboards. For an individual dictating emails and notes, the defaults are a reasonable tradeoff for accuracy. For a lawyer dictating client confidences, a doctor dictating patient notes, or an employee under a strict data policy, the right move is to check the plan-level controls before dictating anything sensitive, and to treat the opt-out settings as part of setup rather than an afterthought. Against Apple's and Microsoft's built-in dictation, Wispr wins on cleanup quality and cross-app behavior and loses on privacy architecture, since built-in tools can run on-device; against one-time-purchase rivals, it wins on polish and loses on lifetime cost.

# Nebulock — autonomous threat hunting that never sleeps

Nebulock sells an agentic threat hunting platform to enterprises whose security teams are drowning in noisy alerts and brittle detection rules while attackers use AI to move faster — generating polymorphic malware, automating lateral movement, and evading traditional detections. Instead of waiting for an alert to fire, Nebulock connects to a customer's identity, endpoint, and cloud telemetry and hunts continuously, forming hypotheses, testing them against live data, and surfacing real findings before an attacker entrenches. It is listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #19. The company was founded by Damien Lewke, who previously led product for AI and threat intelligence at Arctic Wolf and worked at CrowdStrike from its roughly $25M ARR days through IPO, and who studied at MIT's Computer Science and AI Lab. Pricing is not published.

Nebulock's system is built around a single observation: the hardest part of defense, threat hunting, was still manual, brittle, and single-threaded even at companies with thousand-person security operations centers, where elite analysts spent nights replaying logs and rewriting the same detection logic. Nebulock's answer is to automate the hunter's loop itself. It ingests telemetry from endpoints, identity systems, cloud environments, networks, and SaaS applications, builds a contextual behavior graph — a baseline of normal activity across a unified timeline — and hunts continuously for deviations: stolen credentials used oddly, lateral movement, attackers blending into normal traffic. When it finds something, it does not merely alert; it builds a detection, tests it against the customer's environment, checks for logic drift, and rewrites or improves it automatically, with the customer able to review or let it deploy. A simulation engine using synthetic data and reinforcement learning, currently in development, is meant to test detections before they ship. The company was founded by Damien Lewke, formerly product lead for AI and threat intelligence at Arctic Wolf and an early CrowdStrike product leader, and is backed by Decibel. Pricing and named customers are not public.

## Continuous hunting, drift-aware detections, and the behavior graph

Nebulock's pitch has three parts. Continuous threat hunting: no playbooks required, no human prompting needed — the system hunts 24/7 across EDR, identity, and cloud telemetry and raises anomalies before attackers can entrench. Drift-aware detection engineering: when it finds something, it does not stop at an alert; it builds a detection, tests it against the customer's environment, checks for logic drift, and rewrites or improves it automatically, with the customer able to review or let it deploy. Behavior over signatures: most serious breaches are behavioral — a stolen credential used oddly, lateral movement, someone blending in — so Nebulock builds a contextual behavior graph, a baseline of normal activity across a unified timeline, and flags deviations from it. That is how it positions itself against signature-based detection and against traditional threat hunting, which Lewke describes as still largely manual, brittle, and single-threaded, with analysts spending nights replaying logs and rewriting the same detection logic.

## What Nebulock is building next, and who it competes with

In the background, Nebulock is building a simulation engine that uses synthetic data and reinforcement learning to test detections before they ship — so that when it calls a threat real, it has already watched that attack play out in simulation. Its stated long-term goal is to make elite autonomous threat hunting available to enterprises that cannot afford a large in-house hunting team or hire the talent. Its competitive set includes managed detection providers with human hunting teams, such as Huntress and Arctic Wolf, and the large endpoint and XDR platforms such as CrowdStrike Falcon and Cisco XDR; Nebulock's argument against both is that human hunting does not scale and alert-driven tooling waits too long. What is not public: named customers, pricing, and independent validation of detection outcomes — the company is early, backed by Decibel, and the public record is strongest on its architecture and founder story rather than on proven deployments.

## The founder's path, and why it shapes the product

Damien Lewke's career explains Nebulock's design. Out of school he joined Northrop Grumman on the nuclear modernization program, where his job was to threat-model an entire system end to end — software, physical supply chain, communications infrastructure, and the analog-to-digital transitions across the stack — under Department of Defense Top Secret clearance. He then joined CrowdStrike at roughly 200 employees and about $25 million in annual recurring revenue, working across marketing, product, sales, and solutions engineering, helping build and launch Falcon Complete, Discover, and Spotlight and building Dell and VMware OEM integrations that delivered Falcon to millions of endpoints, staying through the IPO. At Arctic Wolf he led product for AI and threat intelligence across a thousand-person security operations center, where he watched elite analysts spend their nights chasing alerts, revalidating detections, and rewriting the same logic. At MIT's Computer Science and AI Lab he explored how deep learning could reason over large, noisy telemetry datasets and simulate the hypothesis generation that threat hunters do instinctively. Nebulock is that synthesis: a system that hunts the way a human hunter does, but never sleeps, never tires, and improves with every iteration.

## What to ask before buying Nebulock

Because Nebulock does not publish pricing or named customers, a buyer has to do more diligence than the website allows. The questions that matter: which telemetry sources does it ingest beyond EDR, identity, and cloud — network, SaaS applications, and email are named in third-party listings, but the buyer should confirm coverage for their own stack; how does the human review workflow operate when Nebulock proposes a detection — can the team review before deployment, and what does the approval trail look like; how does the simulation engine's synthetic data relate to the customer's real environment, and what evidence exists that a detection validated in simulation holds up in production; and what happens to hunting coverage when telemetry sources go dark or change format. The answers to those questions, not the architecture diagram, determine whether agentic hunting replaces manual hunting or merely adds another console. Nebulock's vision — elite autonomous threat hunting available to all enterprises, not just those that can afford it — is compelling precisely because the talent shortage in security is real; the burden of proof is on the platform to show it in a customer's environment.

Sources: Decibel investment announcement and founder Q&A with Damien Lewke; Slashdot and SourceForge Nebulock product listings. Accessed 2026-10-30.
