# Basic Capital — a 401(k) built around a retirement mortgage

Basic Capital is a 401(k) recordkeeper and third-party administrator that sells employers a bundled retirement plan — its own recordkeeping system, administration, a mobile-first participant portal, a sponsor portal, and a distinctive investment product it calls the Retirement Mortgage. The idea: most employees undersave, and the standard advice ladder (get the match, max the IRA, return to the 401(k)) is unrealistic for people whose monthly surplus is small. Basic Capital's answer is to let participants use financing inside the plan to get more market exposure with every contribution. It is listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #20. The company was founded in 2021 by Abdul Al-Assad, a former Goldman Sachs executive, and is based in New York. It sells to plan sponsors — employers — and makes money from plan administration and the financing product's fees, which vary with the financing chosen.

Basic Capital operates as both recordkeeper and third-party administrator on its own recordkeeping system, which is the unglamorous foundation the Retirement Mortgage sits on: automatic payroll sync, built-in investment education, always-on compliance monitoring, a mobile-first participant portal, and a sponsor portal, with an investment menu of more than 6,000 funds plus a brokerage window for single stocks, ETFs, crypto, and private investments. A direct integration with Rippling feeds employee data into participant records automatically. The Retirement Mortgage itself works through that brokerage window: a participant elects preferred-equity financing — explicitly not a margin loan — to increase market exposure with every contribution, paying it off over 10 to 30 years, with no margin calls and no personal recourse, and can invest within the tool up to 100% in S&P 500 among other index and private-debt options. Financing costs vary and additional fees apply. The product's controversy is inseparable from its pitch: critics describe it as a leveraged bet on interest rates, noting example terms around 6.25% financing cost and a five-year lockup, while Basic Capital argues that financing against stable direct-lending assets is what can actually move retirement readiness, where merely adding alternatives adds only about 1% in expected annual returns according to a Mercer report it cites.

## The Retirement Mortgage, in concrete terms

The Retirement Mortgage is an optional tool offered through a 401(k) brokerage window. A participant elects it and uses preferred equity — Basic Capital is explicit that it is not a margin loan — to make a larger upfront investment and pay it off over 10 to 30 years. The financing is secured against stable, income-generating alternative assets: Basic Capital accesses 40 Act funds in the direct lending space, whose predictable cash flows and low volatility are meant to support the leverage. Participants customize a portfolio and can invest within the tool up to 100% in S&P 500 among other options, including US and international stock index funds, bond index funds, and actively managed private debt. The company stresses there are no margin calls and no personal recourse, and that alternatives exposure and asset financing are entirely optional. Its broader 401(k) platform offers more than 6,000 fund options, an open architecture, an embedded brokerage window for single stocks and ETFs, crypto and private investments through that window, payroll sync, and a direct integration with Rippling that feeds compensation, hire date, and birth date into participant records automatically. AI agents help sponsors identify compliance issues and streamline employee communications.

## Why the Retirement Mortgage is controversial

Basic Capital's own framing is that alternatives alone add only modest value — it cites a Mercer report finding that adding alternatives raises annualized expected returns by about 1% with no meaningful volatility reduction — and that financing against them is what can meaningfully change retirement readiness. Critics argue the opposite: one detailed public critique describes the structure as swapping a decades-long bet on American growth for a leveraged bet on interest rates, noting an example where a participant borrows $4 for every $1, pays around 6.25% for the financing, and must lock money up for five years, with bond yields covering the interest cost and only the remainder in stocks. That critique is an outside opinion, not a regulator finding, but any buyer should weigh it: leverage inside a retirement account magnifies losses as well as gains, and the product's value depends heavily on the spread between financing cost and asset returns over a long horizon. Regulatory context matters too: a Trump executive order in August 2025 directed the Department of Labor to reevaluate fiduciary guidance on alternative assets in retirement plans, building on 2020 guidance permitting private equity in diversified target-date funds — a tailwind for Basic Capital's category, but not a mandate. Basic Capital does not publish a price list; employers buy the bundled platform, and financing carries additional fees.

## The bundled platform, beyond the Retirement Mortgage

The Retirement Mortgage gets the attention, but most of Basic Capital's day-to-day value is the bundled 401(k) platform around it. It is a full recordkeeper and third-party administrator built on its own recordkeeping system, with automatic payroll sync, built-in investment education, always-on compliance monitoring, and a mobile-first participant portal plus a sponsor portal. Sponsors can bring their own advisor and administrator or use Basic Capital for everything, and the investment menu holds more than 6,000 fund options from managers participants recognize, plus the embedded brokerage window for self-directed single-stock and ETF investing and, through that window, crypto and private investments. AI agents help sponsors identify compliance issues and streamline communications to employees about them. The Rippling integration shows the platform's philosophy: employee data — compensation, birth date, hire date, name — flows automatically from Rippling into Basic Capital to create participant records, removing the manual enrollment work that makes small-company 401(k) administration painful. One customer voice on Basic Capital's site, the CEO of Footprint, cites scalable pricing based on actual value creation rather than excessive fees, and a 401(k) aligned with a young, financially engaged team.

## Who the Retirement Mortgage suits, and who should skip it

The Retirement Mortgage is best understood as a tool for a specific employee: young, with a long horizon, whose problem is insufficient investing power rather than insufficient discipline. For that employee, financing that increases market participation inside a tax-advantaged wrapper, with no margin calls and no personal recourse, and a 10-to-30-year payoff, can plausibly change retirement readiness in a way that simply adding alternatives cannot. For an employee near retirement, the same leverage is dangerous: a market decline close to retirement leaves little time to recover, and the financing cost — which varies, with additional fees — eats returns in flat markets. For a plan sponsor, the decision is fiduciary as much as financial: offering leveraged investing inside a retirement plan invites scrutiny, and the sponsor should understand the financing structure, the fee schedule, and the downside scenarios before enabling it, even though participation is optional per employee. Basic Capital's own educational material is unusually candid that alternatives alone deliver only modest improvement; a sponsor should hold the Retirement Mortgage to the same candor and ask for the downside math, not just the upside illustration.

# Midi Health — virtual menopause care, covered by insurance

Midi Health is a virtual clinic for perimenopause and menopause care: women book a video visit with a clinician who specializes in midlife hormones, get a personal Care Plan, and have prescriptions sent to their pharmacy, with visits covered by most major insurance plans and no referral needed. The pitch is aimed at a specific failure of ordinary primary care — rushed 10-minute visits where hot flashes, sleep disruption, mood changes, joint pain, and weight changes get brushed off. Midi's clinicians take a 30-minute first visit to dig into symptoms, history, and goals, then 15-minute follow-ups to adjust the plan. It is listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #21. Midi says more than 500,000 women use it, and it operates in all 50 states. Money comes from insurance reimbursement for visits plus self-pay visits, not from a membership fee.

Midi's model is insurance-first in a way that distinguishes it from most telehealth startups: virtual visits and prescriptions are covered like any other specialty care under most PPO plans, with no referral needed, and the company says most patients pay about $50 a visit with insurance. The visit structure is fixed and published: a 30-minute first visit for $250 self-pay, where the clinician reviews symptoms, history, and goals and builds a Care Plan, and 15-minute follow-ups for $150 self-pay to track progress and adjust the plan. The plan itself may include FDA-approved hormone therapy in pill, patch, ring, cream, or gel form, compounded estradiol and progesterone, non-hormonal options such as gabapentin, GLP-1 medications, and compounded testosterone cream in 25 states, plus targeted labs for bone, heart, thyroid, and metabolic health. Midi operates in all 50 states and says more than 500,000 women use it. The exclusions are equally fixed: no Medicaid or Medi-Cal patients even as self-pay, and Medicare out of network, with Medicare beneficiaries welcome only as self-pay patients who cannot submit claims. For an employer or plan buyer, Midi's value is a defined benefit for a commercial PPO population; for a patient on Medicaid or Medicare, it is not an option at all.

## Hormone therapy, non-hormone options, and the visit prices

Midi prescribes FDA-approved hormone replacement therapy — pill, patch, ring, cream, and gel — plus compounded estradiol cream and gel and progesterone, and non-hormonal options including gabapentin. It also offers GLP-1 medications (brand-name to the patient's pharmacy, and compounded versions) and compounded testosterone cream in 25 states. Targeted labs can be ordered to rule out other causes or check bone, heart, thyroid, and metabolic health, and clinicians add supplements and lifestyle support to the plan. Self-pay prices are published: $250 for the 30-minute first visit and $150 for the 15-minute follow-up, with prescriptions and labs billed separately; Midi says most patients pay about $50 a visit with insurance, while deductibles, coinsurance, and copays still vary by plan. HSA and FSA funds can pay for visits. Two hard edges: Midi does not take Medicaid or Medi-Cal patients, even as self-pay, and Medicare is out of network — Medicare beneficiaries can be self-pay patients but cannot submit claims for Midi visits, medications, or services.

## Midi for employers, and the menopause telehealth field

Midi for Employers is offered to organizations whose health plans already recognize Midi as a participating provider, with no fees, no contracts, and no complicated integration — essentially a landing page and communications so employees know the benefit exists, including partnerships such as Delta Dental's Next Stage women's health program and MultiCare's employee health plan. Midi's rivals are the other menopause telehealth platforms: Alloy, Evernow, and Winona. The differences that matter to a buyer are coverage and format: Midi is in-network with most PPO plans and uses live video visits, while Evernow's video visits are covered by UnitedHealthcare, Aetna, Anthem, and Blue Cross Blue Shield plans with a $150 cash rate otherwise, and Winona is a different model built around asynchronous care. Midi's advantage is insurance breadth plus live specialist visits; its gap is the Medicaid and Medicare exclusion, which shuts out the oldest and lowest-income patients who often need this care most.

## The care plan in practice

A Midi visit starts with the 30-minute first appointment, where the clinician reviews symptoms, age, menstrual and medical history, and goals, and builds a Care Plan that may include hormone or non-hormone prescriptions, targeted labs, supplements, and lifestyle support. Follow-ups run 15 minutes and adjust the plan as symptoms change — a cadence that matters because menopause treatment is rarely set-and-forget: hormone doses, formulations, and non-hormone options often need tuning over months. Patients do not need to know their exact menopause stage before booking; the clinician works that out from history and symptoms, since menopause itself is defined as 12 consecutive months without a period but the perimenopause transition is gradual and messy. Prescriptions go to the patient's pharmacy, and the plan is covered like any other specialty care under most PPO plans, billed directly to claims. Midi's clinicians specialize in hormones and menopause rather than general primary care, which is the point of the whole model: a patient who has been told to simply live with hot flashes, night sweats, joint pain, and weight changes gets a clinician whose entire practice is those symptoms.

## Midi's coverage map, and where it stops

Midi's coverage strength is breadth within commercial insurance: in-network with most PPO plans nationwide, available in all 50 states, with state-level carrier lists — in California, for example, Aetna (PPO and HMO), Cigna (PPO and OAP), Anthem (Select PPO and HPN), Blue Cross Blue Shield, Blue Shield of California, Health Net, and UnitedHealthcare. Employer partnerships extend that reach: Delta Dental's Next Stage women's health program and MultiCare's employee health plan both route members to Midi, and the employer program carries no fees, contracts, or complicated integration for organizations whose plans already cover Midi. The hard edges remain Medicaid, Medi-Cal, and Medicare: Midi cannot treat Medicaid or Medi-Cal patients even as self-pay, and Medicare beneficiaries can only be self-pay patients who cannot submit claims. For a benefits buyer, that means Midi is a strong addition to a commercial PPO population and no help at all to a Medicaid or Medicare population — a coverage gap that should be named in any benefits communication rather than discovered by an employee at booking.

## Aura AI, revenue recognition, and multi-entity close

Aura AI is Rillet's agent layer, and it works on live general-ledger data rather than last period's batch. It answers plain-English questions against the books ("What accruals are missing from October?") with draft journal entries attached, and its embedded agents handle close management, reconciliation, flux analysis (comparing actuals to prior periods, flagging anomalies, and drafting variance narratives), accruals, AR collections, and AP coding — proposing entries that a human approves, with a full audit trail. Revenue recognition is a core strength: real-time sync from Salesforce or HubSpot pulls closed-won contracts and generates revenue patterns and deferred revenue schedules automatically, covering sales-led, product-led, and usage-based models under ASC 606, with drill-down into ARR, net revenue retention, logo retention cohorts, SaaS P&L, and GAAP financials. Multi-entity consolidation, intercompany eliminations, and currency translation run on rules the finance team defines. Native integrations number more than 50, including Stripe, Salesforce, Snowflake, Ramp, Brex, Rippling, Gusto, and major banks, and Rillet's proprietary models automatically match a reported 90% of bank transactions.

## Rillet's implementation model, and the crowded AI ledger field

Rillet's implementation is CPA-led and runs 4 to 8 weeks at a company-stated cost around $20,000, with accountants who close the customer's first books alongside them — against the 6 to 18 months and $150,000 to $400,000 Rillet cites for legacy ERP implementations. Named customers reported by third-party coverage include Function, Mercor, Temporal, Scribe, Sotheby's, Kickstarter, and Foursquare, with more than 600 customers claimed by the company, and a Series C at a reported $1 billion valuation led by ICONIQ, as reported by TechCrunch in August 2026. The risk for a buyer is the same as with any system of record: switching costs are high once live, and Rillet's zero-day close claim is a company positioning statement, not an independently audited benchmark.

## The close in practice, from bill sync to board package

Rillet's continuous close is best understood as a chain reaction. When a bill syncs from an expense platform, the system simultaneously records the bill, creates department allocations, posts journal entries, and proposes the accrual — and any change cascades instantly, so month-end becomes verification of work already done rather than reconstruction of a month's activity. Bank feeds match automatically, foreign-exchange transfers reconcile without manual intervention, and discrepancies surface immediately; hours of Stripe payout reconciliation become minutes. The flux agent compares actuals to prior periods, flags anomalies, and drafts variance explanations — Rillet says 80% of the board package narrative before a human opens a spreadsheet. A 13-week cash forecast that once took days can be generated in minutes. The audit trail is structural: timestamped entries, role-based permissions, and propose-and-approve workflows, so every action is traceable and every agent proposal requires a human approval. Rillet sells direct to finance teams, but it also sells through accounting firms: it publishes an accounting partner track aimed at practices serving client companies, and third-party coverage names partnerships with Armanino and Wiss. # Listen Labs — AI-moderated customer interviews at massive scale

Listen Labs runs AI-moderated customer interviews for companies that need to understand what customers think, but cannot wait four to six weeks for a traditional research agency to recruit a dozen people and write up a report. Its platform designs the study, recruits participants, conducts the interviews with an AI interviewer that asks dynamic follow-up questions, analyzes the responses, and delivers consultant-quality reports, slide decks, and video highlight reels — in under 24 hours, at roughly a third of the cost of traditional research according to the company. It is listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #24. Listen Labs was founded in 2023 by Alfred Wahlforss and Florian Juengermann in San Francisco. Money comes from enterprise contracts; reported pricing starts around $20,000 a year plus $300 to $400 per completed interview.

Listen Labs compresses a research cycle that traditionally takes four to six weeks into less than 24 hours, at roughly a third of the cost according to the company, by automating every stage: AI-assisted study design, recruitment from a network of more than 50 million verified respondents across 45-plus countries and 120-plus languages, AI-moderated audio and video interviews with dynamic follow-ups, automated analysis with emotional-intelligence signals, and consultant-quality deliverables including reports, slide decks, and video highlight reels. Quality Guard monitors every interview in real time for fraud, low-effort responses, and repeat respondents, and participants are capped at three studies a month. The company says it has run more than 1 million interviews for customers including Microsoft, Google, Anthropic, Sony, Sweetgreen, Perplexity, Robinhood, Procter & Gamble, Skims, Levi's, Boston Consulting Group, and Nestlé. It also sells digital twins — AI simulations built from earlier interviews that estimate customer reactions before real participants are asked — which are useful for pre-testing but are estimates, not evidence from real people. In September 2026 Salesforce announced a definitive agreement to acquire Listen Labs for undisclosed terms, reported at about $2 billion, with closing expected in Salesforce's fiscal fourth quarter of 2027.

## The 50-million participant network, Quality Guard, and digital twins

The engine is the participant network: more than 50 million verified respondents across 45-plus countries and 120-plus languages, from which Listen Labs recruits for a study, with participants limited to three studies a month. Interviews are audio and video, AI-moderated, with emotional-intelligence analysis of tone of voice, word choice, and micro-expressions, and a Visual Insights feature that lets the interviewer observe on-screen behavior and react when a participant acts differently from what they said. Quality Guard monitors every interview in real time for fraud, low-effort responses, and repeat respondents, and every finding links back to a timestamp, verbatim quote, and AI reasoning chain. The company says it has run more than 1 million interviews, names Microsoft, Google, Anthropic, Sony, Sweetgreen, Perplexity, Robinhood, Procter & Gamble, Skims, Levi's, Boston Consulting Group, and Nestlé among its customers, and claims roughly 15% of the Fortune 100. It holds SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 27701, and ISO 42001 certifications, is GDPR compliant, and says it never trains its AI models on customer data. Separately, Listen Labs sells digital twins: AI simulations built from earlier interviews that estimate how a group of customers might react to a product or message before any real person is asked — useful for quick tests, but a simulation is not evidence from real participants, and the distinction matters.

## The Salesforce acquisition, and what it changes

In September 2026, Salesforce announced a definitive agreement to acquire Listen Labs; financial terms were not disclosed by the companies, though multiple outlets reported a price of about $2 billion. The deal is expected to close in Salesforce's fiscal fourth quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approval, and Listen Labs will join Salesforce AI Labs, with Wahlforss remaining CEO and Juengermann remaining CTO. Salesforce says Listen Labs will complement Marketing Cloud and Service Cloud and give its AI agents additional customer context — which makes qualitative research a data source inside CRM workflows rather than a report that lives outside them. For buyers, the open questions are integration (Salesforce has not detailed which agent workflows will use Listen Labs data) and independence (whether a Salesforce-owned research platform stays equally useful to companies that compete with Salesforce's ecosystem). Listen Labs raised a $69 million Series B led by Ribbit Capital in January 2026 at a reported valuation above $500 million; reported annualized revenue of about $30 million comes from TechCrunch reporting, not a company filing.

## A study in practice, from brief to board-ready deliverable

A Listen Labs study runs as a single workflow rather than a relay between vendors. The team designs the study with AI assistance, building screener questions and discussion guides; Listen Labs recruits from its verified network, with fraud screening handled by Quality Guard; the AI interviewer conducts audio and video interviews with dynamic follow-ups, reading emotional signals and on-screen behavior as it goes; analysis is automated, with themes, sentiment, and quantitative cuts; and the deliverables — consultant-quality reports, PowerPoint decks, and video highlight reels — arrive in under 24 hours, with auto-generated reports available in under a minute for some formats. The Research Library stores studies, highlight reels, and matrices in one searchable workspace, so insights compound across studies instead of disappearing into slide decks. That compounding is a real, underappreciated advantage over agencies: the tenth study on a category starts from the previous nine rather than from zero. For a single researcher, the operational change is scale: hundreds of AI-moderated interviews in a day, producing a statistically meaningful sample, instead of the five to fifteen interviews that constrain most qualitative projects.

## Digital twins, carefully, and the governance behind the platform

Digital twins deserve a separate, careful paragraph, because they are the part of Listen Labs most easily misunderstood. A digital twin is an AI simulation built from earlier interview data, intended to estimate how a group of customers might react to a product, message, or idea before any real person is asked. That is useful for cheap, fast pre-testing — but a twin's output is a model's estimate, not a participant's words, and it should never be quoted to a stakeholder as if customers said it. Listen Labs' own framing preserves the distinction: interviews capture what recruited participants say, simulations estimate what customers might say or do. The governance around the real interviews is the stronger story: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 27701, and ISO 42001 certifications, GDPR compliance, participants capped at three studies a month to prevent professional respondents, and a stated policy of never training AI models on customer data. For a buyer in a regulated industry, those controls, plus the traceability of every finding to a timestamp and verbatim quote, are what make AI-moderated research defensible in a way that a chatbot summary of public opinion never is.

Actively's product is a system, not a tool: a persistent AI agent for every account in a company's market, built on custom reasoning models trained on that company's products, positioning, and historical data, that works each account around the clock and tells reps the next best action every day. The agents identify opportunities, develop strategies to break into accounts, research, prospect, and execute the work to move deals forward, learning from every interaction and sharing learnings across the system so the whole deployment compounds. ## Per-account agents, custom reasoning models, and the Samsara proof point

Actively's agents are not a shared chatbot. Underneath are custom-trained reasoning models that analyze a company's data to identify high-impact opportunities, optimal outreach timing, and personalized messaging, plus a deep reasoning engine that synthesizes CRM data, communications, and external signals into account profiles. Actively raised a $45 million Series B in April 2026, co-led by TCV and First Harmonic with Bain Capital Ventures, First Round Capital, and Alkeon participating, bringing total funding to $68 million by the company's own statement. The daily experience of Actively is a prioritized list, not a dashboard. # Cyera — data security that starts by finding the data

Cyera sells an AI-native data security platform to enterprises that have lost track of where their sensitive data lives: customer PII in a forgotten S3 bucket, a finance spreadsheet shared to an entire Google Workspace domain, an unencrypted snapshot of a production database sitting in a dev account. The platform discovers data across cloud, SaaS, on-premises, and endpoints, classifies it with AI, maps who — human and machine — can access it, and prioritizes the exposures worth fixing. It is listed as LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 — US #30, and it also appears on the Israel 2026 list. Cyera was founded in 2021 by Yotam Segev (CEO), Tamar Bar-Ilan (CTO), and Yonatan Itai (VP of R&D), engineers who previously built and ran the cloud-security division of Israel's Unit 8200, and is headquartered in New York with Tel Aviv R&D. Money comes from enterprise subscriptions; pricing is not published.

Cyera's platform answers a question most security teams cannot answer: where is our sensitive data, and who can reach it. Its agentless DSPM engine deploys in minutes, scans petabytes across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Snowflake, Databricks, and SaaS applications, and classifies data with a company-claimed precision above 95% using hundreds of out-of-the-box and learned classifiers. On that classification sit the rest of the platform: Omni DLP, built from the October 2024 acquisition of Trail Security, which protects data in motion, at rest, and in use with far fewer false positives than legacy DLP; Data Access Governance for right-sizing entitlements; Access Trail for auditing how humans and AI systems touch data; AI-SPM for inventorying AI models, applications, copilots, and agents; and AI Protect and Agent Guardian for runtime enforcement on AI interactions. In July 2026 Cyera agreed to acquire Oasis Security for roughly $1 billion, adding non-human identity governance — because AI agents and service accounts now touch sensitive data at machine scale. Reported scale figures include a $600 million Series G in June 2026 at a reported $12 billion valuation, more than $150 million in annual recurring revenue, and roughly one in five of the Fortune 500 as customers, with named references including Paramount, AT&T, Chipotle, DocuSign, and Peloton. Cyera was founded in 2021 by Yotam Segev, Tamar Bar-Ilan, and Yonatan Itai. Pricing is not published.

## DSPM, Omni DLP, and the AI security modules

The flagship is data security posture management (DSPM): an agentless engine that deploys in minutes, scans petabytes across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Snowflake, Databricks, and SaaS applications, and classifies sensitive data with a company-claimed precision above 95% across structured and unstructured datasets, using hundreds of out-of-the-box and learned classifiers. Everything else runs off that classification. Omni DLP, built from the October 2024 acquisition of Trail Security ($162 million), protects data in motion, at rest, and in use, using DSPM context to cut the false positives that bury legacy DLP teams. Data Access Governance maps who can reach what data and supports right-sizing entitlements. Access Trail audits how humans and AI systems touch sensitive data. AI-SPM inventories AI models, applications, copilots, agents, and knowledge bases and maps them to identities and data stores, while AI Protect and Agent Guardian enforce runtime controls on AI interactions, including blocking risky PHI sharing or prompt injection attempts in real time. Cyera holds SOC 2, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS certifications with GDPR, HIPAA, and CCPA attestations, and was named a Leader in the Forrester Wave for Sensitive Data Discovery and Classification Solutions in Q2 2026, with the highest score in the strategy category.

## Cyera's acquisitions, scale claims, and the DSPM field

Cyera's acquisition run shows where it thinks the market is going: Trail Security for DLP, Otterize and Shape AI in 2025 for runtime and non-human identity, and Oasis Security in July 2026 for roughly $1 billion, folding non-human identity governance into the platform — because AI agents are now identities that touch data, and governing them is becoming as important as governing employees. Reported scale figures: a $600 million Series G in June 2026 at a reported $12 billion valuation, more than $2.3 billion raised in about 18 months, more than $150 million in annual recurring revenue reported as tripled in 2025, and roughly one in five of the Fortune 500 as customers — all third-party or company-reported figures, not audited financials. Named customers and references include Paramount, AT&T, Chipotle, DocuSign, Peloton, Mercury Financial, and Valvoline. Cyera's direct rival in DSPM is BigID; its broader competitive set includes the cloud security platforms adding data classification and the legacy DLP vendors. Its argument is that AI-native, agentless classification is the foundation everything else depends on, and that a platform built on that foundation beats a collection of point tools. The number to treat with care is the 95% precision claim: it is Cyera's own figure, not an independently audited benchmark.

## Cyera in a healthcare deployment

Healthcare shows Cyera's platform at its most demanding, because the data is patient data and the regulations are unforgiving. Cyera inventories PHI, PII, and research data by system and geography, identifies over-privileged or duplicate identities and third-party users touching PHI, and right-sizes entitlements to minimize blast radius. It detects unvetted AI assistants used by clinicians or back-office staff, maps which PHI they touch, and enforces policies — including monitoring prompts and responses and blocking risky PHI sharing or prompt injection attempts in real time. It maintains updated records of data locations, classifications, access trails, and controls to streamline HIPAA, HITRUST, and internal reviews, and it rationalizes sprawling clinical datasets to shrink the PHI attack surface while cutting infrastructure spend and backup bloat across electronic health records, picture archiving systems, research lakes, and SaaS tools. Cyera's Oasis acquisition is the clearest signal of where data security is heading: from protecting data to governing the identities that touch it, including non-human identities. AI agents, service accounts, automation scripts, and third-party integrations now access sensitive data at machine scale, and they do not behave like employees — they do not take vacations, they do not respond to training, and their access often accumulates silently. # AfterQuery — Expert reasoning, captured as training data

AfterQuery is an applied research lab that sells training data to frontier AI labs and enterprises, built on one argument: models plateau when trained on final answers, and improve when trained on how experts actually work — the decisions, tradeoffs, and context behind an answer. It does not sell a model or an app. It sells datasets and training environments built with verified practicing professionals, aimed at labs building foundation models and companies post-training models for professional work. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #31. Its pitch to buyers is concrete: off-the-shelf datasets for immediate use, or custom datasets and evaluation suites built around the exact capability gaps a lab is trying to close. Its network, by its own count, spans 300,000+ verified practitioners across medicine, law, finance, engineering, and other professional fields — the people whose working judgment the datasets encode. The commercial logic is straightforward: frontier labs already have compute and base models; what they lack is expert reasoning traces at quality, and AfterQuery charges for producing them. A public proof point: with Hebbia, AfterQuery post-trained NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL open model on expert-written public credit tasks, and perfect solves on a 100-task held-out set rose from 47% to 74%, as reported on its blog in October 2026. Pricing is not published; engagements are sold as data products and custom projects, not self-serve subscriptions.

The timing matters. Frontier labs spent 2023 and 2024 scaling on web text, then hit the same wall in professional domains: public data teaches models to sound competent, but professional work is judged on decisions under uncertainty — which diagnosis to prioritize, which clause creates exposure, which credit deserves a downgrade. That judgment lives in practitioners' heads, not in documents, which is why AfterQuery's pitch is capture rather than collection. The company frames itself as an applied research lab rather than a data vendor, and its blog publishes failure-mode research (for example, where Nemotron and Qwen models break on GDP-related documents) alongside product announcements — a deliberate signal to lab buyers that it understands the science, not just the supply chain. Its customer list is not published, which is normal for this sector: labs do not disclose their training-data suppliers. The Hebbia post-training result is therefore doing heavy work as public proof, and it is specific enough to check: expert-written public credit tasks, a 100-task held-out set, perfect solves up from 47% to 74%. The products themselves show the same research-first instinct: loss analyses that map failure modes before datasets are designed, and custom evals that let a lab measure exactly which capability gap a dataset closes.

## SFT pairs, rubrics, and RL environments

AfterQuery's catalog breaks into distinct data products, each aimed at a different stage of post-training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) pairs give models prompt-response examples plus chain-of-thought demonstrations, teaching behavior across complex tasks before reinforcement learning begins. Rubric- and verifier-based reinforcement learning pairs expert-crafted grading rubrics with automated verifiers, so model outputs get graded the way a seasoned professional would — rewarding nuance, penalizing shortcuts — across reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following. Tool-calling RL environments are built on real APIs, MCP servers, and developer tools, letting agents learn to call, chain, and recover from errors across service workflows, with automated evaluation at every step. Computer-use and browser-use environments pair high-fidelity browser and desktop environments with expert-demonstrated trajectories, teaching agents to navigate interfaces and complete multi-step workflows the way a domain expert would. RLHF captures preference comparisons — what makes one response genuinely better than another — across thousands of pairs. Code generation data spans expert-written code, test cases, and debugging traces aimed at production-quality software and architectural reasoning. Deep research data covers long-horizon tasks: gathering evidence across sources, synthesizing findings, and producing analyses that mirror skilled researchers. Loss analyses study where and why models fail in professional contexts, and feed back into how every dataset is designed.

## Who buys, and how the work is sold

The buyers are frontier foundation-model labs and enterprises doing serious post-training — the kind of customer that measures a dataset by held-out task performance, not by volume. AfterQuery sells two ways: ready-to-deploy datasets across high-demand capability areas for labs that want validated training data without a custom engagement's lead time, and custom evaluation suites and training datasets designed from scratch around a customer's specific capability targets. A second line, Data Partnerships, announced in October 2026, works with business owners to realize value from their underlying data while holding to AfterQuery's research, trust, and privacy standards — a sign the company is sourcing proprietary enterprise data, not just commissioning expert labor. Its research-first posture is part of the sales pitch: every domain has its own failure patterns, and AfterQuery studies where models break in real professional contexts before designing the data to fix it.

## AfterQuery against generic data labeling

The distinction AfterQuery draws against conventional labeling vendors is process over answers. Generic labeling grades or produces final outputs; AfterQuery records the working process — step-by-step decisions, rejected alternatives, and the reasoning a professional applies mid-task. It also draws an expertise line: datasets are built with verified practicing professionals, not general annotators, which is what lets it claim coverage of tacit knowledge that textbooks leave out and synthetic data cannot replicate. The risk to that claim is verification: buyers must trust that the "verified practitioners" are genuinely expert in the domains sold, and AfterQuery's public material does not publish its vetting methodology in detail. Its other exposure is concentration: its value rests on frontier labs continuing to pay for human expert data rather than closing the gap with synthetic data and self-improvement, a bet the whole training-data sector is making at once.

## Data Partnerships and the synthetic-data question

The October 2026 Data Partnerships announcement points to AfterQuery's second supply channel: partnering with business owners to unlock value in their underlying data under research, trust, and privacy standards. That matters because commissioned expert labor alone scales linearly with headcount, while proprietary enterprise datasets compound — each partnership adds data no competitor can buy off the shelf. The open question for the whole sector is whether synthetic data and model self-improvement close the expert-data gap faster than vendors can widen it. AfterQuery's answer, implicit in its product design, is that reasoning traces from real professionals remain the hardest data to synthesize well, because a model generating its own training data inherits its own failure modes. Buyers should still ask the hard question in diligence: how much of a given dataset's lift survives when the same tasks are trained on the lab's own synthetic data at a fraction of the cost. AfterQuery does not publish head-to-head comparisons, and its pricing opacity means buyers cannot easily benchmark cost per unit of capability gain against rivals.

# Phantom — The wallet that became a trading app

Phantom started in January 2021 as a crypto wallet for Solana and now presents itself as a home for trading crypto, prediction markets, and perpetual futures, plus spending and sending money — used, by its own count, by more than 20 million people. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #32. The business model is a consumer finance platform built on top of a self-custodial wallet: users hold their own funds (Phantom states it never has access to them), and Phantom monetizes trading activity — in-app token swaps, perps, and prediction markets — alongside a prepaid Visa debit card for spending. It began with a 40,000-person beta, raised a $9 million Series A in July 2021 led by a16z with Variant and Jump Capital, and in January 2025 raised a $150 million Series C co-led by Sequoia Capital and Paradigm at a reported $3 billion valuation, explicitly to build what it calls the world's biggest consumer finance platform. The team is 100+ people, led by CEO Brandon Millman, CTO Francesco Agosti, and CPO Chris Kalani. Phantom is not a bank; the card is issued by Lead Bank under Visa licensing, with Bridge Ventures as program manager.

The arc from wallet to trading app is the story. Phantom launched on Solana when that chain's ecosystem was small, won users on design at a time when wallets were built for developers, and then expanded chain by chain — Ethereum, Bitcoin, Base, Sui — rather than staying a single-chain tool. Each expansion added a user segment: Bitcoin holders who wanted one home for their coins, Ethereum users who wanted the same clean swap experience, and traders who wanted perps and prediction markets without opening a separate exchange account. The social layer — usernames, profiles, sending money to friends — pushes the same direction: a wallet that behaves like a payments app is easier to recommend than one that behaves like a key manager. The 24/7 support team and instant scam flagging are part of that mainstreaming bet, since self-custody's biggest adoption barrier is fear of irreversible mistakes. Phantom's own timeline marks the milestones: 40,000 beta testers in 2021, 1 million users by the swap launch, 3 million by the Series A, 15 million by the Series C, and 20 million-plus today. The education layer supports the same mainstreaming: Crypto 101 guides for Solana, Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Polygon, explainers on wallets, stablecoins, and bridges, and scam-avoidance guides, all aimed at users who are new to crypto rather than native to it.

## Swaps, perps, prediction markets, and Terminal

Phantom's trading surface has widened well past the original wallet. In-app token swaps launched in June 2021 and passed $1 billion in volume by October of that year. The current lineup adds prediction markets — trading on cultural moments — and perpetual futures, letting users go long or short with leverage, plus Terminal, a desktop trading toolset. The wallet itself remains multichain, covering Solana, Ethereum, Bitcoin, Base, and Sui, with features aimed at mainstream users: usernames and profiles for sending money to friends, scam detection that flags malicious transactions, Ledger hardware-wallet support, and 24/7 support. The spend side is a prepaid Visa debit card usable anywhere Visa is accepted, plus Apple Pay and Google Pay support, for users 18 and older, with fees per the cardholder agreement. Phantom also publishes Crypto 101 guides and developer documentation, and has grown by acquisition — Solsniper in August 2025, SimpleHash in February 2025 for token data, and Parallax joining in June 2025.

## Phantom against MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet, and exchanges

Phantom's edge against wallet incumbents is design and breadth in one place: it pairs self-custody with an exchange-like trading surface, so users who would otherwise split activity between a wallet and a centralized exchange can trade, bet on events, and run perps without leaving the app. Against centralized exchanges, its argument is custody — users keep control of funds — and against pure wallets, its argument is that trading, social features, and spending are built in rather than bolted on through third-party dApps. The risks are the ones that come with that breadth: perps and prediction markets draw regulatory scrutiny in many jurisdictions, self-custody means user error is unrecoverable by design, and the card business puts Phantom in the regulated payments chain through partners it does not control. Its growth also depends on crypto market cycles: the jump from 40,000 beta users to 3 million by the Series A, 15 million by the Series C, and 20 million-plus today tracks bull-market onboarding as much as product quality. What is not public: revenue, swap fee rates, and perps volume, none of which Phantom publishes.

## Where Phantom makes money, and what it does not disclose

Phantom's revenue engine is trading flow: swaps, perps, and prediction markets generate fees or spreads, while the card business earns through its issuing partners. That makes Phantom's economics sensitive to crypto market cycles in a way a pure wallet's would not be — trading volume, not user count, pays the bills, and the user-count milestones it publishes do not translate directly into revenue. Phantom does not publish revenue, fee schedules for swaps, or perps volume, so the size of that engine is not verifiable from public material. Its acquisitions point to where it is investing the Series C money: Solsniper (August 2025) for trading tooling, SimpleHash (February 2025) for token data quality, and Parallax (June 2025) joining the team — all infrastructure for a trading-first product rather than a wallet-first one. The regulatory exposure grows with the same breadth: perps and prediction markets are restricted or contested in several major jurisdictions, and Phantom's ability to offer them everywhere it has users is not guaranteed. Self-custody remains the philosophical core — "controlled by you, secured by us" — but the product's center of gravity has moved from custody to trading, and that shift is the thing to watch.

# Rogo — AI agents that do bankers' deal work

Rogo sells an AI platform to financial institutions — investment banks, private equity firms, and other finance houses — that executes end-to-end deal workflows using finance-specific agents, and it claims more than 450 leading firms in finance as customers. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #33. The product is not a chatbot that answers finance questions; it is a system that runs work: building LBO models, refreshing public comps, reading investment memos, checking relationship notes, and updating deal stages, with every answer citing the filing, model, or document it came from so the work can be checked line by line. Its revenue model is enterprise software sold to firms, deployed with guided implementation and a "Forward Deployed Bankers" team — former bankers and investors who embed with the customer from day one through firmwide rollout. Pricing is not published; deals are enterprise contracts. Rogo's public endorsements include Truist Securities CEO Tom Hackett, who credits the integration with boosting productivity, reducing risk, and freeing bankers to focus on relationships and growth. Rogo has also announced a strategic investment to accelerate expansion across EMEA and APAC, with terms not disclosed.

A deal in Rogo runs as a chain of small, checkable steps rather than one big answer. A banker opens a project for a live deal, and agents pull the relevant pieces: the target's filings, the firm's prior work on comparable companies, relationship notes from past pitches, and the current model file. The LBO agent reviews the model, flags inconsistencies, and drafts updates; a comps agent refreshes trading multiples from public data; a memo agent reads the investment memo and extracts the thesis, risks, and open questions. Each output carries its source, so a senior banker can audit the chain — the filing page, the model cell, the memo paragraph — before anything goes to a client or an investment committee. Usage is tracked by project, which gives firms a concrete handle on cost and adoption: which teams use it, on which deals, and how much agent work each deal consumes. That audit trail is also Rogo's answer to the trust problem that stalls AI adoption inside banks: the work is only useful if a professional will sign it, and signing requires checking. The platform's integrations, including Dow Jones data, feed the same workflow: agents work from data the firm already trusts, rather than from a separate research silo.

## Agents, Intelligence, Projects, Watchtower, and Notes

Rogo's platform is organized as five parts. Agents run thousands of finance-specific workflows against a firm's existing data and processes — the LBO model build, the comps refresh, the precedent-deal search. Intelligence captures a firm's people, deals, and expertise into a reusable, governed knowledge base: a search for a previous deal surfaces relationship notes, memos, and deal history as structured records. Projects let teams ingest data rooms, execute deal requests alongside the deal team, and run full processes inside Rogo, with usage tracked by project. Watchtower is the governance layer: it governs models, spend, permissions, and policies in one place, so firms can deploy AI at scale with controls. Notes is compliant AI notetaking that turns meetings into reusable firm context. Underpinning all of it is a permissions model that carries a firm's existing entitlements through to every agent, so people only ever see data they already could — a requirement for banks, where information barriers are legal obligations, not preferences. Rogo lists SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, GDPR, and CCPA compliance, and positions itself for EU AI Act readiness.

## Rogo against Harvey, generic copilots, and in-house builds

Rogo's named competitive set is instructive: it competes against legal-AI vendor Harvey for professional-services AI budgets, against general-purpose copilots that lack finance-specific workflows and cited sources, and against banks' own in-house AI efforts. Its differentiation is specificity and auditability: workflows built for finance tasks rather than general question-answering, answers that cite sources line by line, and governance (Watchtower, entitlement-aware permissions) designed for regulated institutions. The risk is concentration and proof: 450+ firms is a strong claim, but Rogo does not publish revenue, retention, or the share of work its agents complete without human correction, so buyers must verify output quality in pilots. Its other exposure is model dependence: the agents run on frontier models Rogo does not own, so its moat is workflow design, firm-specific memory, and deployment expertise rather than model ownership — durable only as long as that workflow layer stays ahead of what banks can assemble themselves.

## Forward Deployed Bankers and the deployment bet

Rogo does not sell self-serve software. Its deployment model pairs each customer with Forward Deployed Bankers — former bankers and investors who embed with the team from day one through firmwide rollout, shaping Rogo around the firm's existing process rather than asking the firm to adopt a generic workflow. That high-touch model explains both its traction and its cost structure: 450+ firms is a large customer count for a company that deploys this way, and it implies a services-heavy organization behind the software. The strategic investment for EMEA and APAC expansion suggests the model is being exported rather than replaced, with the same embedded approach in new regions. For buyers, the diligence question is whether Rogo's value survives the departure of its deployed team — whether the firm's institutional memory, once captured in Rogo's Intelligence layer, keeps paying off without constant hand-holding, or whether usage fades when the bankers leave. Rogo's public material does not answer that, and its pricing opacity means the total cost of a firmwide rollout, including the deployment team, is not visible before a sales conversation.

# Qualified Health — The governance layer for hospital AI

Qualified Health sells health systems a single enterprise platform for building, deploying, and governing AI across clinical and administrative work — and its central claim is that governance, not model quality, is what stops hospital AI from scaling. Founded in late 2023 by Justin Norden, a computer scientist, Stanford-trained physician, and former founder who sold Trustworthy AI to Waymo, the Palo Alto company (a public benefit corporation) now reports more than 500,000 users across health systems representing roughly 7% of U.S. hospital revenue. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #34. Its customers include Mercy, Emory Healthcare, Jefferson Health, University of Rochester Medicine, and all eight institutions of the University of Texas System, including MD Anderson Cancer Center and UT Southwestern. The platform wraps AI agents in what it calls enforceable governance — access controls, risk alerts, privacy protections, and hallucination safeguards that hospitals can audit after the fact — and bundles pre-built workflows that go live in weeks, plus upskilling modules so nurses and administrators work alongside the tools. The money story, as reported in March 2026: a $125 million Series B led by New Enterprise Associates, valuing the company between $500 million and $1 billion, bringing total raised to $155 million, after a $5 million seed and a $25 million Series A in January 2025. Anthropic invested both directly and through the Menlo Ventures Anthology Fund, and supplies Claude for clinical workflows. Pricing is not published; deals are enterprise platform contracts, delivered with engineers embedded inside health systems.

The governance layer itself deserves a closer look, because it is the product. Qualified Health's platform wraps agents in access controls that limit who can see what, risk alerts that flag uncertain or unsafe outputs, privacy protections for patient data, and hallucination safeguards that catch confident-sounding errors before they reach a clinician. Every action is auditable after the fact, which is what lets a health system's compliance and legal teams sign off on deployment: when something goes wrong, the system can show what the agent saw, what it recommended, and who approved it. The platform also ships pre-built workflows that go live in weeks rather than quarters, and upskilling modules that teach nurses and administrators to work with the tools instead of around them — a recognition that failed AI deployments are usually adoption failures, not model failures. The company's team composition mirrors the pitch: former health system executives, frontline physicians from leading institutions, clinical transformation experts, and Silicon Valley engineers, combining the domain depth hospitals trust with the engineering speed they lack in-house.

## Care-gap detection at UT System, and the $15 million UTMB result

The deployment that best explains Qualified Health is the University of Texas System rollout with Anthropic, where the platform continuously analyzes clinical datasets to find patients who meet evidence-based criteria for guideline-recommended care and surfaces them, with supporting clinical context assembled, directly into care-team workflows for review. The problem it attacks is mundane and large: across a big system, patients who qualify for recommended care routinely go unidentified because no one has a continuously updated, population-level view of care gaps. At UT Medical Branch specifically, Qualified Health reports more than $15 million in measurable run-rate impact within the first six months, achieved by establishing a secure data foundation and pushing automated workflows into production. UTMB's chief AI and digital officer, Peter McCaffrey, frames the value as compounding: lessons learned on one use case feed back into the platform and benefit all 15,000 UTMB users. That compounding claim is the platform argument in miniature — one deployment's governance, data plumbing, and workflow library makes the next deployment cheaper and safer.

## Why hospitals buy a platform instead of point solutions

Qualified Health's founding insight, per Norden, came at a 2023 HIMSS conference where health system leaders complained that buying AI from multiple vendors had left them with no control over their own technology roadmap. The company's bet is that healthcare AI adoption will look like enterprise software deployment, not consumer app downloads: one trusted platform partner rather than a sprawling vendor portfolio. Its platform combines workflow automation, agent development, clinical safeguards, real-time monitoring, and end-to-end governance, with an Agent Factory product for hospitals to build and monitor AI agents inside the platform. Its delivery model is deliberately high-touch — engineers embedded directly inside health systems — which the company presents as depth and which analysts note is hard to scale quickly. It also turns away clients that want narrow, single-use solutions, limiting near-term revenue in favor of long-term platform depth. That selectivity is a real strategic choice: it keeps the customer base to systems willing to standardize on one platform, and it means Qualified Health's growth depends on winning enterprise-wide commitments, not accumulating small pilots.

## Qualified Health against Epic, point-solution vendors, and in-house AI teams

The competitive field has three poles. Electronic health record vendors, notably Epic with its own Agent Factory, bundle AI into the system hospitals already run — Qualified Health must prove its cross-vendor, model-agnostic platform is worth buying on top. Point-solution vendors offer a better tool for one workflow — documentation, scheduling, prior authorization — and Qualified Health's answer is that fifty point solutions recreate the governance mess it exists to solve. In-house AI teams at large systems argue they can build the governance layer themselves; Qualified Health's answer is speed and the shared learning across its customer base. Its exposure is the same as its pitch: if the governance layer becomes a commodity feature of EHR platforms or model providers, its moat narrows to workflow libraries and embedded expertise. Its other exposure is evidence: the UTMB $15 million figure is company-reported, and independent, peer-reviewed outcome data for its deployments is not public. What is verifiable is the customer roster and the funding — both substantial for a company founded in late 2023.

# Parallel Web Systems — Live web data, sold as APIs for AI agents

Parallel (parallel.ai) sells web infrastructure for AI agents: APIs that let agents search, extract, monitor, and reason over live web information, with citations attached. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #36. The problem it solves is that AI models train on frozen data, so any assistant, copilot, or coding agent that answers from its own weights alone goes stale — it cannot tell you what changed in the EU AI Act this month, what a competitor's pricing is today, or whether a clinical trial posted yesterday. Parallel's APIs give agents fresh, cited facts fast enough for a chat thread: a Search API for ranked URLs with compressed excerpts, an Extract API for full page contents, a Task API for deep research with structured outputs, a Decisions API that returns typed answers grounded in web evidence, a Responses API (OpenAI-compatible) for cited answers in seconds, a Monitor API for continuous change tracking, and a Find All API for building structured datasets from a text query. The pricing model is pay-as-you-go with a free tier of up to 5,000 requests per month: Search runs $0.001–$0.005 per request for 10 results, Extract is $0.001 per request, Decisions is $0.001 per up to 100 questions, Responses is $0.01–$0.25, Monitor is $0.003–$0.01, Find All is $0.03–$1 per match, and Task API work runs $0.005–$2.40 per request depending on depth. Rate limits run from 300 to 2,000 requests per minute depending on the API, and the platform is SOC 2 certified. Named customers on its site include Granola, Lovable, Harvey, Notion, Pfizer, LangChain, Modal, Replit, Profound, and Rogo — a mix of AI startups and a Fortune 500 pharmaceutical company.

## The Decisions API and the move from links to answers

The Decisions API is Parallel's most telling product move: instead of returning ranked links for an agent to read, it returns typed answers grounded in web evidence, with citations, in 200 milliseconds to 1 second, priced at $0.001 per up to 100 questions. That is a different job from search. Search serves an agent that will read and reason; Decisions serves an agent that needs a structured fact — a headcount, a funding round, a trial status — to fill a field, qualify a lead, or check a guardrail condition. It competes less with search APIs and more with data vendors and internal research teams, and its pricing (a tenth of a cent per question at the low end) is built for high-volume enrichment where each answer is cheap but the volume is large. The risk for Parallel is that the model providers add decision-grade grounding to their own agent products, collapsing the layer Parallel sells. Its defense is that Decisions is one of seven APIs sharing one crawling, extraction, and citation infrastructure — a customer using Search, Monitor, and Decisions together gets a consistent, cited view of the web that a bundled model feature would struggle to match across use cases.

## Monitor, Search, and Deep Research in practice

Parallel's four headline use cases show what the APIs are for. Monitor watches the things a business runs on — portfolio companies, target accounts, competitor pricing, regulations — and sends a structured alert the moment something material changes, so teams hear only what matters: a new Phase 2 trial posting on clinicaltrials.gov, an FDA Fast Track grant, a competitor's positive Phase 3 topline. Search puts fresh facts inside a product, giving an assistant or coding agent current, cited answers from live docs, breaking news, and real-world context. Deep Research takes an objective and returns hundreds of finished, cited reports in minutes — an account brief before a call, an investment memo, a competitive picture — analyst-grade work embedded in a workflow. Enrichment takes a list of companies or people and returns live, structured profiles with every field cited and confidence-scored, ready for a CRM or pipeline. The Decisions API, introduced as the first decision engine with world knowledge built in, is the newest piece: instead of returning documents, it returns typed answers with citations, aimed at data enrichment, lead qualification, and agent guardrails where a structured answer matters more than a list of links. Latency varies by design: Search answers in 200 milliseconds to 3 seconds, Decisions in 200 milliseconds to 1 second, Extract under 3 seconds, while Task API research runs 5 seconds to 30 minutes asynchronously and Find All takes 10 minutes to an hour.

## Parallel against Tavily, Exa, and the model providers' own browsing

Parallel competes in a crowded field of web-data APIs for AI. Tavily and Exa sell search and extraction for agents; Brave and Bing sell search APIs; and the model providers themselves bundle browsing into their assistants and agent products. Parallel's differentiation is breadth with citations at every layer: seven APIs covering search, extraction, monitoring, decisions, and dataset-building, all returning cited, confidence-scored results rather than raw text, and all SOC 2 certified for enterprise buyers. Its customer list is doing argumentative work here — Harvey and Rogo are themselves AI companies selling to professionals, so their use of Parallel is a vote for its data quality from demanding buyers. The risks are the ones every web-data vendor faces: dependence on the open web's accessibility (sites that block crawlers shrink coverage), price pressure as search becomes a commodity feature of model APIs, and the possibility that model providers bundle good-enough browsing for free. Parallel's answer is specialization: monitoring and decision-grade structured answers are harder to commoditize than a ranked list of links, and its pricing table — with per-request costs down to a tenth of a cent for extraction — is built to make it cheap enough to leave running inside products at scale.

## Citations, confidence scores, and SOC 2

The API design reflects a specific view of what agents need from the web. Every result carries citations, and enrichment results carry confidence scores, because an agent that acts on a fact — qualifying a lead, flagging a trial, briefing an account — needs to know how much to trust it and where it came from. The platform offers a playground and onboarding prompts for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, plus agents.md support, signaling that Parallel is built to be wired into coding agents and agent frameworks, not just called from a dashboard. Rate limits are generous for production use (600 requests per minute on Search, Extract, and Decisions; 2,000 per minute on Task API; 300 per minute on Responses and Monitor) and the free tier of 5,000 requests per month lets a team validate quality before paying. SOC 2 certification across all seven APIs matters for the enterprise buyers on its customer list: a pharmaceutical company like Pfizer cannot pipe web data into internal workflows without security attestation, and Parallel's pricing page lists SOC 2 on every API row as a deliberate reassurance. The company's positioning — "web infrastructure for AI agents" rather than "search API" — is a claim that the web itself needs a new access layer now that the readers are machines, not people browsing pages.

# Monaco — A revenue engine that replaces the CRM for startups

Monaco sells startups an AI-native revenue platform that replaces a legacy CRM and a stack of disconnected sales tools: it builds a company's total addressable market, runs outbound, captures every interaction, and manages pipeline in one place. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #37. The pitch, endorsed by investors Garry Tan and Peter Thiel and by Flexport founder Ryan Petersen, is aimed at founders without sales backgrounds: Monaco claims to solve go-to-market risk for them, with one investor quoted as saying no product sells itself, though Monaco comes close. The product works like this: agents find every company and buyer worth pursuing, score them, and show the reasoning behind every score, so the market stays current without anyone maintaining a list; agents act on real-time buying signals and reach the right buyer with the right message at the right time, with the customer approving the campaigns that matter and the rest running on its own; agents draft emails, send reminders, take notes, and update records as deals progress, so founders step in only for the conversations that close. Every interaction — emails, calls, meeting recordings, messages — is automatically captured, summarized, and turned into structured records, and agents research each account to fill in what is missing. Onboarding is white-glove: Monaco sets up the TAM, scores all accounts, overlays signals, builds sequences, and imports pipeline on day one, pairing each customer with a forward-deployed sales executive, and it claims value in days rather than months, with new meetings generated within the first week.

## What Monaco replaces, tool by tool

The consolidation claim becomes concrete when listed against the stack it displaces. The TAM and account list that a founder would build in Clay or a data vendor comes pre-built and scored, with reasoning shown for every score. The sequences and inbox follow-ups that would run in an outbound sequencer run inside Monaco's Demand Gen agents, acting on live signals rather than static lists. The call recording and note-taking that would come from a conversation-intelligence tool are captured automatically and turned into structured records. The pipeline tracking and forecasting that would live in a CRM live in Monaco's pipeline agents, which draft follow-ups and flag risks as deals progress. The RevOps work of keeping the database clean — deduplication, enrichment, list maintenance — is done by agents continuously. For a startup, the saving is not just subscription fees but headcount: Monaco's own framing is that agents take the grunt work off SDRs, AEs, and RevOps, so the same motion runs on a fraction of the team. The counter-argument a buyer should test is whether one system does each of those jobs as well as the best point tool, or whether consolidation trades depth for convenience — and whether AI-drafted outbound, sent at machine scale, helps or hurts a young brand's reputation with the buyers it most wants.

## Usage credits instead of seats: the $10,000 commit

Monaco's pricing is the most distinctive part of its pitch. There are no seats and no platform fee: customers fund an account once with a $10,000 upfront commit that buys 1,000,000 credits at one cent per credit, and the balance moves only when the system does work. After the credits, billing switches to monthly pay-as-you-go with no lock-in and no long-term commitments, and a live breakdown in the product shows what is driving spend. Spending rolls up into four categories: Data (building and improving the TAM, keeping accounts and contacts enriched and current), Signals (custom and inbound signals overlaid on accounts, showing who to reach, when, and why), Demand Gen agents (outbound that runs itself — sequences, context-adapted messages, inbox follow-ups, campaign agents inside customer guardrails), and Pipeline agents (meetings captured and summarized, opportunities created and updated, risks flagged, follow-ups drafted). Monaco says the $10,000 commit covers roughly the first three months for most customers, with the real driver being how much work the system does: TAM size, signals run, outbound sent. The model aligns Monaco's revenue with customer usage rather than headcount, which is the opposite of per-seat CRM pricing — but it also means costs scale with activity, and a startup running aggressive outbound can burn credits faster than it expects. Named customers on its site include Gamut, Nowadays, Simple AI, BackOps, and Parley, with BackOps' co-founder quoted as saying Monaco replaced its CRM, outbound tools, and half the manual work overnight.

## Monaco against Salesforce, HubSpot, Clay, and the outbound stack

Monaco's competitive claim is consolidation: one platform instead of a CRM plus a data vendor plus an outbound sequencer plus a call recorder plus a pipeline tracker. Against Salesforce and HubSpot, its argument is that legacy CRMs start empty and demand constant hygiene, while Monaco starts working on day one with a pre-built TAM and agents that maintain records automatically. Against Clay and the modern data-enrichment stack, its argument is that enrichment is built into the revenue workflow rather than sold as a separate tool. Against outbound point solutions, its argument is that sequences, signals, and pipeline live in one system of record, so nothing falls between tools. The risks are execution and trust: AI-drafted outbound at scale can damage a young company's reputation if messages miss the mark, and customers must hand Monaco their entire go-to-market motion — TAM, messaging, pipeline — which makes switching away costly and makes Monaco's quality a single point of failure for revenue. Its investor endorsements are unusually loud for a company at this stage, which cuts both ways: they signal confidence from people who have seen many sales tools, but they also set expectations Monaco must meet in customer results, not quotes. What is not public: customer count, revenue, retention, or meeting-booking rates, so the "value in days" claim rests on testimonials.

## The system of record, in practice

What "system of record" means in practice is the difference between Monaco and a CRM with AI features bolted on. In a legacy CRM, the record is what a rep typed after the call, and it decays the moment anyone gets busy; in Monaco, the record is built by the system itself from captured interactions, enriched by agents, and kept current without human data entry. That is why the onboarding promise matters so much: a TAM built on day two, sequences running the same day, meetings generated within days — as Nowadays' co-founder describes it — is only possible if the system arrives with data and works immediately, rather than asking a founder to spend months configuring it. The forward-deployed sales executive paired with each customer is the human side of that promise: someone who has run go-to-market motions before, helping build and operate the customer's motion rather than handing over documentation. The investor quotes on the site — Tan on go-to-market risk for founders without sales backgrounds, Thiel's "no product sells itself, though Monaco comes close," Petersen's "every founder needs to put their startup on Monaco before their competition" — are unusually strong for a young company, and they frame Monaco as a founder tool first: the buyer is often a technical founder who knows the product cold and has never run sales.

Higgsfield AI is an all-in-one AI creative studio for video and image creation, built to give creators, marketing agencies, and filmmakers cinematic-quality output without filmmaking expertise. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #38. Launched in 2025 and headquartered in San Francisco, it reports more than 25 million users, 850 million-plus generations created, about 6 million generations per day, 300 million-plus videos created, and about 2 million videos per day, with more than 200 releases shipped since launch. The product brings together cinematic intelligence and a unified creative workflow: users generate from text, image, or link input, with automatic camera logic and pacing for first-time creators and professional camera lenses, cinematic parameters, and color grading for filmmakers. Its surface spans image, video, and audio generation, plus an MCP integration for Claude, an API, a ChatGPT plugin, and tools with names that map to jobs: Cinema Studio for multi-minute cinematic video, Genjutsu for motion recasting (take a motion and recast it with different characters, locations, or products), Content Factory for turning trending styles into ready-to-post series, Playable for making a mobile game from a single prompt, AI Influencer for building virtual creators, Katana, Ads Studio for product-URL-to-ad generation, and a Supercomputer agent.
