## The credit economy, and why plans keep changing

Higgsfield's credit system is where creators feel the product's economics. Every generation costs credits depending on model, clip length, and resolution, and the plan comparison translates credits into yields: Starter's 200 credits buy roughly 100 Nano Banana Pro images, Plus's 1,000 buy roughly 500, and Ultra's 3,000 buy roughly 1,500, while video costs run far higher per take — a Seedance-class video costs on the order of 15 credits, and third-party trackers put some premium video takes far above that. Subscription credits reset each billing cycle and do not roll over, while separately bought credit packs last 90 days, and credit-based generations run in a priority queue while unlimited-model generations run in the standard queue. The repeated plan changes through 2026 — Starter, Plus, and Ultra repriced and re-credited several times, with promotional unlimited windows on named models — reflect a company still searching for the price point where creators feel they get value and the company covers model costs. For a buyer, the practical advice is to price a month of actual work (how many videos, at what length and resolution, on which models) rather than comparing headline credit counts, and to check the current pricing page before subscribing, since the numbers move.

## Cinema Studio, Genjutsu, and the creator workflow

Higgsfield's flagship workspace is Cinema Studio, positioned for agencies producing multi-minute cinematic videos — the hard case for AI video, where consistency across scenes matters more than a single good clip. Genjutsu is the motion product: a creator takes an existing motion and recasts it with their own characters, locations, and products, or swaps specific elements while keeping the rest untouched, which is how brands reuse a proven ad format with new talent or products. Content Factory turns trending styles into ready-to-post series for social, optimized for TikTok, Reels, and Shorts with built-in hook timing and native pacing. Ads Studio takes a product URL and generates trend-matched video ads for campaigns at scale. The platform also aggregates third-party models — Seedance, Kling, Veo, Sora appear across its model lineup — behind one subscription, so a creator does not need separate accounts and credit balances for each model provider. Higgsfield Academy teaches creation step by step, and Higgsfield Earn lets creators monetize talent and grow professionally. The company says its features are built by award-winning filmmakers, producers, and researchers driven by creative needs, and that Fortune 500 agencies use it for campaigns and launches. Its values page commits to creator trust with a dedicated Trust page covering terms, policies, and support operations.

## Higgsfield against Runway, Kling, and the model providers directly

Higgsfield's competition is threefold. Against Runway and other creator platforms, it competes on breadth — image, video, audio, and influencer tooling in one studio — and on cinematic controls borrowed from real film terminology. Against Kling and other single-model providers, it competes as an aggregator: one subscription reaches many models, with the workflow (storyboards, pre-production visualization, campaign variation) layered on top. Against the model providers' own apps, its argument is workflow and curation: the right model for each shot, camera logic, and pacing, rather than a raw prompt box. The structural risk is that aggregation is a thin moat — if the underlying models become directly accessible and cheap, the studio layer must justify its margin with workflow that creators will not rebuild themselves. The credit economy is the other pressure point: creators judge a plan by what it actually buys (Higgsfield's own math puts a Seedance-class video at roughly 15 credits and a Nano Banana Pro image at about 2), and frequent plan changes through 2026 have made that math a moving target, which is itself a trust issue for paying creators. What is not independently verified: the 25 million user and 850 million generation counts, which are company-reported.

## Reading the 25-million-user claim

The scale figures deserve a careful read. Twenty-five million users and 850 million generations are company-reported, and they describe a platform where most users generate occasionally and a smaller core generates constantly — 6 million generations a day across 25 million users averages out to a fraction of a generation per user per day, which is consistent with a social-creator product where many accounts are casual. The commercially important cohort is agencies and professional creators producing client work at volume, and Higgsfield's product decisions — Cinema Studio for multi-minute work, pre-production storyboarding, campaign variation at scale, enterprise plans with custom credits and rollover — are aimed at that cohort rather than the casual user. The company's launch timing also matters: founded in 2025, it entered a market where AI video models were improving monthly, and its strategy from the start was aggregation plus workflow rather than training its own foundation model. That choice let it ship fast and ride every model improvement, but it also means its fate is tied to providers whose pricing and access terms it does not control.

Juicebox's product breaks into four linked pieces. Candidate Search is the front door: describe the person in plain language, get ranked, deduplicated profiles with verified contacts and a written rationale per candidate. Juicebox Agents are the always-on layer: autonomous sourcing that never sleeps on an open role, profile analysis with reasoning, adaptive learning from every approval and rejection, and follow-ups drafted for approval rather than sent blindly. Outreach is the conversion layer: verified contact data, personalized multi-step sequences, and opens, clicks, and replies tracked in one dashboard, so recruiters see which messages work. # Icarus — Solar aircraft that live in the stratosphere for weeks

Icarus (Ikaros Industries, Inc.) builds solar-powered, autonomous stratospheric aircraft — "stratospheric birds" — designed to fly above 60,000 feet for weeks without landing, providing persistent sensing and connectivity that satellites cannot match on latency and that conventional aircraft cannot match on endurance. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #40. The company was founded in 2023 by Henry Kwan, who built autonomous drones at NASA and designed spacecraft for building factories in space, after concluding that orbital mechanics constrain what space platforms can do: satellites pass overhead intermittently, roughly 10 minutes per orbit pass, while a stratospheric aircraft can loiter continuously over one area. Kwan started from first principles in a barn in upstate New York, drove a 1996 Ford Bronco to California, and assembled a team; in 2024 the vision became APOLLO, the company's first fully solar-powered, autonomous aircraft, which flew and worked. Icarus designs, manufactures, and assembles its aircraft at its Los Angeles headquarters — engineering, manufacturing, and business under one roof — and tests them at a flight development site in the Mojave Desert, where every major system is proven from launch to recovery before operational deployment. The leadership team includes a former Army Apache pilot as head of business and a TOPGUN instructor from the Navy Fighter Weapons School as head of operations. The customer is, by the company's own statement of focus, singular: one mission, one product, one customer — defense and intelligence users who need persistent overhead capability.

The company's discipline is part of the product story. Icarus states its focus as one mission, one product, one customer — a deliberate rejection of the platform sprawl that kills hardware startups, where a team splits across products before any of them works. The team reflects that focus: Kwan's background is autonomous drones at NASA and spacecraft designed to build factories in space, where he saw firsthand how orbital mechanics constrain space platforms; the head of business is a former Army Apache pilot; the head of operations is a TOPGUN instructor from the Navy Fighter Weapons School. The Los Angeles headquarters concentrates design, manufacturing, and assembly under one roof — one of the few places, the company says, where an entire stratospheric drone is designed, built, and brought to life in a single facility — and the Mojave Desert test site provides wide-open airspace and rugged terrain for rapid testing, iteration, and validation of full flight systems from launch to recovery. The culture page is blunt about who it wants: no tourists, no bystanders, only builders, with values named as hyper focus, extreme ownership, and best idea wins. Backing, per the site, comes from world-class investors, though names and amounts are not published.

## The team, the factory, and the testing regime

Hardware credibility for Icarus rests on two facts: APOLLO flew in 2024, and the company can build the next one in Los Angeles and prove it in the Mojave without waiting on outside suppliers for the airframe. That vertical integration is unusual for a startup at this stage and deliberate — stratospheric aircraft are sensitive to weight, power, and thermal design in ways that make outsourced, multi-vendor integration slow and fragile. The Mojave site's role is equally important: every major system is proven there from launch to recovery before operational deployment, which is the difference between a demonstrator and a deployable product. The open question is production rate. A single flying APOLLO proves the design; a fleet proves the factory, and Icarus has not published production numbers, delivery timelines, or the size of its order book. Its hiring posture — "if you're a fit, we'll move fast, no bureaucracy, no waiting" — suggests it is scaling the team now, ahead of announced contracts, which is a bet that demand for persistent stratospheric capability arrives on the timeline its thesis assumes.

## APOLLO: endurance, sensing, and direct-to-device comms

APOLLO's pitch rests on three capabilities that follow from stratospheric flight. Rapid aerial intelligence: ultra-high-resolution, real-time sensing with continuous pinpoint coverage, replacing the revisit gaps of satellite passes. Always-on connectivity: high-throughput, secure communications direct to device — phone or radio — above interference and infrastructure limits, without requiring a satellite terminal. Persistent wide-area coverage: monitoring more than 1,000 square miles with continuous autonomous flight for weeks, without refueling or orbit constraints. The aircraft is solar-powered and autonomous, operates above 60,000 feet where it is above weather and unreachable by most threats, and deploys in hours to station for weeks. Icarus frames the stratosphere as a forgotten frontier: explored in the Cold War with the U-2 at 70,000 feet and the SR-71 at Mach 3, then abandoned as satellites took over, now reopened by solar power, autonomy, and lightweight sensing. Its own argument for why now: commercial persistent high-altitude intelligence becomes viable as FAA rules loosen and the cost basis shifts from capital expenditure to operating expenditure — a matter of when, not if, in the company's telling.

## Icarus against satellites, HAPS rivals, and the defense primes

Icarus competes against satellite constellations on one side and other high-altitude pseudo-satellite (HAPS) efforts on the other, plus the defense primes that sell the aircraft and drones the military already flies. Against satellites, its argument is latency and persistence: no orbits, no waiting, no gaps — continuous coverage of one area rather than periodic passes. Against HAPS rivals (Airbus Zephyr, Aerostar, and similar programs), its argument is a product that has actually flown and a manufacturing base under one roof in Los Angeles, with rapid Mojave testing and iteration. Against primes, its argument is cost: extreme endurance at a fraction of the cost of crewed or large uncrewed platforms, with tactical precision from proximity that satellites cannot match. The risks are regulatory and physical: stratospheric flight operates in airspace regimes that are still being defined, solar-powered endurance depends on seasonal and latitudinal sunlight, and a single-product company lives or dies on APOLLO's reliability in operational conditions. What is not public: funding, contract values, flight-hour totals, or customer names, so Icarus's traction rests on the fact of APOLLO's flights and the team's background rather than disclosed business metrics.

# Unconventional AI — Computing with physics instead of transistors alone

Unconventional AI is rethinking the foundations of computing to bring biology-scale efficiency to artificial intelligence, and its founding claim is that the current path — scaling digital compute — will not solve AI's energy problem. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #43. Founded by experts in AI systems, analog circuits, computing theory, and neuroscience, the company builds what it calls dynamical-system hardware: AI that computes with physics — coupled oscillators, gyroscopes, springs, and differentiable physical systems — rather than simulating neural networks on conventional digital chips. The goal it states publicly is 1,000x AI compute efficiency, and its argument for why that is necessary is that memory, not compute, is the real bottleneck in AI energy efficiency: data movement dominates power consumption, and Amdahl's Law limits what faster arithmetic alone can achieve. The company pursues that goal through research it publishes openly: Un-0, an image generator powered by a simulated system of coupled oscillators, reaches FID 6.74 on ImageNet 64x64 — matching the quality of leading conventional image generation methods when they were first published — with weights, training, and ablation code all open. Its sparsity work shows coupled oscillator networks cutting up to 98.4% of connections in the Un-0 model while improving performance by 1.9 FID on the same benchmark. It has introduced DS-ISA, the first Instruction Set Architecture for dynamical system hardware, giving software a vocabulary to program AI that computes with physics. And it runs the Unconventional Grant, which drew nearly 100 submissions and awarded five projects $100,000 each in its first cohort, at Stanford, UT Austin, Yale, MIT, and UC Berkeley, funding new computational paradigms across hardware, systems, neural architectures, and theory.

## The NeuReality acquisition and the 4-dimensional roadmap

Unconventional AI's path from research to product accelerated with its acquisition of NeuReality, which added AI inference technology and a systems and silicon engineering team and, in the company's words, compressed the timeline to its 4-dimensional computing roadmap. The acquisition matters because Unconventional's core challenge is not theory but translation: turning dynamical-system prototypes into silicon that runs real inference workloads at the promised efficiency. NeuReality's inference technology and engineering team give it that bridge — systems and silicon expertise alongside its physics and neuroscience bench. The company's research agenda shows the breadth of the bet: system modeling and digital twins as the substrate for neural co-evolution, machine learning with dynamics using gyroscopes and springs for sequence classification, and rethinking the memory stack — relaxing error rates so each memory technology, from PCM to eDRAM, finds its job in the age of AI. The throughline is that the universal memory never arrived, and AI efficiency will come from matching each part of the system to the physics that suits it, rather than forcing every workload through the same digital pipeline. The company is explicit that analog is not dead but returning in mixed-signal form: future AI hardware will combine analog dynamics with digital control, and the winners will be the teams that design for that mix from the start.

## Unconventional AI against NVIDIA, analog startups, and the scaling consensus

Unconventional AI's competition is, in effect, the entire AI hardware consensus: NVIDIA's GPUs and the digital accelerator industry built around them, plus a field of analog and neuromorphic startups pursuing related efficiency bets. Its argument against the consensus is thermodynamic: scaling digital compute alone hits energy walls that no process node fully removes, because moving data costs more than computing on it. Its argument against other analog startups is breadth and openness: it publishes research, open-sources Un-0, funds outside researchers through the Grant, and is building the software layer (DS-ISA) that a whole ecosystem would need, rather than guarding a single device. The risks are the classic deep-tech ones: dynamical-system hardware must prove itself not on benchmarks but in production inference at scale, the NeuReality integration must deliver silicon on a timeline the roadmap implies, and the 1,000x efficiency goal is an aspiration, not a measured product result. The company's own research is careful on this point — Un-0 is a simulated system, and the gap between simulation and silicon is where hardware startups usually fail. What is not public: funding totals, headcount, product timelines, or any customer or deployment, so Unconventional AI should be read as a research-stage company with a hardware roadmap, not a product company with revenue.

## Open research as a strategy

The research program behind the company is unusually open for a hardware startup. Un-0's weights, training, and ablation code are public, letting other researchers verify the coupled-oscillator image generation results rather than taking them on trust. The sparsity results — cutting 98.4% of connections while improving FID by 1.9 on ImageNet 64x64 — are the kind of finding that matters beyond the company, because they suggest dynamical systems have inductive biases that make them more efficient learners, not merely more efficient hardware. The Grant program extends that openness outward, funding researchers at Stanford, UT Austin, Yale, MIT, and UC Berkeley to pursue new computational paradigms the company itself might not have chosen. It ranks LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 US #44. The platform reports more than 1 million developers using it, with workloads running across 31 global regions and more than 30 GPU SKUs, from B200s and H200s down to RTX 4090s and A40s. Its site also publishes case studies from teams running inference, agents, and fine-tuning workloads. Clusters run multi-node GPU jobs for distributed training and inference. Hub deploys open-source models and templates, and a Deployments/Models control plane manages a developer's own compute or Runpod's from one place. The use cases Runpod names are inference (real-time model serving on low-latency GPUs), agents (AI agents that run, react, and scale instantly), fine-tuning (faster training on scalable compute), and compute-heavy tasks (massive workloads with no bottlenecks). ## Pods, Serverless, and the experiment-to-production path

Runpod's core design decision is that one account covers the whole lifecycle. A developer experiments on a Pod, fine-tunes on the same infrastructure, pushes a handler to Serverless for a live inference endpoint, and scales to Clusters for distributed jobs — no migration between stages, no second vendor for production. Serverless handles the operational pieces developers would otherwise build themselves: managed orchestration that queues and distributes tasks, failover for enterprise-grade uptime, and real-time logs, monitoring, and metrics without custom frameworks. The October 2026 Batch Inference launch fills a gap in that story: not all GPU work needs real-time latency, and batching deferrable work separately from live traffic cuts cost for training-data generation, offline evaluation, and bulk processing. Runpod's own decision framework, published in October 2026, benchmarks when a Serverless endpoint costs less than an always-on Pod on a single A40, and what latency, storage, and debugging tradeoffs come with the switch — a sign the company is selling to developers who price their infrastructure carefully rather than to enterprises buying on contract. Its Fall 2026 State of AI Compute report publishes data on deployment patterns, infrastructure demand, and model scaling trends, positioning Runpod as a source of ground truth on what developers actually run.

## Runpod against AWS, CoreWeave, Lambda, and Modal

Runpod competes against the hyperscalers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) on one side and the GPU-native clouds (CoreWeave, Lambda, Together, Modal) on the other. Against hyperscalers, its argument is speed and simplicity: a GPU pod in under a minute, per-second billing, and no enterprise procurement process, for developers who want to start now. Against GPU-native rivals, its argument is breadth and the developer experience: 30-plus SKUs, 31 regions, Pods plus Serverless plus Clusters in one account, and a Hub of deployable models and templates. The 1-million-developer figure is its proof of developer adoption, though it does not disclose paying-customer counts or revenue, so the conversion from free experimentation to paid production is not visible. The developer experience is deliberately low-friction at every step. A Pod launches in under 30 seconds with the developer's own containers, framework, and code — no ticket, no procurement, no waiting for a quota increase. Serverless endpoints scale from zero to hundreds of concurrent workers in under 250 milliseconds, so a demo that goes viral does not fall over, and a quiet weekend costs nothing. That whole design reflects who Runpod serves: individual developers and small teams who measure cloud platforms by time-to-first-result, not by enterprise feature checklists. The 1-million-developer figure, the 31 regions, and the 30-plus SKUs are all chosen to signal the same thing — that whatever GPU a developer wants, wherever they are, Runpod has it available now.

Pronto sends a trained, background-verified house helper to your door in about 10 to 15 minutes. Founded in 2025 by Anjali Sardana — a former Bain Capital investor who studied biology at Georgetown and worked at 8VC — the Bengaluru company takes India's informal domestic-help market and puts structure around it: neighbourhood micro-hubs where workers wait between shifts, in-person training and background verification for every worker, called a "Pro", and an app that books, tracks and bills the visit. Customers pick from 20 services — sweeping, mopping, utensil washing, kitchen and bathroom cleaning, fridge and fan cleaning, laundry and ironing, wardrobe resets, vegetable chopping and basic meal prep — as single tasks or stacked into one visit, or as hourly slots from 30 minutes to 3 hours, booked instantly, scheduled ahead or on a recurring daily or weekly cadence. Pricing is shown live in the app for the customer's address, per task or per hourly bundle, with no per-bedroom multipliers, no advance deposits and no cash: payment runs in-app via UPI, debit and credit cards or wallets. Pronto operates in 11 cities — Bengaluru, Delhi, Faridabad, Ghaziabad, Gurgaon, Hyderabad, Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Noida, Pune and Thane — across more than 150 micromarkets, and reports handling 18,000 bookings a day, up from about 1,000 a day a year earlier, though Forbes has separately reported 46,000 regular daily bookings; the two figures are reported, not reconciled.

The booking itself is deliberately simple: pick a service or stack several into one visit, choose instant, scheduled or recurring, and pay only per visit with no setup charge for recurring bookings. That simplicity hides the operational load — recruiting, training, uniforming and rostering thousands of Pros, running micro-hubs in 150-plus neighbourhoods, and keeping arrival times honest when demand spikes. Pronto's reported growth, from about 1,000 daily bookings a year ago to 18,000 a day, and more than 500,000 bookings in its first 11 months after the May 2025 public launch, suggests the hub model can scale, but the funding history shows how expensive that scale is: $2 million at seed, $11 million in August 2025, $25 million in March 2026 and a $20 million extension two months later. The company's next test is price: promotional rates near ₹25 an hour cannot last, and the move from ₹79 and ₹99 phases to about ₹129 an hour is only the first step toward rates that cover labour, transport, hubs and management. Expansion is the other test: from one city to 10 in seven months, and now 11 cities, the company must replicate hub density street by street rather than by marketing spend, since a thin hub network cannot hit 15-minute arrivals at all. Pronto's test is whether hub density, higher prices and recorded sessions can co-exist in a business without losing the trust the model rests on. The next year answers that, street by street, hub by hub.

Micro-hubs and the 15-minute promise
The speed promise rests on a small room, not an algorithm. Pronto stations Pros in micro-hubs inside residential clusters — rooms with water, toilets and first aid — so the worker starts near the customer instead of crossing the city. Early coverage advertised 10-minute arrival; the current app listing says 15 minutes for instant bookings, and that is an arrival claim conditional on location and capacity, not the time to finish the chore. When a Pro cannot make a booking, the system reassigns automatically. Support runs 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., and cancellations made well in advance are free while late cancellations may carry a small charge for the reserved slot. The hub model is also the cost model: hubs, training, uniforms and managers are fixed costs that only pay when bookings are dense and back-to-back in the same locality.

Pros on shifts, not gig piecework
Pronto's labour pitch is the inverse of a gig marketplace. Pros work structured shifts meant to give more predictable income than informal arrangements, and the company's press kit describes health insurance, an SOS function, legal assistance and an incident-response team. That structure is the product as much as the app: customers are buying a vetted stranger in their home, and trust is the scarce resource. The core team is small — about 60 employees, with roughly 15 to 16 across engineering, product and design — while the Pro workforce scales through the hubs. Pilots now running include cooking, car washing and dog washing, with salon services under exploration, but sweeping, mopping and utensil cleaning remain the most-used services.

The discount war and the ₹129 hour
Pronto's economics are the open question. The app has charged around ₹129 for an hour of service, up from earlier ₹79 and ₹99 phases, while one analyst estimate puts labour plus transport alone near ₹116 per booking before onboarding, training, discounts and management overhead — leaving only about ₹15 of gross contribution per order in an ideal case. Promotional pricing has gone far lower: first bookings for as little as ₹1 and hourly rates near ₹25 have been reported across the instant house-help segment, where Urban Company's InstaHelp and Snabbit compete for the same customer. Snabbit reportedly went from 400 jobs a day to 50,000 in about a year. Pronto's funding — a $2 million seed, an $11 million Series A in August 2025 co-led by General Catalyst and Glade Brook Capital with Bain Capital Ventures, a $25 million Series B in March 2026 led by Epiq Capital, and a $20 million extension in May 2026 from Lachy Groom, taking disclosed funding to $58 million at a reported $200 million valuation — buys time to raise prices toward sustainability, but the segment's history says discounts end only when someone stops paying for them.

Cameras in the home: Pronto Verified and Provision Labs
The sharpest scrutiny Pronto faces is not pricing but privacy. In May 2026 it launched Pronto Verified, an opt-in service that records service sessions and uses anonymised footage for AI training, and founder Anjali Sardana has since set up Provision Labs, a US physical-AI venture focused on collecting real-world data to train and test robots and machines, backed by Lachy Groom, General Catalyst and Bain Capital Ventures. The company frames recording as opt-in and anonymised; the concern is structural — a platform that puts cameras in customers' homes and workers' workplaces, and monetises the footage as training data, is a different business from one that sells cleaning. How Pronto handles consent, retention and worker surveillance will matter more to its durability than the next funding round, because trust is the only moat in a market where the service itself is a commodity chore.

Kela is ranked #4 on LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 in Israel. Echo is an Israeli cybersecurity company that rebuilds the software supply chain so that the code enterprises run starts clean — and, since October 2026, patches flaws that AI finds before anyone else even knows they exist. Founded by Eilon Elhadad and Eylam Milner, veterans of Israel's intelligence units whose previous startup Argon was acquired by Aqua Security, Echo raised $50 million in its first ten months, including a $35 million Series A led by N47 with Notable Capital, Hyperwise Ventures and SentinelOne participating. Echo is ranked #5 on LinkedIn Top Startups 2026 in Israel. Its original product is a "software compilation factory": instead of scanning existing container images for vulnerabilities, Echo rebuilds images from source, including only essential components, hardening them with aggressive security configurations to SLSA Level 3 supply-chain standards. The result is a catalogue of more than 600 secure images — containers, libraries, OS packages and virtual machines — that the company describes as zero-vulnerability by default, with self-healing patching as new flaws appear. Named customers include UiPath, Varonis, Vectra AI and EDB.

The compilation factory is Echo's answer to a security model it considers broken. Official container images can carry more than 1,000 known vulnerabilities, most in packages the running application never uses, and security teams burn their time patching software they did not write. Echo rebuilds from source, includes only essential components, hardens configurations to SLSA Level 3, and ships a catalogue of 600-plus images whose attack surface is a fraction of the originals, with AI agents monitoring thousands of threats and patching autonomously. That is the known-CVE answer. Echo Frontier is the unknown-flaw answer, and the more consequential one: frontier models now find vulnerabilities faster than maintainers and the CVE system can respond, and Frontier runs those same models against customer software, validates findings against working exploits, backports fixes, compatibility-tests them through the full application, and delivers patched software privately before disclosure. The OpenEXR case — a high-severity flaw patched and delivered in about two days, about two months before an upstream fix — is the proof point, and the company's own cited counter-evidence, that 54% of AI-generated patches fail or introduce new flaws, is why validation rather than generation is the product. Echo's risks are the ones that come with touching a customer's supply chain: a wrong patch that breaks an application is worse than a known flaw with a workaround, and trust must be earned image by image. Its $50 million raised in ten months, its Rising in Cyber 2026 listing, and customers like UiPath, Varonis, Vectra AI and EDB suggest the market takes the thesis seriously. Whether Frontier becomes a service or a niche for the most exposed estates depends on how often frontier models find exploitable flaws in open source.

The compilation factory: rebuilding instead of patching
Echo's founding insight is that the standard approach to container security is a losing game. Official images can contain more than 1,000 known vulnerabilities, and security teams spend their time patching flaws in software they did not write and do not need — most of an image's packages are never used by the application running on it. Echo's factory compiles binaries and libraries directly from source, strips out everything non-essential, and applies hardened configurations, so the delivered image has a far smaller attack surface and a clean bill of materials. Its AI agents monitor thousands of new threats from official databases and unstructured sources like developer forums, and patch autonomously when a vulnerability appears in a component Echo ships. CEO Elhadad positions Echo as the "enterprise AI native OS", drawing the parallel to how Red Hat professionalised open-source Linux for corporate use: a hardened, curated foundation for the AI and agentic era, where every workload runs on software Echo has vetted. CTO Milner's comparison is blunter: running an official image is like plugging a computer found on the sidewalk into a corporate network.

Echo Frontier: patching AI-discovered zero-days before disclosure
Echo Frontier, launched on October 14, 2026, is the product that made Echo's LinkedIn ranking story. Frontier AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI now find vulnerabilities in open-source software faster than maintainers, scanners and the CVE system can respond — Anthropic research cited by Echo found an open-weight model producing working exploits in 50 of 410 ExploitBench attempts, close to Claude Mythos Preview's 56. Frontier runs those same frontier models against the open-source software its customers depend on, hunts for unknown flaws, validates each finding against a working exploit, develops and backports a fix, compatibility-tests it through the full application in a cloud environment, and delivers the patched software privately through JFrog or Nexus repositories — before public disclosure. Customers then move to the official upstream fix once available, in a sequence Echo calls Discover, Validate, Fix, Protect, Disclose, Converge. Echo is also an authorised CVE Numbering Authority, giving it a role in the formal disclosure process. The proof case it cites is OpenEXR, the open-source image library: Echo found a high-severity denial-of-service flaw, validated and patched it, and protected customers in about two days, roughly two months before an upstream fix appeared. The counter-evidence Echo itself cites is sobering: 1Password's Off-by-1 Labs found 54% of 6,080 AI-generated patches either failed to fix the flaw, introduced a new one, or both — which is why Frontier's validation and compatibility testing, not just patch generation, is the product.

The supply-chain bet and its limits
Echo's bet is that the software supply chain is the next enterprise security frontier, and that AI makes it urgent in both directions: AI finds flaws faster, and AI-generated patches fail more than half the time without rigorous validation. Its catalogue of 600-plus hardened images and its Frontier service are two answers to the same problem — known CVEs handled by rebuilding, unknown flaws handled by pre-disclosure patching. The risks are operational and reputational: a wrong patch that breaks a customer's application is worse than a known vulnerability with a workaround, and Echo's private-patch model depends on customers trusting a startup to modify their software supply chain. Competition includes the container-security incumbents, the cloud vendors' own hardened images, and every scanner vendor adding AI remediation. Echo's inclusion in Notable Capital's Rising in Cyber 2026 list, alongside 13 other Israeli companies, and its $50 million raised in under a year, suggest the market takes the thesis seriously. Whether Frontier becomes a standard enterprise service or a niche for the most exposed software estates depends on how often frontier models actually find exploitable flaws in widely used open source — and on Echo never shipping a patch that breaks what it was meant to protect.

# Notch — AI agents for regulated insurance operations

Notch (notch.cx) builds an AI operating system for insurers, brokers, managing general agents, and financial institutions — the companies whose daily work is high-stakes, document-heavy, and bound by compliance rules. Its platform has three parts that work together: an AI Workspace where human teams handle the decisions in front of them, an AI Workforce of agents that run the repeatable work end to end, and ADAM (AI Dialogue and Automation Mindframe), the operating brain that connects agents, teams, workflows, and business systems into one governed foundation. Notch sells to carriers, MGAs, and brokers, and it makes money on enterprise contracts sold through demos, with approval gates in front of every agent action so nothing moves without a traceable, audit-ready record. LinkedIn ranked Notch #7 on its 2026 Top Startups list for Israel. The pitch that matters is narrow: regulated operations cannot hand work to generic chatbots, because every intake, claim, and servicing decision has to be compliant, traceable, and accurate — Notch's whole product is built around that constraint, and its go-live claim is 4 to 6 weeks to production. Pricing is not published; sales are enterprise-contract only. Notch at notch.cx is not the similarly named marketing-automation startup at usenotch.ai. The customer stories show the same pattern in different corners of insurance. Phoenix, a $173 billion EMEA insurance group, deployed governed AI agents across voice, web, app, and text to transform policy servicing in weeks. EarnIn turned employer-specific support knowledge into agents that process more than 1,000 payroll documents a week. A global broker automated carrier-report reconciliation and cut manual work by 75%, shrank its backlog by half, and reduced cases needing a human by 65%. Notch's own site figures are 99% submission intake accuracy, 22 million production interactions, and servicing time six times faster. The company has more than 90 people across Tel Aviv and New York, says dozens of enterprise customers run on Notch in production, and raised a $30 million Series A in March 2026 led by Headline, bringing total funding to $45 million. Its pricing philosophy is outcome-based: the TRUE Model — Ticket Resolved, Unmanned, End-to-end — charges for full case resolution rather than per-seat software, though no price list is published. Workspace, Workforce, and ADAM
The Workspace is where staff work alongside AI on the case in front of them: documents get chased, compared, and summarized, and the agent drafts replies and routes work while the human decides. ## Submission intake, claims, and servicing in practice
Notch's published customer stories show where the platform actually runs. EarnIn processes more than 1,000 payroll documents a week through Notch, after turning employer-specific support knowledge into dependable agents. ## The MGA origin and why governance is the product
Notch was founded in 2021 and first launched as an MGA itself, going live in 47 states backed by partnerships with Hartford Steam Boiler and Munich Re. The software the team built to solve its own MGA problems became the Notch platform, and the company retired the MGA to sell the platform. That origin is the reason governance is the product rather than a feature: the founders ran insurance operations first, then built the tools they wished they had. The company now has more than 90 people across Tel Aviv and New York, and says dozens of enterprise customers run on Notch in production. Its first Tier 1 carrier deployment and its New York office both came after the pivot from MGA to platform.

## Rivals: Fin, Zendesk, Salesforce, and the gen-1 support vendors
Notch's competitive fight is against first-generation support automation — Fin, Zendesk, and Salesforce are the names its own coverage cites it winning contracts against — and against insurers building in-house. The argument Notch makes is that gen-1 tools resolve simple tickets but cannot run regulated back-office workflows end to end with auditability. Its pricing philosophy points the same way: Notch introduced the TRUE Model — Ticket Resolved, Unmanned, End-to-end — aligning price with outcomes so customers pay for full case resolution rather than per-seat software. Whether outcome pricing holds up at Tier 1 carrier scale is the open commercial question; the company has not published price lists or per-customer economics.

## Traction and funding
Notch announced a $30 million Series A on March 25, 2026, led by Headline with Lightspeed Venture Partners, Jibe Ventures, Illuminate Financial, and Phoenix Insurance, bringing total funding raised to $45 million. ## Pricing by outcome, not by seat
Notch's TRUE Model deserves its own note because it changes what the customer is buying. Traditional enterprise software charges per seat or per module, which rewards the vendor when usage grows regardless of results. Outcome pricing charges for resolved cases, which aligns the vendor with the customer's metric — fewer open tickets, faster servicing, cleaner intake. The risk is definitional: what counts as "resolved, unmanned, end to end" has to be agreed case by case, and a carrier that disputes resolutions will dispute invoices. # Mate Security — the agentic SOC built on a Security Context Graph

Mate Security (mate.security) sells an AI-native security operations center to enterprises whose security teams are drowning in alerts that human analysts can no longer triage at machine speed. Its product is an open platform of AI agents that detect, investigate, respond to, and hunt threats as one continuous cycle, and its core claim is architectural: agents fail when they are fed data structured for humans, so Mate first rebuilds a customer's security knowledge into a Security Context Graph — a graph of "memories" that captures how an organization actually investigates — and only then lets agents reason over it. Mate was founded in early 2025 in Tel Aviv by CEO Asaf Wiener, chief product officer Oren Saban, and CTO Guy Pergal, veterans of Wiz, Microsoft, Axonius, and Apex, and it sells to Fortune 500 enterprises and managed security providers on enterprise contracts; pricing is not published. LinkedIn ranked Mate Security #8 on its 2026 Top Startups list for Israel. The company says it has grown more than 500% since the third quarter of 2025, has raised more than $50 million, and employs around 50 people, with about 40 in Israel and the rest in the United States. The product's operating loop is continuous detection and continuous response: detections compress into investigations, and investigations feed the next detection, so both stay rooted in the customer's changing reality instead of decaying like static rules. Mate claims its platform investigates 100% of the alert queue, including informational alerts, closes false positives itself, and cuts mean time to respond sharply — one company-published chart shows MTTR falling from about 2,300 minutes to about 100 minutes over five months. Customers named on Mate's site include Bridgewater Associates, Merlin Entertainments, OCBC, and AlphaSense, where the CISO says nearly 100% of investigations moved into Mate, and Water-IT, a managed security provider that says Mate made it stack-agnostic. In August 2026 Mate added Gamebooks, structured investigation procedures that bound what agents may do: what to investigate, what evidence to establish, when to change course, which actions are permitted, and when to escalate, stop, or seek approval. Funding is a $15.5 million seed in November 2025 and a $35 million Series A in July 2026 led by Canaan Partners, and Mate joined the 2026 Cybersecurity Startup Accelerator run by CrowdStrike, AWS, and NVIDIA. The Security Context Graph and Reason Mining
When Mate integrates with a customer, it builds that customer's context graph within 24 hours, ingesting SIEM logs, tickets, documentation, SOPs, CMDB records, messaging apps, and configurations. Mate's investors include Canaan Partners, Microsoft's M12, Insight Partners, and Team8.                                                                                                                                                                        

## Gamebooks: procedure wrapped around agent reasoning
In August 2026 Mate launched Gamebooks, its investigation framework for AI agents, and the distinction from old SOAR playbooks is the point. A Gamebook is a structured investigation procedure that specifies five things: what must be investigated, what evidence must be established, which conditions change the course of the investigation, which actions are permitted, and when an agent must escalate, stop, or request approval. Mate's summary line is "deterministic where it matters, dynamic where it helps": agents reason and adapt, but inside procedures the customer controls and can extend with its own requirements, while Mate owns the agent engineering, evaluation, testing, and execution as models and environments change. Gamebooks are the third foundation Mate has introduced, after the Security Context Graph and its continuous detection / continuous response framework.

## Continuous detection, continuous response
Mate's operating loop is CD/CR: detections compress into investigations, and investigations feed the next detection, so both stay rooted in the customer's changing reality instead of decaying like static rules. The company claims its platform investigates 100% of the alert queue, including informational alerts, closes false positives itself, and reduces mean time to respond — one company-published chart shows MTTR falling from about 2,300 minutes in January to about 100 minutes in May, a 93% reduction. Customers named on Mate's site include Bridgewater Associates, Merlin Entertainments, OCBC, and AlphaSense, where the CISO says nearly 100% of investigations moved into Mate, and Water-IT, a managed security provider that says Mate made it stack-agnostic and expanded its addressable market. Mate integrates with SIEM, EDR, email security, and the rest of the existing stack rather than replacing it.

## Agentic SOC rivals and the trust problem
Mate's market is the crowded AI SOC field, where every vendor promises autonomous triage and the buyer objection is always the same: can an agent be trusted to act? Mate's answer is structural — a context graph built before any agent runs, plus Gamebooks that bound what agents may do — rather than a bigger model. Its backers and channels reinforce the enterprise pitch: a $15.5 million seed in November 2025 led by Team8 with Insight Partners, then a $35 million Series A in July 2026 led by Canaan Partners with Microsoft's M12, Insight Partners, and Team8, and participation in the 2026 Cybersecurity Startup Accelerator run by CrowdStrike, AWS, and NVIDIA. The risk to the thesis is concentration: if the graph is wrong about an organization, every agent downstream inherits the error, and Mate's public evidence is customer testimonials and company charts rather than independent benchmarks.

## What Mate does not replace
Mate layers over the existing security stack rather than replacing it. SIEMs still collect logs, EDRs still sit on endpoints, email security still filters mail, and SOAR playbooks still exist for the workflows customers choose to keep. What changes is who reads the output: Mate's agents, fed by the context graph, triage and investigate across those tools instead of analysts opening six consoles. The analyst's job shifts to supervisor — guiding agents, handling the escalations Gamebooks route upward, and owning the decisions agents document. That shift is the adoption risk: a SOC that buys Mate but keeps its old triage process running in parallel gets two systems and the cost of both, while a SOC that hands the queue to Mate has to trust the graph on day one.

# Eon — turning cloud backups from dead storage into a queryable data lake

Eon (eon.io) sells cloud backup posture management to large enterprises whose data is scattered across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud and whose backups have historically been write-only: expensive insurance that nobody can search, use, or restore quickly. Eon's platform autonomously scans, maps, and classifies a customer's cloud resources, then makes the backed-up data visible, searchable, and usable — for instant file-level recovery, for ransomware and disaster recovery, and as a queryable data lake that feeds AI and analytics. The company was founded in January 2024 in New York and Tel Aviv by Ofir Ehrlich, Gonen Stein, and Ron Kimchi, the team behind CloudEndure, which AWS acquired in 2019 after the founders had run its disaster recovery technology inside AWS. Eon sells enterprise contracts to large companies; pricing is not published. LinkedIn ranked Eon #9 on its 2026 Top Startups list for Israel. Its funding pace is the story in itself: $500 million raised since founding, with a $300 million Series D in December 2025 at a $4 billion valuation, against revenue that Globes estimated only in the millions up to about $10 million — a multiple the same coverage called very high. Deployment is deliberately light: a single read-only IAM role, with no agents, appliances, or clusters inside the customer's environment, and continuous discovery across accounts so backup policy applies automatically — including to the buckets and databases no policy currently covers. Recovery is granular: individual objects and database records restored without rebuilding the surrounding environment, which is what separates Eon from whole-environment restore tooling. The funding history is unusually fast: a $20 million pre-launch round led by Sequoia, a further $30 million led by Lightspeed, a $77 million Series B in summer 2024 at a $750 million valuation, a $70 million round in November 2025 led by BOND at $1.4 billion, and the $300 million Series D in December 2025 led by Elad Gil's Gil Capital at $4 billion, with Sequoia, Lightspeed, Greenoaks, and others participating. Globes counts one of the largest banks in the United States among Eon's customers, unnamed, with another significant contract reported close to signing, and estimates revenue only in the millions up to about $10 million — a multiple the same coverage called very high. From backup jobs to a queryable data lake
Traditional backup tooling answers one question — can we restore after a failure — and does it slowly, per account, per region, per cloud. Eon's pitch is that the backup copy is the most complete copy of an enterprise's data, and it should behave like a database: scanned once, classified, and then searchable across clouds so teams can find a file, a record, or a dataset without rebuilding the environment around it. Eon's investors include Sequoia, Lightspeed, Greenoaks, and Gil Capital.                                     

## How Eon deploys: one read-only role, no agents
Deployment is deliberately light: a single read-only IAM role, with no agents, appliances, or clusters running inside the customer's environment. Eon discovers resources continuously across accounts and applies backup policy automatically, which addresses the coverage problem that per-account native configuration creates — the buckets and databases no policy covers. Because the platform controls backup posture centrally, it can enforce consistent policy across clouds instead of relying on each team to configure its own native tooling. For recovery, the emphasis is granularity: individual objects and database records restored without rebuilding the surrounding environment, which is what separates Eon from whole-environment restore tooling in third-party comparisons.

## The CloudEndure lineage and the AWS connection
Ehrlich and Stein co-founded CloudEndure in 2013, built technology for moving workloads into the cloud and recovering them, and sold it to AWS in 2019 for a reported $200 million after raising only about $18 million. At AWS they met Kimchi, who had run disaster recovery and cloud migration in Israel on CloudEndure technology. Eon is, in effect, the same team's second attempt at the same problem from the opposite direction: CloudEndure moved data into the cloud, Eon manages and activates the data once it is there. That lineage is also the investor story — Sequoia led the $20 million pre-launch round, Lightspeed led a further $30 million, the Series B in summer 2024 raised $77 million at a $750 million valuation, a $70 million round in November 2025 led by BOND reached $1.4 billion, and the December 2025 Series D led by Elad Gil's Gil Capital tripled the valuation to $4 billion, with Sequoia, Lightspeed, Greenoaks, Eight Roads, Vine, and Meron Capital among the backers.

## Druva, Commvault, and the incumbent backup vendors
Eon's named competitors are the established data protection vendors: Druva, the cloud-native platform from 2008, and Commvault, the public company founded in 1996. The competitive argument is not that incumbents cannot back up data — they can — but that their backups remain passive storage, while Eon's are queryable and AI-ready. The risk runs the other way: the incumbents have decades of enterprise relationships, and Eon's valuation demands growth far faster than its reported revenue. Globes noted Eon may be growing faster than even Wiz did at the same stage, and also that its revenue multiple is very high. Eon's granular restore — a file, a record, a dataset, without rebuilding the environment — shortens that conversation from days to minutes, and its continuous discovery answers the follow-up question about coverage gaps. The AI-and-analytics argument is the expansion revenue: once the backup copy is queryable, teams that never cared about backup start querying it. # Encore AI — revenue agents trained on a company's own calls

Encore AI trains AI agents on the customer conversations a company has already had — its recorded calls, emails, and text messages, joined to its CRM data — and then deploys those agents to sell, collect, and serve like its best employees do. The company, founded in 2022 as Insait IO by CEO Dvir Ginzburg and rebranded as Encore AI in July 2026, is headquartered in New York with presence across APAC and EMEA, and it sells to enterprises in regulated industries, mostly financial institutions. Its agents work autonomously or alongside live teams across voice, chat, SMS, WhatsApp, IVR, and live form-fill, converting leads, closing applications, recovering balances, and driving upsell and cross-sell. Encore sells enterprise contracts; pricing is not published. LinkedIn ranked Encore AI #11 on its 2026 Top Startups list for Israel. The company says it has more than 40 enterprise customers globally and that annual recurring revenue is up more than five times since its seed round less than eighteen months ago; it does not disclose absolute revenue or valuation. The mechanics are specific. Encore ingests call recordings, emails, and text messages, joins them to CRM data, splits customer journeys into stages, and identifies which rep behaviors at each stage produced successful outcomes — explanations, responses, examples, even the jokes and anecdotes top relationship managers use. Those behaviors become playbooks, and playbooks become agents that work autonomously or assist live staff with suggested responses during conversations, across voice, chat, SMS, WhatsApp, IVR, and live form-fill. The agents convert leads, close applications, recover balances, and drive upsell and cross-sell, and they go live in weeks because they build from the company's actual operating reality instead of from scripts. Encore says it has more than 40 enterprise customers globally, mostly financial institutions, with annual recurring revenue up more than five times since its seed round less than eighteen months ago, without disclosing absolute revenue or valuation. The $30 million Series A in July 2026 was led by Team8 with Planven and The Garage, alongside Lukatz and several large banks and insurers that first came on as customers and invested after seeing the impact. Interaction Mining: the call archive as training data
Encore's core technology is what Ginzburg calls Interaction Mining, and it is patented. The platform ingests call recordings, emails, and text messages, connects them to CRM systems, splits customer journeys into stages, and works out which rep behaviors at each stage actually produced successful outcomes. Those behaviors — explanations, responses, examples, conversational styles, even the jokes and anecdotes top relationship managers use — become playbooks, and the playbooks become agents. Encore's investors include Team8, Planven, and The Garage.                                                     

## Revenue agents vs deflection bots
Encore's positioning is a deliberate inversion of the support-automation market. Most AI agents are built to deflect calls and reduce the number of customers who ever reach a human. Encore's are built to increase revenue from every customer interaction. The distinction matters commercially: deflection bots are bought by cost centers and measured on tickets avoided, while Encore's agents are bought by revenue teams and measured on applications closed, balances recovered, and cross-sells completed. The agents also work in assist mode, recommending responses and tactics to employees during live conversations, so a company can deploy them as copilots before trusting them autonomously. The open question is whether interaction mining travels beyond sales into compliance coaching and customer support inside the same accounts — Encore's next test, by its own coverage's account.

## Regulated sales: compliance as the moat and the risk
Encore's early base is concentrated in financial services, where sales interactions involve complex products, compliance requirements, and long customer journeys. That concentration is both moat and exposure: regulated call data is hard for competitors to obtain and harder to handle, since recordings from financial customers move under US and EU privacy rules, and the reporting on Encore does not detail retention, consent, or how recordings are governed. The company's claim is that its agents meet the compliance requirements of the most stringent regulated environments, and its investor list supports the enterprise story — the $30 million Series A in July 2026 was led by Team8 with Planven and The Garage, alongside Lukatz and several large commercial banks and insurers that first came on as customers and invested after seeing the platform's impact on their own operations.

## Salesforce, SAP, Zoho, HubSpot building the same layer
Encore's structural risk is that the CRM vendors already own the data it mines. Salesforce, SAP, Zoho, and HubSpot are all adding AI agents to their platforms, and they sit on the customer records Encore connects to. Encore's counterargument is that records are not conversations: CRM data says what happened, while call archives say how the best rep made it happen, and that behavioral layer is what its agents replicate. Whether buyers agree will show up in the next two things to watch: whether Encore's 40-plus customers expand from one workflow to several, and whether any large CRM vendor acquires or clones the interaction-mining approach instead of partnering for it.

## The assist-first deployment path
Encore's assist mode is the deployment path most regulated buyers actually take. Before trusting an agent to talk to customers autonomously, a bank or insurer runs it beside live staff, suggesting responses and tactics during real conversations, and measures whether the suggestions match what top performers would say. That trial is low-risk and high-signal: it tests the playbooks against live traffic without exposing customers to an unsupervised agent, and it gives compliance teams transcripts to review. If the assist phase works, autonomy follows workflow by workflow — collections first, then sales, then the complex applications. If it does not, the buyer still keeps a coaching tool. The assist-first path is also why Encore's ARR growth claim is plausible without a large customer count: expansion inside 40-plus accounts matters more than logo count.

# Limitless Labs — physical AI for CNC manufacturing

Limitless Labs (limitless-labs.ai) builds AI for precision manufacturing: software that turns a 3D design into the instructions that guide a machine through cutting and shaping a mechanical part. Its product is an agentic physical AI platform for CAD/CAM — the computer-aided design and manufacturing software that programs CNC machines — built on a foundation model trained not on text but on the physics of metal cutting, CAD geometry, and the operational constraints of real machines. The company was formerly LimitlessCNC, is based in Tel Aviv with an office in Oradell, New Jersey, and is led by CEO David Priev with chief scientist Shahaf Finder and CTO Assaf Peleg. Limitless sells enterprise software to manufacturers; pricing is not published. LinkedIn ranked Limitless Labs #12 on its 2026 Top Startups list for Israel, listing 35 employees. The claim that sets it apart is deployment: production use at Blue Origin and Cadillac F1, which is rare for industrial AI at Series A stage. The product surface is a CAM Agent that works inside Mastercam, NX, and Creo, the CAD/CAM systems engineers already use: it identifies machinable features in a design, recommends tools, sequences operations, and generates toolpaths that produce shop-floor-ready programs. The company says it cuts CNC programming time by up to 50%, which matters because programming is the bottleneck between design and part — a design drawn in hours can take days to program, and every program carries the risk of a production-stopping error. Production deployments at Blue Origin and Cadillac F1 are the proof points, in environments where a bad toolpath destroys expensive hardware or misses a race deadline. The platform is ITAR-compliant and deployable on AWS GovCloud, which is what lets it into defence and aerospace shops. Limitless raised $4.1 million in March 2025 and a $20 million Series A in June 2026 co-led by Dell Technologies Capital and Square Peg Capital, with Grove Ventures, Meron Capital, and Kinetica participating, and counts about 35 employees. A foundation model trained on metal cutting, not text
Most AI foundation models learn from language. Limitless's learns from machining: how metal behaves under a cutter, what geometries are machinable, which tools suit which features, and what real machines can and cannot do. That is the company's central technical bet — that CNC programming knowledge, which today lives in the heads of a small number of experienced programmers who are hard to find and impossible to scale, can be captured in a model the way language knowledge was captured in LLMs. The platform is described as the world's first agentic physical AI platform for CAD/CAM in mechanical manufacturing, and the company says it cuts CNC programming time by up to 50%. Limitless's investors include Dell Technologies Capital and Square Peg.                                                                                              

## The CAM Agent inside Mastercam, NX, and Creo
The product surface is a CAM Agent that works inside the CAD/CAM systems engineers already use — Mastercam, NX, and Creo — rather than asking shops to adopt a new platform. The agent identifies machinable features in a design, recommends tools, sequences operations, and generates toolpaths that produce shop-floor-ready programs. The workflow matters because CNC programming is the bottleneck between design and part: a design that takes hours to draw can take days to program, and every program carries the risk of a production-stopping error if a tool, speed, or sequence is wrong. By putting expert-level CAM knowledge at every programmer's fingertips, Limitless argues it lets junior programmers produce senior-grade programs and lets senior programmers spend their time on the hardest parts instead of the routine ones.

## Blue Origin, Cadillac F1, and defence-grade deployment
Production deployments at Blue Origin and Cadillac F1 are Limitless's strongest evidence, because both are environments where a bad toolpath destroys expensive hardware or misses a race deadline. Aerospace and motorsport parts are high-complexity, low-volume, and unforgiving — exactly the segment where programming time dominates and where a 50% cut matters most. The ITAR compliance and GovCloud deployment options point to the same market: defence and aerospace manufacturers whose work cannot leave controlled infrastructure. The risk is symmetric: any security lapse or machining failure in a defence or aerospace context could end the business, and the company is still small — around 35 people — selling into organizations with procurement cycles far longer than its own fundraising cycles.

## Why CNC programming is the bottleneck
Precision manufacturing is one of the most knowledge-intensive disciplines in modern industry, and its experts are scarce. A shop's throughput is set not by its machines but by the programmers who tell those machines what to do, and the knowledge those programmers carry — which tool for which alloy, which sequence avoids chatter, how to hold tolerance on a thin wall — is rarely written down. Limitless raised a $4.1 million round in March 2025, then a $20 million Series A in June 2026 co-led by Dell Technologies Capital and Square Peg Capital, with Grove Ventures, Meron Capital, and Kinetica participating. The funding question is whether a physics-trained model can generalize across the long tail of machines, materials, and parts fast enough to outrun larger automation incumbents building the same capability.

## The programmer shortage behind the product
Limitless's market exists because CNC programmers are scarce and getting scarcer. The programmers who master precision machining are experienced, hard to find, and impossible to scale, in the company's own framing — and every machine shop's throughput is set by how many programs its programmers can produce, not by how many machines it owns. A junior programmer with Limitless's CAM Agent can produce senior-grade programs, and a senior programmer can spend time on the hardest parts instead of the routine ones. That is the economic argument a shop owner understands immediately: the product does not replace programmers, it multiplies the ones you have. The counterargument is deskilling — if the model is wrong about a tool or a sequence, a junior operator may not catch it — which is why production deployments at Blue Origin and Cadillac F1 matter more than any benchmark: they prove the output survives expert review.

# Adaptive6 — treating cloud waste like a vulnerability

Adaptive6 sells cloud cost governance to enterprises whose cloud bills keep growing while nobody can say which code is responsible. Its platform — Cloud Cost Governance and Optimization, or CCGO — scans cloud environments in real time, traces waste back to the specific lines of code and the developer who wrote them, and routes fixes directly into engineers' workflows through Jira, Slack, or ServiceNow. The company borrows its playbook from cybersecurity: instead of finance dashboards that highlight problems nobody can fix, Adaptive6 treats waste like a vulnerability to be scanned, traced, and patched. It was founded in Tel Aviv by CEO Aviv Revach, Eyal Brosh, and CTO Omer Muller; Revach is a former Israeli Military Intelligence Unit 8200 security researcher and former head of strategy at Taboola, and Revach and Brosh previously sold Commerce Sciences to Taboola. Adaptive6 sells enterprise contracts; pricing is not published. LinkedIn ranked Adaptive6 #13 on its 2026 Top Startups list for Israel. Its customers include Ticketmaster, Bayer, and Norstella, and the company claims 15% to 35% reductions in total cloud spend at deployed enterprises. The distinctive move is attribution. Most cost tools stop at the resource — this cluster costs too much — while Adaptive6 continues to the code: this commit, by this developer, created the waste, and here is the fix, routed personally to that developer in Jira, Slack, or ServiceNow. The platform hunts Shadow Waste, the hidden inefficiencies in architecture, application logic, or outdated software versions that traditional tools miss because they look for idle servers while the wasteful resources stay busy. It operates agentlessly through standard cloud APIs, scanning AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure plus Databricks, Snowflake, and Kubernetes, and it analyzes provisioned throughput for AI workloads so engineers commit only to the capacity they need. It also integrates with CI/CD pipelines to block costly architectures before deployment, like a security scanner for spend. Customers include Ticketmaster, Bayer, and Norstella, the company claims 15% to 35% reductions in total cloud spend, and it announced $44 million in funding at its January 2026 emergence from stealth, including a $28 million Series A led by U.S. Venture Partners. Shadow Waste: the cost FinOps dashboards cannot see
Adaptive6's central concept is Shadow Waste: hidden inefficiencies buried in architecture, application logic, or outdated software versions that traditional cost tools miss because they look for idle servers and over-provisioned resources. A misconfigured workload, an inefficient query pattern, or an old library version can burn money for months while every dashboard shows green, because the resources are busy — just wastefully. Adaptive6's investors include U.S. Venture Partners.                                                                                                       

## Cloud-to-code tracing and the Jira ticket to the right developer
The product's distinctive move is attribution. Most cost tools stop at the resource: this cluster costs too much. Adaptive6 continues to the code: this commit, by this developer, created the waste, and here is the fix. The recommendation goes personally to the developer who wrote the code, in the tool they already work in, which is why the company frames the problem as engineering rather than finance. Finance teams cannot rewrite code; developers can, but only if they know which of their changes cost money. In one case the company cites, correcting a single misconfiguration saved more than $1 million in annual cloud costs — a company claim, not an audited figure, but a useful illustration of how concentrated cloud waste can be.

## Shift-left cost checks in CI/CD
Adaptive6 is also proactive: it integrates with CI/CD pipelines to block costly architectures before deployment, the way a security scanner flags vulnerable code before it ships. The shift-left argument lands harder as AI-generated code spreads, because generated code is often inefficient in ways its author never reviewed — the company argues that tools like Amazon Bedrock and AI coding assistants increase waste rather than solving it, since they produce code that ignores resource efficiency. The industry context supports the size of the problem: public cloud spend keeps rising sharply, and Flexera's State of the Cloud reporting has put wasted spend at up to 32% of enterprise cloud budgets, while Adaptive6's own framing puts total industry waste at about $200 billion a year out of $1 trillion in cloud spending.

## Finout, CloudZero, Turbonomic, and the FinOps field
Adaptive6 does not operate in a vacuum. The FinOps field includes Cloudability (sold to IBM), CloudZero, and the Israeli startup Finout, which Adaptive6's coverage explicitly contrasts: Finout and its peers manage cost reporting, while Adaptive6 manages consumption at the code level. Its closest competitive comparison, by Globes's account, is Turbonomic, acquired by IBM for $1.8 billion, which also optimizes resource consumption automatically. Adaptive6 announced $44 million in funding at its January 2026 emergence from stealth, including a $28 million Series A led by U.S. Venture Partners. The open question is whether code-level attribution scales beyond the largest enterprises: the product's value depends on engineering teams actually acting on its tickets, and that depends on whether cost becomes an engineering metric or stays a finance report.

## AI-generated code as a new waste source
Adaptive6's timing argument is that AI coding assistants made its problem worse. Generated code is often inefficient in ways its author never reviewed: over-provisioned resources, redundant queries, outdated patterns, and architectures chosen for convenience rather than cost. A developer who writes ten lines by hand reviews them; a developer who accepts a thousand generated lines reviews almost none. Adaptive6 argues that tools like Amazon Bedrock and AI co-workers increase waste rather than solving it, because they produce code that ignores resource efficiency. Whether that claim holds across the industry, the direction is clear: as more code is generated rather than written, the cost of that code becomes a property of the generator, and someone has to audit it. Adaptive6 wants to be that auditor, embedded in the pipeline rather than in the finance department.

Sphere, Hero, and Atlas
Dream's product line has three parts. Sphere, its first product, provides AI-enabled cyber defence for governments and critical infrastructure, built to think like both a defender and an attacker. Hero finds and patches software vulnerabilities autonomously. Atlas, launched in June 2026, is the sovereign AI platform: it connects government data and deploys models inside government-controlled environments, so a state can build and run dedicated AI models on its own infrastructure without relying on external cloud providers. ## Sovereign AI: models on the customer's own iron
The sovereign AI argument is that AI has become critical infrastructure, and a country that depends on American providers for its models risks having access curtailed or its most sensitive data exposed to foreign systems. Dream's answer is technological sovereignty with zero foreign reliance for AI and cyber defence: models the customer controls, data the vendor cannot see, deployment on infrastructure the customer owns, including GPU clusters that press coverage describes as hundreds of Blackwell 200 GPUs. ## The NSO past and the trust argument
Dream's founding story is also its largest liability. Hulio led NSO Group for a decade before leaving in 2022. NSO's Pegasus spyware was used to hack the phones of journalists, activists, and officials around the world, the company was later blacklisted by the US government, and it lost a lawsuit brought by WhatsApp over Pegasus-related hacks. Dream's pitch is the defensive inversion: the same offensive expertise, applied to shielding nations and vital infrastructure rather than surveilling targets. Reuters's coverage of the June 2026 round drew that contrast directly. Whether governments accept it depends on whether they judge Dream by its products or by its founder's record — and the fact that Dream sells to more than a dozen countries suggests many have already decided, while the Financial Times headline framing the pitch as "Pegasus spyware founder urges governments to trust his tech" shows how the other half of the argument will always be made.

Dream does not publish its customer list, which is normal for government cyber work and also convenient: the claim of a dozen-plus countries cannot be checked against named deployments beyond the two Atlas countries. Atlas being live in two countries is both Dream's strongest proof point and its most frustrating disclosure. Two live sovereign AI deployments mean the platform works outside a demo: real government data, real infrastructure, real models running under customer control. But the countries are unnamed, the scale is undisclosed, and the difference between a pilot and a national deployment is enormous. The two-country figure should be read as evidence that Atlas is real software with real users, not as evidence of market dominance. What would change the assessment is a named deployment at national scale, or a second funding round explicitly tied to Atlas expansion rather than to the broader cyber defence business.

Synctera is a banking-as-a-service and embedded finance platform that lets companies build and launch banking products without becoming a bank. Its platform brings three kinds of businesses together — fintechs that want to offer financial services, sponsor banks that provide the legal framework and regulated infrastructure, and service vendors that supply specialized pieces like card production and identity checks — and manages their interactions through one set of APIs and a dashboard called the Synctera Console. Synctera was launched in 2020, is a technology company rather than a bank, and sells platform contracts to banks and fintechs; pricing is not published. LinkedIn ranked Synctera #2 on its 2025 Top Startups list for the United States. Its pitch is compliance as a product: in sponsor banking, the bank carries the regulatory risk, so the platform that gives the bank complete visibility and control over every fintech program it sponsors is the platform that gets deals done. The platform's product families cover the full stack of a banking program: ledger and customer views, card issuance and processing, money movement through ACH transfers and mobile remote deposit capture, and risk services including KYC verification, document verification, and transaction fraud monitoring, all exposed as REST APIs alongside the Synctera Console where humans at both the fintech and the sponsor bank work — operators handling customer updates and card reissuance, administrators managing API keys, logs, and webhooks, and bank overseers watching transaction activity, KYC status, AML alerts, and reconciliation reports in real time. Matching a fintech to a sponsor bank
The first step in a fintech's relationship with Synctera is onboarding, during which Synctera determines what banking resources the fintech needs, finds a sponsor bank that can provide them, and establishes the business relationship between the two. That matching is a real service, not a directory: sponsor banks differ in risk appetite, geography, and product focus, and a mismatch kills programs. ## The Ledger, the Cards API, and money movement
Synctera's products cover the full stack of a banking program. Its native services include setting up customers and accounts, reconciling transactions with the sponsor bank, and reporting compliance activities. Its product families include ledger and customer views, card issuance and processing, money movement through ACH transfers and mobile remote deposit capture, and risk services including KYC verification, document verification, and transaction fraud monitoring. The REST APIs expose each piece directly: Customers and Accounts APIs for records and relationships, KYC Verification, Disclosures, and Watchlist APIs for compliance, Transactions and Remote Check Deposit APIs for money movement, and Cards APIs for issuing, activating, and managing cards. Vendor services — debit card creation, KYC checks, card transaction processing — are available through the platform without separate setup, contracts, or connections. The Synctera Console is the browser-based interface where humans at both the fintech and the sponsor bank work with the platform.
