The platform sits alongside a bank's existing core system and requires no direct core integration, which is the selling point for community banks that want sponsor banking revenue without a core conversion. Synctera's market is embedded finance: every non-bank brand that wants to offer accounts, cards, or payments, and every community bank that wants the deposits and fees from sponsoring those programs. # Underdog Sports — fantasy contests, then a federally regulated prediction market

Underdog Sports, founded in 2020 by CEO Jeremy Levine, is a sports gaming company that started in daily fantasy sports and became, in July 2026, the first sports company to hold a complete prediction market license stack of its own. Its app — renamed "Underdog: Sports, Games & Rips," with underdogfantasy.com now redirecting to underdogsports.com — runs fantasy contests across more than a dozen sports led by the NFL, NBA, and MLB, and an exchange where users trade event contracts. Pick'em sets a projection for a player stat and the user picks higher or lower, with fixed payouts; Champions is a related player-stat format; Best Ball is a season-long snake draft where the roster is set once and scoring is automatic; and draft tournaments include Battle Royale, Sit & Go, and Weekly Winners, plus Ladders and promotional Gimme Picks. Availability is a patchwork: Best Ball reaches 41 states plus Washington DC, classic Pick'em only 15 states, and the prediction market exchange 38 states, with nine states blocked entirely. The app holds 4.8 stars from 327,000 iOS ratings. Pick'em, Champions, and Best Ball
Underdog's fantasy products are fourfold. Pick'em is the flagship: the platform sets a projection for a player stat — passing yards, points, rebounds — and the user picks higher or lower, with fixed payouts that do not change based on the pick direction. Champions is a related player-stat format. Best Ball is a season-long snake draft game: draft a roster before or early in the season, never touch it again, and scoring is automatic, with the best performers counting each week. The app also runs draft tournaments including Battle Royale, Sit & Go, and Weekly Winners, plus variants like Ladders for higher-upside multi-leg entries and Gimme Picks, promotional picks treated as winners regardless of the athlete's performance. Underdog's CEO and co-founder is Jeremy Levine.                          

## The prediction market exchange: a full CFTC license stack
Underdog's exchange is the strategic leap. It launched its own prediction market exchange on July 18, 2026, after acquiring the Aristotle Exchange clearing and market entities, and it operates the exchange under Designated Contract Market status with CFTC oversight — the first sports company holding the complete license stack, by its own account. Before that, Underdog partnered with external exchanges including Crypto.com and Kalshi; owning the exchange gives it control over pricing, features, and rollout. The exchange lists event contracts on sports and other topics across 38 states, reaching users in states where sports betting is not legal, because event contracts are federally regulated rather than state-licensed gambling. Third-party coverage reported roughly $6.49 billion in total trading volume on the platform. The exchange also puts Underdog into direct competition with Kalshi and Polymarket, and into a policy fight: 2026 proposals aim to limit contracts tied to player injuries or specific in-game actions while allowing broader outcome contracts.

## The state-by-state map: 41, 15, and 38
Underdog's availability is a patchwork that every dossier about it has to state plainly. Best Ball drafts reach 41 states plus Washington DC. Classic Pick'em reaches only 15 states. The prediction market exchange reaches 38 states. Underdog is blocked entirely in nine states, including Washington, Nevada, and Louisiana. The map exists because fantasy law is state law, and each format is regulated differently: season-long drafts are the most widely permitted, house-banked player-stat contests the least. New customers were offered a Play $5, Get $50 bonus-entry offer after a first $5 contest entry as of August 2026, terms applying, and the platform enforces age verification, geolocation checks, deposit limits, and self-exclusion tools.

## The New York settlement and the line between fantasy and prop betting
New York is the cautionary tale. In October 2023 the New York State Gaming Commission adopted rules that fantasy contests shall not be based on proposition betting or contests mimicking it, which excluded Underdog's house-banked and peer-to-peer Pick'em. In March 2025 the Commission announced a settlement in which Underdog agreed to pay $17.5 million, according to SBC Americas and Vixio, and to stop offering certain contest types in New York unless permitted under state law. Underdog held its New York permit through Synkt Games, which it bought in December 2022, paused all New York operations after the deal, and relaunched around May 15, 2025 with draft-style contests only — Best Ball tournaments and daily snake drafts, with no Pick'em and no sign-up offer in the state. The settlement is the clearest public marker of the legal line Underdog now navigates everywhere: drafts are fantasy, player-stat props are the contested territory, and the exchange is the federal route around the state fight.

## Entry fees and the exchange take
Underdog's money model has two engines. Fantasy contests take entry fees: players pay to enter Pick'em, Champions, Best Ball, and draft tournaments, and Underdog's revenue comes from the contest economics — the difference between entries collected and prizes paid, plus promotional mechanics like Gimme Picks that are accounted as marketing. The exchange takes its revenue from trading: event contracts bought and sold on a regulated market, where the operator earns from the market structure rather than from taking positions against users. That distinction matters for the regulatory story: a fantasy operator takes a rake, an exchange operates a market, and Underdog now does both under different regulators. The $6.49 billion in reported trading volume is a scale signal, not a revenue figure, and Underdog has not published the take rate on either engine.

Cellular devices — blood-pressure cuffs, scales, and glucose meters that transmit on their own with no smartphone required — capture daily vitals at home. Clinical Intelligence software watches every patient continuously, surfaces risk, and catches care gaps before they become emergencies, resolving most alerts inside Cadence's own team. ## HypertensionOS and the FDA TEMPO pilot
Cadence's most distinctive product is HypertensionOS, prescription software as a medical device for clinician-supervised Stage 2 hypertension titration. In August 2026 HypertensionOS was selected as the second participant in the FDA's Technology-Enabled Meaningful Patient Outcomes (TEMPO) pilot for digital health devices. The distinction matters and Cadence's own coverage states it: TEMPO selection is enforcement discretion, not HypertensionOS approval, and it limits the commercial claims the company can make. The product's logic is titration at machine speed — blood pressure readings flow in daily, the software proposes dose adjustments against protocol, and a clinician supervises — instead of the standard pattern where a patient waits months between visits while their pressure stays uncontrolled. HypertensionOS is the product to watch because it moves Cadence from monitoring into treatment, which is both a larger market and a heavier regulatory burden.

## What the outcome numbers actually say
Cadence publishes outcome numbers more aggressively than most remote-monitoring companies, and they deserve precise reading. A Mayo Clinic Proceedings retrospective analysis reported in August 2026 found patients at goal blood pressure rose from 19% to 36% in Cadence's hypertension program, with inpatient costs falling about $88 per Medicare patient per month. Peer-reviewed studies cited in company coverage report a 70% relative increase in blood-pressure control and a 27% reduction in hospital admissions. A June 2026 funding report also noted heart-failure emergency visits cut 50% and total cost of care down 23% in earlier coverage. These are program results, not randomized trials of the whole platform, and they come from a company with every incentive to publish its best cohorts — but the volume of published numbers, and the health-system partnerships behind them, is itself the differentiator in a field where many remote-monitoring companies have promised outcomes and faded.

## The Medicare billing engine underneath
Cadence's business model runs on Medicare billing codes for remote patient monitoring, chronic care management, and CMS Advanced Primary Care Management. Remote patient monitoring became a covered Medicare benefit in 2019, and Part B payments for RPM devices and services rose from $109 million in 2018 to $1.3 billion in 2023; CMS added two new RPM billing codes in the 2026 Physician Fee Schedule, and 42 state Medicaid programs covered RPM as of May 2026, with Anthem, UnitedHealthcare, and Cigna covering it broadly for chronic conditions. That reimbursement tailwind is what makes the model work: the health system does not pay out of pocket for a new cost center, it shares in a reimbursed service, and Cadence's fees tie to performance and utilization. Cadence raised a $100 million Series C in June 2026 led by Spark Capital at a reported $1.2 billion valuation, with Memorial Hermann and Duke Health investing, bringing total funding to a reported $241 million. The company's stated mission is life-changing care for more than one million chronic patients by the end of the decade — ten times its current census.

The clinical gap Cadence fills is the months between visits. A hypertension patient sees a doctor, gets a prescription, and then nothing happens until the next appointment — while blood pressure drifts, medication adherence fades, and the next data point arrives only when something goes wrong. Cadence's daily readings close that gap: trends are visible within days, titration proposals arrive within the care protocol, and a clinician reaches out before a rising pressure becomes an emergency. The model only works if patients actually take readings, which is why the devices transmit on their own and need no smartphone: the fewer steps between the patient and the data, the fewer gaps. The open clinical question is durability — whether daily monitoring sustains engagement over years, or whether readings fade after the novelty wears off and the program becomes another unenrolled device in a drawer.

Charlie Health's programs run Monday through Saturday.       

## Kids, teens, and adults: three different programs
Charlie Health does not run one program for everyone; the three age bands get different treatment. Adults get intensive virtual support designed around adult life — regaining stability, building practical coping skills, and moving through serious mental health or substance use challenges without putting work, family, or caregiving on hold — treating major depressive disorder, anxiety and panic disorders, PTSD and trauma-related conditions, and substance use disorders. Teens get intensive care in supportive peer groups, building confidence, coping skills, and emotional skills while staying connected to school, friends, and family, treating depression, anxiety and school avoidance, self-harm and suicidal thoughts, and marijuana use. Kids get engaging, kid-friendly virtual care designed for how children think, feel, and learn, treating anxiety and excessive worry, sadness and irritability, school refusal, and social withdrawal. The clinical core is curated peer groups plus individual therapy plus family therapy, delivered with modalities including dialectical behavior therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, and motivational interviewing. Around that core sits what Charlie Health calls a 360-degree treatment ecosystem: a dedicated 24/7 crisis line, care coaches who provide resources, encouragement, and mentorship throughout treatment, more than 20 free virtual family support groups, and free alumni groups and events after discharge. Specialty tracks cover Spanish speakers, LGBTQIA+ patients, neurodivergent patients, BIPOC patients, eating disorders, and substance use disorders. What Charlie Health has built that is hard to copy is the operating system for running high-acuity group care virtually at scale — scheduling, staffing, and clinical consistency across age bands and states.

The product is a bovine colostrum concentrate: more than 400 bioactive nutrients — immunoglobulins, bioactive proteins, peptides — processed through a proprietary Cold-Chain BioPotent pasteurization technology that the company says preserves those nutrients in bioavailable form while removing compounds the body does not need. The mechanism claimed is barrier-first: colostrum reinforces the mucosal barrier, where nearly 80% of the immune system resides, and fortifies gut barrier layers. The brand sells direct to consumers on subscription through tryarmra.com: an unflavored jar with 120 servings, blood orange travel sticks with 30 servings, and bundles pairing them, stirred into cool liquid or food and never heated, because heat degrades the compounds. Sourcing is claimed calf-first — only overflow colostrum after calves are fully fed — from grass-fed, pasture-raised cattle on family-owned US farms, with no hormones. Review aggregators report mixed experience: immunity, energy, digestion, and hair gains for many, no measurable benefit for others, plus complaints about clumping, stevia taste, rigid returns, and subscription issues. On September 22, 2026, the nonprofit Animal Partisan sued Rahal Biosciences in DC Superior Court alleging deceptive health and animal-welfare claims, no peer-reviewed human trials, and lab tests alleging an undisclosed ingredient — allegations, not findings. Colostrum, concentrated: the 400-nutrient claim
ARMRA's core claim is concentration plus preservation. ARMRA is owned by Rahal Biosciences Inc. of Florida.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       

## Cold-Chain BioPotent and calf-first sourcing
Two process claims carry the brand. Cold-Chain BioPotent pasteurization is ARMRA's proprietary low-heat process for preserving bioactives that conventional pasteurization would damage; it is the technological answer to the obvious question of why a processed powder should retain the properties of fresh colostrum. Calf-first sourcing is the ethical answer to the equally obvious question of where the colostrum comes from: ARMRA says it collects only overflow colostrum after calves are fully fed, from grass-fed, pasture-raised cattle on family-owned US farms, with no hormones, and that its products are free from casein, gluten, GMOs, antibiotics, fat, oils, and glyphosate. Both claims are now contested, which is why they belong in the dossier as claims rather than facts — the lawsuit below alleges the welfare and purity claims do not hold up.

## Jars, sticks, and the subscription model
ARMRA sells the way modern supplement brands sell: direct to consumer, on subscription, in formats built for routine. The unflavored jar holds 120 servings; the blood orange travel sticks hold 30 servings; bundles pair them, like the Catalyst Bundle combining an unflavored jar with blood orange sticks. The ritual is one scoop a day, and the business model is retention: a daily habit, a subscription that renews, and a product line that extends from the core colostrum into flavored sticks and bundles. Review aggregators report mixed customer experience: many reviewers report stronger immunity, steadier energy, improved digestion, and thicker hair after weeks to months, while others report no measurable benefits and discontinue, and complaints cite clumping, stevia-heavy flavored blends, stale taste over time, rigid returns, subscription issues, and unresponsive support. No prices were verified from the sources reviewed, and third-party revenue estimates were omitted as low-confidence.

## The lawsuit and the evidence gap
On September 22, 2026, the nonprofit Animal Partisan sued Rahal Biosciences in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia, alleging misrepresentations about ARMRA's human health benefits and animal welfare practices. The complaint alleges that ARMRA provides no peer-reviewed human clinical trials to substantiate its benefit claims, relying instead on consumer surveys and one cell culture study, and that laboratory test results prove ARMRA contains an ingredient the company asserts is not present. These are allegations in a lawsuit, not findings, and ARMRA has not been found liable on this record. But the evidence gap the suit points to is real and structural: colostrum supplements are only loosely regulated by the FDA, the industry is growing rapidly in the US and globally, and ARMRA's own cited evidence — a 60-person open-label survey over three months at 2 grams daily, with individual results varying — is not the same as peer-reviewed human trials. A briefing agent for ARMRA has to say that plainly whenever a health benefit is claimed.

## The supplement regulation gap
ARMRA operates in a regulatory gap that shapes its whole story. Dietary supplements in the United States are only loosely regulated by the FDA: products reach the market without pre-approval, claims are policed after the fact, and the burden of proof for deceptive marketing falls on challengers like Animal Partisan rather than on the seller. That gap is why the colostrum category can grow rapidly on influencer marketing and testimonials while accumulating almost no peer-reviewed human trial evidence, and why a lawsuit, rather than a regulator, is the mechanism forcing the evidence question. For a briefing agent, the gap means every ARMRA benefit claim has to carry its evidence status with it: company-cited survey, lab model, or peer-reviewed trial — three very different things that marketing copy treats as one.

# Inworld AI — the Character Engine for AI NPCs

Inworld AI builds the Character Engine, a platform for creating non-player characters that talk, remember, feel, and act like people instead of reciting scripted lines. Game developers, studios, and storytellers use it to design characters with personalities, backgrounds, motivations, memories, and goals, then deploy them into games, virtual worlds, training simulations, and interactive experiences where they respond to players in real time. The platform combines voice, text, animation, emotion, gestures, and actions into multimodal characters, orchestrates across multiple large language models for low-latency interaction, and ships with Unity and Unreal SDKs plus APIs for web and mobile. Inworld sells a free tier for prototyping and paid plans for production use; public pricing detail is thin, and one 2026 review lists a $10-per-month Pro tier for the character product. LinkedIn ranked Inworld AI #10 on its 2025 Top Startups list for the United States. Its best-known deployment outside games is Disney's Droid Maker, built with Lucasfilm's ILMxLAB immersive storytelling studio. The Character Engine's difference from a chatbot is persistence plus embodiment. A character remembers past interactions and carries that memory forward, so relationships with players evolve instead of resetting each session; characters hold dynamic emotional states, pursue goals autonomously, and make decisions based on motivations and game states. They communicate multimodally — dialogue through text and natural voice, expression through animation and gesture — kept coherent with the logic, lore, and fantasy of the game's world, with safety parameters, content controls, custom knowledge, and narrative controls so characters stay in character. Developers design characters in a visual interface — personality, background, motivations, voice profile — then integrate through Unity or Unreal SDKs or the API and deploy across platforms, with the platform orchestrating across large language models for low-latency interaction. Multi-character conversations let several characters interact with each other and the player at once. Beyond games, the platform serves training and education simulations, brand and customer-experience characters, and interactive storytelling, with Disney's Droid Maker built with Lucasfilm's ILMxLAB as the prestige deployment. The platform is freemium — free for prototyping, paid for production — and one 2026 review lists a $10-per-month Pro tier for the character product. The Character Engine: voice, memory, and emotion in one NPC
The Character Engine's difference from a chatbot is persistence plus embodiment. A character remembers past interactions and carries that memory into future ones, so relationships with players evolve over time instead of resetting each session. Inworld's best-known deployment outside games is Disney's Droid Maker.                                                                     

## Unity, Unreal, and the developer workflow
Inworld's workflow is built for working game teams, not demos. A creator designs a character in a visual interface — personality, background, motivations, voice profile — then integrates through Unity or Unreal SDKs or the API, and deploys the same character across platforms. The platform handles real-time optimization itself: orchestrating across LLMs to deliver high-quality interaction with faster inference and lower cost, which matters because an NPC that pauses for seconds breaks immersion in a way a chatbot's pause does not. Developers can also upload proprietary models for unique character personalities and behaviors. Use cases beyond games include AI-powered quests generated and managed through autonomous NPCs responding to player behavior, game prototyping and testing of complex NPC behaviors, and personalized learning experiences and interactive simulations in training and education.

## Beyond games: training, brands, and interactive stories
Inworld's market extends wherever a believable interactive character has value. In training and education, characters become patients, customers, or adversaries that trainees practice on. For brands and customer experience, they become spokescharacters that hold conversations instead of menu trees. For writers and interactive storytellers, persistent characters with memory generate endless interactive stories that branch on player choices rather than pre-written paths. The Disney Droid Maker project with ILMxLAB is the prestige proof point: characters built with Inworld technology inside a Lucasfilm storytelling experience. The company's funding is described in third-party coverage as significant, making it one of the best-funded startups in AI and gaming, though no verified funding total was found in the sources reviewed.

## The pricing fog and the indie-vs-studio split
Inworld's commercial picture is the least documented part of the dossier, and that is worth stating. The platform is freemium: free unlimited characters for prototyping in some listings, with paid plans for advanced features, scalability, and enterprise capabilities, and at least one 2026 review lists Pro at $10 per month — a consumer-creator price that plainly does not describe an enterprise game-studio contract. The gap between those two prices is the business: indie developers and writers enter free, studios negotiate production terms, and the company's revenue depends on converting the first group and landing the second. The competitive pressure comes from game engines and AI model providers building character capabilities directly into their stacks, which would make a standalone character engine a feature rather than a platform. Inworld's defense is its accumulated character tooling — memory, emotion, safety controls, and multi-character dynamics — which is harder to replicate than a dialogue model.

## Multi-character scenes
Multi-character conversation is Inworld's most distinctive capability and its hardest technical problem. A single NPC answering a player is a dialogue task; several characters talking to each other and to the player at once is a social simulation, requiring each character to track what the others said, maintain its own goals and relationships, and decide when to speak, interrupt, or stay silent. Inworld's platform supports group conversations with persistent memory across characters, which is what makes interactive stories with genuine social dynamics possible rather than branching scripts with voice acting. The capability also has the clearest path beyond games: training scenarios with multiple roles, customer experiences with handoffs between characters, and stories where the player is one participant among several rather than the center of every exchange.

distilled:
Medallion runs the paperwork that decides when a clinician can legally see patients and get paid for it. Before a doctor, therapist, or nurse practitioner can bill an insurer, someone has to verify their license, education, board certification, malpractice history, and exclusion-list status against the original issuing sources, assemble that evidence into a credentialing file a committee will approve, and then enroll that clinician with each payer whose members they will treat. Medallion does that work on one platform, at medallion.co, for provider groups, health systems, payers, digital health companies, and revenue-cycle firms. Its pitch is measured in time to revenue: every week a clinician sits uncredentialed is a week of appointments that cannot be billed, and Medallion pairs AI agents that collect and structure provider data with credentialing specialists who check each file before submission, with contract-backed performance commitments. The company says it powers more than 300 healthcare organizations, and its own site cites 55 million primary source verifications completed. Pricing is not published; sales are enterprise-contract only, priced by provider volume and the modules used. In September 2026 Medallion acquired Andros, an NCQA-certified credentials verification organization operating since 2013, and announced the combined platform covers more than one million providers across nearly 400 healthcare organizations and health plans. That acquisition matters because it gives Medallion the accredited verification arm that payers themselves require, rather than only software that organizes the work.


Andros is the credentialing industry's version of an auditor with a license to audit. A credentials verification organization does not just run software; it is accredited to verify qualifications on a payer's behalf, and Andros has held NCQA accreditation across 11 out of 11 standards, according to coverage of the acquisition, while processing roughly 300,000 credentialing files a year. That accreditation is what lets a payer delegate credentialing decisions instead of redoing them in-house, and it is what Medallion bought: not just a customer list, but the right to be the verifier of record. For a provider group, the practical difference is fewer duplicate submissions; for a payer, it is a single file to trust instead of a stack of attestations. The combined company's claim to be the largest AI-native credentialing platform in the country rests on that combination of volume, accreditation, and automation, and it will be tested on whether payers that already trust their own verification teams are willing to share a network with competitors.

The question for any buyer is whether Medallion's file is actually faster than the team it replaces. A single provider file carries credentialing, payer enrollment, licensing across states, continuous monitoring, roster management, hospital privileging, payer contract terms, and delegated credentialing.
## Credentialing, enrollment, licensing, and monitoring on a single provider file

Medallion's core product keeps one record per clinician and drives four kinds of work off it. Credentialing is the primary source verification itself: pulling license status from state boards, checking the National Practitioner Data Bank, OIG exclusion lists, DEA registration, and board certification, then building an NCQA-compliant packet for committee review. Enrollment is the payer side: submitting and tracking applications to commercial plans, Medicare, and Medicaid so the clinician becomes billable with each payer, with delegated enrollment where a payer accepts Medallion's credentialing decision directly. Licensing covers state licenses a clinician needs to practice across state lines, a constant problem for telehealth companies hiring nationally. Monitoring is the ongoing piece: licenses expire, sanctions appear, and malpractice coverage lapses, so the file has to be re-verified on a cycle rather than once. Medallion also sells roster management and privileging, the hospital process of granting a clinician permission to practice in a facility, plus payer contract management. The point of bundling all of this is that a provider group expanding into a new state otherwise runs four separate processes with four vendors and four timelines.

## CredAlliance and the payer side of the business

CredAlliance is Medallion's network model for payers, and it is the part of the business that changes the unit economics. Normally every payer credentials the same clinician separately, repeating the same verifications. Under CredAlliance, a provider is verified once and that verification is shared across participating networks, covering Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial lines of business. Medallion claims this runs 3.5 times faster than legacy credentials verification organizations on average, and that customers see a 50% reduction in operating costs on average and 78% less time on operational tasks, all Medallion's own figures. The model only works if enough payers participate, which is why the Andros acquisition matters: Andros brought NCQA certification, roughly 300,000 credentialing files a year, and experience building more than 200 provider networks across all 50 states, according to coverage of the deal. The risk runs the other way too: a payer that already runs its own delegated credentialing, or that trusts an incumbent verification organization, has little reason to join a shared network run by a vendor that also serves provider groups on the other side of the same negotiation.

## Who buys Medallion, and what the sale actually costs

The buyers are operations leaders, not clinicians. A digital health company hiring fifty therapists a month buys Medallion to stop growth from stalling on paperwork; a health system buys it to keep employed physicians billable and compliant; a payer buys the NCQA-certified verification service; a revenue-cycle firm buys it because a claim denied for an unenrolled provider is revenue lost. Tampa General Hospital is one of the customers Medallion names publicly. Pricing is not published anywhere on medallion.co, and third-party listings agree that there is no free version and no free trial: expect a custom quote tied to provider count, product modules, and integrations. That opacity is a real buying cost. A small practice cannot self-serve or even budget from the site; it has to go through sales, and the comparison set includes self-serve or cheaper packet-processing tools. The counterweight is the contract-backed performance claim: Medallion puts its own commitments in the contract, which few pure software vendors in this category do.

## Medallion against Andros, Verifiable, symplr, and CredentialStream

The credentialing category splits three ways, and Medallion sits in the middle. On one side are the legacy credentials verification organizations and incumbents: symplr and CredentialStream sell established credentialing and privileging suites to hospitals and health systems, and their incumbency inside hospital IT is hard to displace. On another side are automation-first tools such as Verifiable, which focus on automated packet processing and verification workflows without the full managed service. Medallion's difference is the combination: AI agents that chase providers for documents, run outreach and follow-up, and populate files, plus human specialists who verify each file, plus the NCQA-certified verification organization itself after the Andros deal. What Medallion is not is an electronic health record, a scheduling tool, or a billing system; it touches the clinician's permission to practice and be paid, and stops there. Its exposure is concentration: credentialing rules are set by NCQA, the Joint Commission, and CMS, and a rule change can raise failure rates and churn across the whole customer base at once, as third-party coverage noted around NCQA's July 2025 rules.

Sources: medallion.co pages (who-we-serve, CVO credentialing, CredAlliance), Medallion's September 15, 2026 Andros acquisition announcement, and third-party coverage of the acquisition and pricing; accessed 2026-10-30.

MagicSchool AI sells time back to teachers. A teacher's week is eaten by work that is not teaching: writing a lesson plan, turning it into a worksheet, building a quiz, writing a rubric, leveling a reading passage up and down, drafting a parent email, and writing IEP goals in the district's required language. MagicSchool, at magicschool.ai, turns each of those recurring jobs into a single-purpose tool: pick the job, enter the grade, subject, and topic, and get a structured draft to edit, instead of coaxing a general chatbot with a long prompt. The company was founded in 2023 in Denver by a former teacher, and it is built for K-12 first, not adapted from a general AI product. It now lists more than 80 teacher tools and more than 50 student tools, plus Raina, its education chatbot, Student Rooms where teachers assign guided AI work, and district controls. The business model is freemium with a district tier on top: individual teachers use a Forever Free plan, heavy individual users pay for Plus, and schools and districts buy Enterprise on a custom quote. MagicSchool reports a community of more than 6 million educators and students and more than 10,000 school and district partnerships, both company-reported figures from its public materials. The reason it matters is distribution: teachers adopt it on their own, for free, and bring it into schools from the bottom up, which is a cheaper way to enter education than selling to a district committee first.


MagicSchool's distribution is the part competitors envy most. Teachers find it on their own, sign up free, and pass it along in staff rooms, which is why third-party reviews describe it reaching 3 million teachers in its first year, a company-reported trajectory. That bottom-up path avoids the district procurement cycle that kills most education software, but it also means MagicSchool's first relationship is with an individual teacher, not with the IT department that will eventually have to approve student data handling. The Enterprise tier exists to convert that bottom-up adoption into a district contract, with the controls and agreements a superintendent needs. The student side is deliberately gated: pupils do not get an open chatbot, they get tools a teacher assigns inside a room, with engagement data flowing back to the teacher. That gating is MagicSchool's answer to the central worry about AI in schools, which is not whether students will use AI, since they already do, but whether a school can see and shape how they use it.

The free tier is also MagicSchool's hardest sales problem. A teacher who gets everything she needs for free has little reason to pay $12.99 a month, so Plus has to sell on volume: unlimited generations, unlimited history, and unlimited rooms for the teacher who uses the platform all day, every day. A single login covers lesson plans, worksheets, quiz generation, rubric generation, slide presentations, IEP drafting, parent communication, text leveling, and guided student rooms.
## Eighty teacher tools, fifty student tools, and Raina in the middle

The teacher catalog maps onto the school week. Lesson Plan Generator, Unit Plan Generator, Worksheet Generator, Multiple Choice Quiz Maker, Rubric Generator, and Presentation Generator cover planning and assessment; text leveling and differentiation tools rewrite a passage for different reading levels, including English learners; IEP tools draft present-level statements and goal language; communication tools draft parent emails and report card comments. Raina sits alongside the tools as a conversational assistant for questions that do not fit a form, and Plus adds the ability to continue Raina threads inside tools, prompt suggestions, and unlimited custom tools. On the student side, MagicSchool for Students offers more than 50 tools, but students work inside teacher-assigned Student Rooms rather than an open chatbot, and teachers get Student Room Insights showing real-time engagement data. AI Slides generation exports to Google Slides, image generation is Adobe-powered, and a web search feature added in 2025 lets tools pull in current information. The design choice that matters most is the form-based tool: a teacher never has to learn prompt engineering, because the grade, subject, and standards context are fields in the tool, not sentences in a prompt.

## What MagicSchool charges teachers, schools, and districts

The pricing page is unusually plain for education software. Forever Free costs $0 for individual teachers and includes the 80-plus teacher tools, Raina, quizzes, class writing feedback, and the student tools, but with standard usage limits rather than unlimited generations, and limited output history. Plus costs $12.99 per month billed monthly, or $8.33 per month billed annually ($99.96 per year), and adds unlimited generations, unlimited output history, unlimited editing of AI output, unlimited student rooms, unlimited AI Slides, and advanced tool features including Studio Mode. New accounts get a 30-day trial of Plus with no credit card required. Enterprise is a custom quote and adds what a district actually needs to approve a tool: single sign-on, integrations with student information and learning management systems, a custom data privacy agreement, centralized tool controls, admin dashboards, and implementation support. The free tier is the growth engine and the risk at once: it gets MagicSchool into classrooms without a procurement cycle, but converting free teachers to paid Plus or to a district contract is where the revenue has to come from, and the free tier already covers most of a casual user's needs.

## MagicSchool against Khanmigo, Brisk, Eduaide, and Diffit

The teacher-AI field divides by shape, and MagicSchool's shape is breadth. Khanmigo, from Khan Academy, is a tutor and teaching assistant tied to Khan Academy's curriculum and known for guided, Socratic student tutoring rather than a catalog of prep tools. Brisk Teaching lives inside Google Docs and Slides and wins teachers who never want to leave the document they are already writing in. Eduaide and Diffit are narrower: Eduaide centers on planning and feedback tools, Diffit on leveled readings and resources from a source text. Almanack goes deep on full curriculum-aligned lessons and grading from a teacher's own uploaded materials, where MagicSchool stays shallow and fast across many jobs. MagicSchool's edge is that one login covers the whole prep list, and its weakness is the mirror image: a lesson draft is a starting point, not a finished plan, and breadth means no single tool goes as deep as a specialist. Its compliance positioning is part of the sale to districts: FERPA, COPPA, GDPR, and SOC 2 coverage plus a Common Sense privacy certification, as checked against its own pages in October 2026, and a stated position that student data is not sold.

## Where MagicSchool's classroom pitch gets tested

Three tests decide whether MagicSchool keeps its place. The first is output quality: AI lesson plans, quizzes, and IEP language contain errors, flatten reading levels unevenly, and carry bias, so every output needs a teacher's review before it reaches students, and a district that treats drafts as finished work will get burned. The second is student data: teachers pasting names, grades, or IEP details into any AI tool is a privacy failure unless the school has approved that tool and its data agreement, and MagicSchool's answer is the Enterprise controls and agreements, not the free tier alone. The third is the student side: giving pupils guided tools inside Student Rooms is a controlled alternative to an open chatbot, but it still requires teachers to set the guardrails and watch engagement data rather than assuming the room runs itself. None of these are reasons to dismiss the product; they are the reasons its buyers are teachers who edit, not schools looking to automate teaching away.

Grow Therapy fixes the most common reason people never start therapy: finding a therapist who takes their insurance, has an open slot, and practices near them or on video. Grow, at growtherapy.com, is a network of independent therapists and prescribers that clients search the way they would search for any professional, filtered by insurance plan, specialty, location, availability, gender, language, and approach, and then book directly. The therapists are not Grow employees; they are independent 1099 contractors who keep clinical control and set their own schedules, while Grow handles the parts of private practice that drive clinicians out of insurance work: credentialing with payers, billing and claims, scheduling, and client referrals. Grow says it has more than 26,000 vetted clinicians in all 50 states, is in-network with more than 125 health plans covering about 90% of commercial lives, and delivers 10 million visits a year across its network, all Grow's own figures. For clients, the model is pay per session through insurance, with the out-of-pocket cost set by the client's own copay and deductible; for employers and health plans, Grow sells itself as a mental health benefit with utilization-based pricing, meaning the buyer pays for care employees actually receive rather than a flat fee. The company also reports that a first appointment is available in under a day on average, and 2.8 days from booking to first completed session.


The client journey is deliberately ordinary, and that is the point. A person searching for therapy is usually doing it at a difficult moment, and Grow's search avoids the usual dead ends: no calling offices to ask whether they take your plan, no waiting lists with no callback date, no discovering after an intake call that the therapist is full. Profiles show specialty, availability, and background, often with a short introductory video, and third-party reviews report most therapists responding within 24 to 48 hours. Sessions run by video, phone, or in person, and the built-in video platform means no separate app to download. For therapists, the mirror image matters: a clinician who wants insurance clients without hiring a biller or spending months getting paneled can join, get credentialed, and start receiving referrals through the directory, with Grow's intake and scheduling team handling booking. The model only works if both sides keep showing up, which is why Grow reports retention and outcome numbers so prominently: a directory with no available therapists, or a network therapists leave, collapses quickly.

The economics underneath Grow explain why therapists join at all. Insurance work pays reliably but slowly, and the administrative cost of getting paneled, submitting claims, and chasing denials drives many clinicians to cash-only practices, which prices out the clients who need care most. One network covers talk therapy, psychiatry, medication management, children's care, crisis support, and employer benefits.
## Therapy, psychiatry, coaching, and the employer's benefit version

Grow's care covers individual adults, couples, teens, and children ages 6 and up, by video or in person where the therapist has an office, with sessions typically 30, 45, or 60 minutes. Beyond talk therapy it offers psychiatry and medication management, coaching, a 24/7 crisis line, critical incident response for employers, and manager consultation, and it routes people to prescribers or higher-acuity support when the intake points that way. Measurement is built into the pitch: Grow embeds measurement-informed care in every session, tracking PHQ-9 for depression and GAD-7 for anxiety, and reports that 81% of members see clinically significant improvement, with depression improvement at 75% against a 40% industry benchmark it cites, anxiety improvement at 75% against 38%, a 90% measure completion rate, 75% retention from session one to session three, and an NPS of 85. Employers get only de-identified, aggregate reporting on utilization and outcomes; Grow states that nothing individual-level is shared with HR or managers, and that it operates on HIPAA-aligned infrastructure. When employer-funded sessions run out, the employee keeps the same provider through their own health insurance, which is the detail that makes the employer version stick: no new search, no re-intake, no broken therapeutic relationship.

## Grow's deal with therapists: free to join, paid through insurance rates

For therapists, Grow is free to join with no membership fee and no minimum visit requirement, and the trade is straightforward: Grow takes over credentialing, enrollment with major payers including UnitedHealthcare, Aetna, Cigna, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Humana, and Anthem, plus Medicare and Medicaid in states where that applies, and guarantees insurance payouts so a denied claim does not mean an unpaid therapist. Providers see an expected payout and payout date per session in the portal, are paid by weekly direct deposit, and keep their own malpractice insurance and an active, unrestricted license in their state as conditions of joining. Third-party reviews of the provider side report credentialing in 5 to 7 days on Grow's current stated timeline, a 5% processing fee on cash-pay sessions, and job listings citing earnings up to $118 per hour for therapists and $143 per hour for psychologists at Grow's negotiated insurance rates, with providers setting their own private-pay rates. Grow also provides a basic EHR, scheduling with Google, Apple, and Outlook calendar sync, secure messaging between sessions, telehealth, AI-assisted documentation drafts that the therapist reviews and edits, free continuing education credits, and a peer community. The EHR is the weak spot named in provider reviews: practices that want a full-featured record system often still pay for one separately.

## Grow against BetterHelp, Talkspace, Headway, and Alma

The online therapy field splits on one question: who pays, and how does the therapist get paid. BetterHelp and Talkspace are primarily subscription products where clients pay a weekly or monthly fee for messaging and live sessions, often without insurance billing at the center. Grow is insurance-first: the client searches in-network providers and pays their plan's copay, and third-party guides put typical session costs at $0 to $125 with insurance, varying by plan, against $75 to $200 without it. The closer competitors are Headway and Alma, which also credential therapists with insurers and handle billing so clinicians can run insurance-based practices; Grow's difference is the size of the consumer-facing directory and the employer and health-plan benefit business built on top of the same network, plus in-person care alongside video. Grow's risks are specific to that model. Medicaid acceptance is limited to select therapists in select states, so the in-network promise thins out for Medicaid clients. Provider reviews also report uneven customer support, and the guaranteed-payout promise depends on Grow's billing operation working: billing corrections driven by federal rules and insurer contracts can adjust payouts well after a session, and insurer-initiated recoupments are absorbed by Grow rather than deducted from the therapist, according to Grow's own provider help pages.

distilled:
Zip is the front door for buying things inside a company. In most companies, an employee who needs software, a contractor, or a laptop starts by emailing finance, or asking in Slack, or filling in a spreadsheet, and the request then wanders between a manager, procurement, IT security, legal, and finance, with nobody able to say where it is stuck. Zip, at ziphq.com, replaces that wandering with one intake form: the employee answers a short set of questions that adapt to previous answers, Zip routes the request to the right reviewers automatically, checks it against company policy, onboards the vendor if needed, and creates the purchase request or purchase order in the company's existing financial system. This is Zip, the procurement software company, not Zip Co, the Australian buy-now-pay-later firm. Zip does not replace a company's ERP or procure-to-pay system; it sits in front of it as a control layer, and that is the whole strategy. Its named customers in coverage include Anthropic, OpenAI, and AMD, and Zip cites Lattice cutting purchase approval cycle times by 50% after adopting it. Pricing is not published on ziphq.com; buyers get a custom quote, although Zip's SAP store listing prices a Starter edition at $50,000 per year for 50 users plus a $15,000 setup fee, with a one-year minimum, which gives a floor for what a small deployment costs through that channel.


The reason buying inside a company feels broken is that nobody owns the request. Finance owns the budget, procurement owns the policy, IT owns the security review, legal owns the contract, and the employee owns the frustration, so a request for a $400-a-month tool can sit for weeks while each team waits for another team. Zip's bet is that the fix is not a better policy document but a single place where the request lives, with every reviewer able to see it, approve it, or ask a question, and the requester able to watch its progress without chasing anyone. That visibility is what finance teams mean when they talk about early spend visibility: a commitment that will hit next quarter's budget is visible the day the request is made, not the day the invoice arrives. The consumer-grade interface is not cosmetic; it is the adoption mechanism, because an intake tool employees avoid is worse than no tool, since it creates a false record of control while spending continues through email and personal cards.

Rogue spend is the number Zip's buyers use to justify the purchase, and it is worth understanding plainly. When an employee buys software on a personal card or through an unapproved vendor, finance loses visibility, security loses the chance to vet the vendor, and legal loses the contract terms, and the company often pays twice when a second team buys the same tool. One request covers guided intake, legal review, and spend visibility. A single request covers guided intake, approvals, vendor onboarding, security review, and legal review. Visibility before money moves is what finance is buying.
## Guided intake, approval chains, and vendor onboarding in one request

A Zip request starts with guided intake, not a blank form. The form asks only the questions relevant to that purchase type and loops in the correct stakeholders automatically, so an employee needs no training to make a compliant request. Approval workflows are dynamic and configurable: a request can route in sequence or in parallel to finance, IT, security, legal, and procurement, with service-level visibility into where each approval sits and the ability to change a workflow while it is in progress. Vendor onboarding runs inside the same request: Zip ingests and categorizes vendors, flags overlaps and duplicates across categories from software providers to staffing agencies, and tracks vendor approvals alongside purchase approvals. Once approved, Zip generates the purchase request or purchase order in the downstream system and gives the requester visibility into the open purchase order amount and number without ERP access. The newer positioning adds an AI concierge that steers requesters to preferred suppliers, correct categories, and active contracts, and AI agents across intake-to-pay and contract review. The pitch to finance is early visibility: commitments become visible at intake, before money is spent, instead of surfacing at invoice time.

## Zip's integrations: SAP, NetSuite, Ironclad, Brex, and the tools employees already use

Zip's value depends on integrations, because a control layer that does not connect to the systems of record is just another form. On the financial side it integrates with ERPs and procure-to-pay systems including SAP S/4HANA, SAP Ariba Buying and Invoicing, SAP Ariba Sourcing, Supplier Lifecycle and Performance, Contracts, and Supplier Risk, plus NetSuite, so approved records appear in downstream systems without duplicate entry. On the contract side it connects to contract lifecycle tools including Ironclad. On the workflow side it connects to Jira, ServiceNow, and Zendesk so stakeholders keep working in their own tools. On the payment side, pairing Zip with Brex lets an approved request be paid immediately with a Brex virtual card carrying the right controls, closing the loop from request to payment. Implementation is not instant: Zip's own materials describe launches in under six weeks, and third-party comparisons warn that setup takes weeks of workflow design, because every approval rule, category, and routing decision has to be modeled before employees use it. Companies that already run SAP can also buy Zip Intake to Procure through the SAP store, where the Starter and Enterprise editions are listed with unlimited user access on Enterprise and price-on-request terms.

## Zip against Coupa, Ramp, Tipalti, Precoro, and Procurify

Procurement software divides into full suites and specialists, and Zip is a specialist that refuses to become a suite. Coupa is the full-suite incumbent: sourcing, contracts, supplier networks, invoicing, and payments in one platform, with the cost and implementation weight that implies. Ramp and Tipalti bundle procurement with spend management and payables, so a company that wants cards, expenses, and invoices in one place will look there first. Precoro and Procurify serve the mid-market with tighter purchase-order control and, unusually, published prices: Precoro lists Core at $499 per month billed annually and Automation at $999 per month. Zip's argument against all of them is that most procurement pain happens before the purchase order exists, in intake and approvals, and that fixing that one stage is a smaller, faster project than replacing the ERP or rolling out a suite. The trade is real: Zip is not a sourcing suite, it does not run supplier networks, and its downstream procure-to-pay capabilities are newer than its intake product, so a company that needs sourcing and contracts still buys those elsewhere. Its G2 rating of 4.6 out of 5 across 139 reviews, as checked in October 2026, suggests the intake experience itself is what customers rate, not the breadth of the suite.

## Who buys Zip, and where the intake fix stops

Zip's buyers are fast-growing companies whose headcount outran their buying process: technology firms adding vendors every week, where a purchase that takes three weeks of email threads is a hiring and shipping delay, not just an annoyance. The buyer is usually finance or procurement leadership, but the daily users are everyone else in the company, which is why Zip's interface is deliberately consumer-grade: if employees hate the intake form, they route around it, and the control layer fails at its one job. That is also why rogue spend is the metric Zip talks about: spend that bypasses policy is not just non-compliant, it is invisible to finance until the invoice arrives. The limit of the fix is scope. A company whose problem is negotiating better prices, running tenders, or managing supplier performance will not solve it with intake software, and a company with no ERP discipline will find Zip faithfully routing requests into a messy downstream system. Zip works best layered over an ERP that already handles purchasing, where the bottleneck is genuinely the front door.

Sources: ziphq.com product pages (via search excerpts), Zip's SAP store listing, Brex's Zip procurement guide, Tipalti's Zip comparisons, and procurement software comparisons; accessed 2026-10-30.

name: Together AI
desc: Together AI — LinkedIn Top Startups 2025 US #25. Open-source model inference cloud. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Together AI rents out the ability to run open AI models without owning the GPUs. A developer who wants to build on Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, Kimi, or Mistral faces a choice: call a closed provider's API and accept its prices and rules, or host the model themselves and pay for hardware, engineering, and uptime. Together, at together.ai, offers the middle path: a cloud of Nvidia GPUs running more than 200 open-weight models behind an API, so a team can call a model by name, pay per token, fine-tune it on their own data, or rent dedicated capacity, without provisioning a cluster. The company was founded in 2022 by a team with roots in Stanford machine learning and systems research, led by CEO Vipul Ved Prakash, and its engineering story is the Together Inference Engine, which uses techniques including FlashAttention-3 and speculative decoding to serve tokens faster and cheaper than a naive deployment. The API is OpenAI-compatible for chat, completions, images, and embeddings, so existing code often moves over with an endpoint and key change rather than a rewrite. Together makes money on usage, not licenses: serverless inference billed per million tokens, dedicated inference billed per minute of running GPU, GPU clusters billed per GPU-hour, and fine-tuning billed per training token. In August 2026 IBM announced a reported $240 million deal to run large-scale open-source inference with Together on Nvidia HGX B300 systems inside IBM Cloud, a sign of how far the company has moved from developer tool toward enterprise infrastructure.


Together's origin explains its product shape. The team came out of Stanford research on making large models run efficiently, including work on FlashAttention, and the company was built around the observation that GPU computing was priced and packaged for an earlier era of computing, not for models that need thousands of GPUs at once. That research background shows up in the Inference Engine, which squeezes more tokens per GPU through optimized attention and speculative decoding, and the savings are passed on as lower per-token prices rather than kept as margin on hardware rental alone. For a developer, the practical consequence is choice without lock-in: models can be swapped by changing a model string, a fine-tune can be downloaded and run elsewhere, and the OpenAI-compatible API means the integration cost of trying an open model is an afternoon, not a migration project. The trade is that Together does not set the direction of the models it serves; it depends on Meta, DeepSeek, Alibaba, and other labs continuing to release strong open weights, and a year in which those labs hold back would leave every open-model cloud thinner at once.

Price is Together's sharpest selling point and its least stable one. One API covers image generation, video generation, and fine-tuning. One API covers chat models, vision models, image generation, and speech transcription. That combination, open weights plus rented GPUs, is the product.
## Serverless inference, dedicated endpoints, and GPU clusters

Together's three serving modes map to three stages of a product's life. Serverless inference is the starting point: call any supported model through a shared API with no provisioning, no replicas to size, and no minimum cost, paying only for the tokens processed. The docs catalog lists per-million-token input and output prices per model, and the spread is wide: OpenAI's open GPT-OSS 120B runs $0.15 input and $0.60 output per million tokens, Qwen3.5 9B runs $0.17 and $0.25, DeepSeek V4 Pro runs $1.32 and $3.96, and Moonshot's Kimi K3 runs $3.00 and $15.00, with cached input priced far lower where offered. Image models bill differently: Black Forest Labs' FLUX.1.1 Pro costs $0.04 per megapixel, so a 1024 by 1024 image runs about $0.042, while a 4096 by 4096 image runs about $0.67. Video models bill per video, audio transcription at $0.0015 per audio minute for the listed speech-to-text models, and a Batch API handles offline workloads at a reported 50% discount to real-time rates. Dedicated model inference is the second mode: a model on GPUs reserved for one customer, billed by the minute per ready replica, at $5.49 per hour for a single H100 and $8.99 per hour for a B200, with H200, GB300, and B300 on a contact-sales basis. GPU clusters are the third: rentable hardware for training and fine-tuning, listed on-demand at $3.99 per hour for an H100, $8.19 for a B200, and $9.99 for a B300, with reserved and preemptible tiers lower. US-only inference, processing kept in the United States via us-api.together.ai, costs 25% more than standard rates.

## Fine-tuning, evaluations, and the open-model catalog

The reason teams stay on Together rather than treating it as a cheap API is customization. Fine-tuning covers LoRA adapters, full fine-tuning, and DPO preference tuning, including multi-node training on models over 100 billion parameters, and a fine-tuned model can be served on dedicated endpoints or downloaded for local inference. An evaluations API judges model outputs against a dataset the customer uploads, with the customer writing the judge instructions and pass thresholds, billed at standard serverless inference rates. The catalog itself is the moat and the limit at once: more than 200 models spanning chat, vision-language, image, video, audio, and embeddings, from Meta's Llama family, DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen, Z.ai's GLM, Moonshot's Kimi, Mistral, Black Forest Labs' FLUX image models, and Google's Veo video models, among others. What the catalog does not contain is any frontier closed model: there is no GPT, no Claude, and no Gemini chat model served as a first-class closed endpoint, so a team that needs those models keeps a second vendor. Licensing also varies by model; open-weight does not mean uniformly permissive, and each model's license governs what a customer can do with the weights and with a fine-tune of them.

## Together against Fireworks, Groq, the hyperscalers, and the closed labs

The inference market has four kinds of rival, and Together competes with each differently. Fireworks AI is the closest peer: another open-model inference cloud with its own speed claims, competing on model coverage, latency, and per-token price. Groq competes on raw speed for a narrower set of models on its own language processing units, winning latency-sensitive workloads but not the breadth of Together's catalog. The hyperscalers, AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, plus DigitalOcean's AI cloud, compete on the full stack: a team already running databases, storage, and networking in one cloud may prefer inference in the same place, and DigitalOcean's comparison notes that Together's 99.9% uptime SLA is enterprise-only, while its own failover is automatic. The closed labs compete on capability: OpenAI and Anthropic sell the most capable models directly, and Together's answer is price and control, running an open model at a fraction of a frontier API bill on workloads where the capability gap does not matter. Together's exposure is that its prices move constantly as new models arrive and rates are repriced, so a bill that looks cheap this month is not a contracted rate, and its enterprise push, including the IBM deal, puts it into procurement contests against vendors with far larger sales organizations.

Sources: Together AI docs (serverless models, dedicated-endpoint pricing), together.ai pricing coverage (October 2026), DigitalOcean's Together AI comparison, and Network World's IBM-Together report; accessed 2026-10-30.

name: Drata
desc: Drata — LinkedIn Top Startups 2025 US #30. Compliance automation for SOC 2, ISO, HIPAA. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Drata, founded in 2020 in San Diego, indeed sells compliance automation to software, fintech, healthcare, and government-contracting companies that need to prove their security controls to enterprise buyers. Its core buyer is a startup or mid-market SaaS team facing its first SOC 2 audit, and its core pitch is that the same evidence, once collected, can satisfy many audits at once. A team connects Drata to its cloud accounts, identity provider, HR system, and developer tools — AWS, Okta, Workday, GitHub, Jamf, CrowdStrike, Wiz, and Confluence are named in its Brex customer story — and Drata pulls evidence automatically, tests controls every day, and flags drift the day it happens instead of at quarter-end. When an auditor asks for proof, the team hands it over from Drata rather than assembling screenshots and spreadsheets.

Drata makes money on annual subscriptions priced by company size, number of frameworks, and modules. Direct pricing is not published; a sales proposal is required. The one public price route is its AWS Marketplace listing, reported by third-party pricing trackers: a Foundation package at $15,000 a year for companies with 1 to 50 full-time employees, and a Platform line at $25,000 a year for capacity up to 100 employees plus $7,500 per framework, so SOC 2 alone on that route totals $32,500 before modules. The independent CPA audit at the end is separate and priced by the audit firm, not by Drata. Drata's own site claims 8,500+ global customers and a 4.8 out of 5 G2 score, and it ranks #30 on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2025 US list. Third-party comparisons report roughly $328 million raised and a $2 billion valuation at its December 2022 Series C; those figures are reported, not confirmed in Drata's own pricing or product pages.

That matters because SOC 2 has become a gate to enterprise revenue: without a report, a vendor cannot close large customers, and with one, it can. Drata's bet is that the gate should be maintained continuously rather than rebuilt before each audit, and that a single control library should cover SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR, and the rest at once. If that bet holds, compliance stops being a one-off project and becomes a standing dashboard a sales team can show a prospect.


For a buyer, the day-to-day work inside Drata is personnel onboarding and policy attestation, access reviews, and evidence tasks assigned to owners, with control status updated daily and drift alerts when a control fails. A security questionnaire from a prospect can be answered from the Trust Center instead of drafted from scratch, and a vendor review can be filed in the same system as the framework evidence. That is the operational pitch: not just a SOC 2 binder, but the place where compliance, risk, and trust work happen every week, so the next audit starts from a dashboard that is already green rather than from a scramble.

Drata also sells through AWS Marketplace and through auditor referrals, and its site names technology, financial services, healthcare, and government contracting as its core sectors, with startups, mid-size companies, and enterprises all in scope.
## SOC 2, ISO 27001, and the 30+ Drata frameworks

Drata's product page lists support for 30+ standard frameworks, with custom frameworks available at the enterprise tier. The named core set is SOC 2, SOC 1, ISO 27001, HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR, CCPA, CMMC, NIST CSF, NIST 800-53, ISO 27701, and DORA, plus newer AI frameworks including ISO 42001 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. The mechanism is cross-framework control mapping: a control is defined once, evidence is linked to it once, and the same control satisfies overlapping requirements across frameworks. Drata calls its shared catalog the Drata Control Framework. In practice this is where multi-framework teams save time — adding ISO 27001 after SOC 2 means mapping existing evidence, not starting a second audit from zero. It is also where Drata's limits show: a framework outside its pre-mapped set, or a bespoke internal standard, has to be built as a custom framework, which is an enterprise-tier capability, and the mapping still has to be reviewed by the customer's auditor.

## Audit Hub, Trust Center, and who actually issues the report

Two Drata products shape the audit itself. Audit Hub centralizes auditor collaboration — evidence requests, approvals, and communication in one hub, with a dedicated auditor view and an integration with Fieldguide so auditors can pull what they need without a Drata login. The Trust Center, built on SafeBase, publishes a company's policies and reports to prospects and automates NDA-gated access, so security reviews run without the security team answering the same questionnaire repeatedly. Drata also offers AI-assisted questionnaire drafting and AI agents for vendor document retrieval and third-party risk assessments.

One fact buyers often miss: Drata does not issue the audit. A CPA firm does, and Drata's auditor relationship is a collaboration tool plus a referral network of 175+ firms reported by third-party guides, not an in-house audit practice. Thoropass, a competitor, bundles audit services; Drata keeps preparation and attestation separate. That separation is standard in the category, but it means the subscription price is never the all-in cost of getting certified.

## Drata's risk management, vendor reviews, and personnel controls

Beyond framework tracking, Drata covers the surrounding GRC work in the same platform: a risk register, vendor risk management, policy and personnel tracking, user access reviews, and third-party vendor assessments. The Brex case is the clearest public example of scale: Brex connected its stack, launched a branded Trust Center, migrated about 1,100 vendors into vendor risk management, and ran internal audits inside Drata, reporting a 5x faster internal audit process. The platform connects to 300+ tools by its own count, or its own API for anything outside that set, and it scans infrastructure during development to catch control gaps before production. For a team whose risk is not one framework but dozens of vendors, access reviews, and policy attestations, this is the part of Drata that replaces the spreadsheet estate, not just the audit binder.

## Who buys Drata, and where Vanta and Secureframe win instead

Drata's named competitors are Vanta, Secureframe, OneTrust, and Thoropass, with Vanta the most frequent head-to-head. Third-party comparisons credit Vanta with a larger install base (16,000+ organizations reported in April 2026 against Drata's 8,500+ claimed) and more integrations (400+ against Drata's 300+), plus hourly rather than daily automated tests and a higher-tier FedRAMP authorization. They credit Drata with stronger auditor collaboration through Audit Hub, higher support scores on G2, and a single AWS-listed package that still covers up to 50 employees where Vanta's listed prices stop at 20. Secureframe is positioned as the simpler, cheaper first-SOC-2 route for teams running one or two frameworks. The practical split: a team running one framework for the first time and price-sensitive will often pick Vanta or Secureframe; a team running three or more frameworks at once, or one that wants its auditor working inside the same tool, is Drata's natural buyer. Drata is weakest where its framework list ends, where a buyer needs audit services bundled, or where per-framework pricing on the AWS route stacks up faster than a flat quote from a rival.

## Drata traction, pricing opacity, and the audit-market risk

Drata's traction is real but its pricing is opaque, and that opacity is itself a risk for buyers budgeting without a sales call. The $15,000 Foundation figure and the $25,000-plus-$7,500-per-framework Platform figures come from marketplace listings reported by third parties, not from a Drata pricing page, and they do not map cleanly onto Drata's Foundation, Advanced, and Enterprise tiers. Module pricing, such as a reported $50,000-a-year risk management line on the AWS listing, adds further variance. No public controversy specific to Drata's audit integrity was found in this crawl; the sector's 2026 scrutiny fell on a smaller rival over alleged fabricated evidence, which if anything raises the value buyers place on an auditor relationship that is independent of the preparation tool. Drata's standing risk is concentration: if enterprise buyers standardize on a rival's trust center, or if auditors stop accepting automated evidence at face value, the daily-monitoring pitch loses its edge. For now, its position is that of the enterprise-polished challenger in a three-way race with Vanta and Secureframe, winning on multi-framework depth and auditor workflow rather than on price transparency.

Sources: drata.com/products/compliance, drata.com/customers/brex, soc2auditors.org Drata pricing, stackscout.net comparisons; accessed 2026-10-30.
