name: Transcarent
desc: Transcarent — LinkedIn Top Startups 2025 US #36. Health and care navigation platform. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Transcarent, founded in 2020 and led by CEO Glen Tullman, sells a single front door for health and care to self-insured employers, health plans, and health systems, who offer it to their employees and members. Its slogan is "One Place for Health and Care," and the product that carries it is WayFinding, an AI-powered navigation experience launched in 2024. A member opens the app, asks a health or benefits question in plain language — what is covered, where to get care, whether a symptom needs urgent attention — and the AI Care Assistant answers in the context of that member's own plan, remembers what their doctor said, and books the next step: 24/7 chat-based care, a same-day video visit with a board-certified physician, virtual mental-health therapy, or an in-person appointment. The point is to replace a stack of separate point solutions — one app for navigation, another for virtual care, another for pharmacy, another for surgery — with one place a member actually opens.

Transcarent makes money on employer and health-plan contracts, not on member subscriptions; members do not buy Transcarent directly, their employer or plan does. Pricing is not published; sales are enterprise-contract only, so no list price or per-member rate can be stated from public sources. Scale is the company's own claim and it is large: after completing its merger with Accolade in April 2025, Transcarent says it serves more than 20 million members through more than 1,700 employer and health-plan clients, and a later company release puts the figure at more than 21 million members. It ranks #36 on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2025 US list. The Accolade deal, valued at about $621 million with Accolade shareholders receiving $7.03 per share in cash, took Accolade off Nasdaq and made it part of privately held Transcarent.

That matters because employer health spending is both huge and badly navigated: employees do not know what is covered, pick high-cost sites of care by default, and delay care until it becomes expensive. Transcarent's bet is that an AI assistant that knows the plan, remembers the history, and can actually book the appointment will steer members to higher-quality, lower-cost care often enough to pay for itself in avoided emergency visits, avoided surgeries, and negotiated surgery prices. If the steering works, the employer saves money and the member gets care faster; if members do not open the app, the whole model stalls, which is why utilization is the number Transcarent's business lives or dies on.


Members reach Transcarent around the clock, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, by app, phone, or chat, and the company says members can connect to care in 60 seconds from its on-demand clinic. Employers can also offer point solutions through Transcarent's Experience Store, so a benefit a member already has is reachable from the same app instead of a separate login. In late 2024 Transcarent was selected to power the Evernorth Health Services oncology benefit program, an early sign that health plans, not only employers, would use its complex-care routing.
## WayFinding: benefits navigation, clinical guidance, and care delivery in one app

WayFinding is organized around three jobs. Benefits navigation: the AI Care Assistant answers questions customized to the employer's benefits and plan design and learns from past interactions to recommend the next best step. Clinical guidance: symptom checking helps a member understand what to do next, with doctors and nurses providing follow-up, and expert medical opinions from 2nd.MD, the Accolade-owned second-opinion service, for high-stakes decisions. Care delivery: intelligent scheduling finds high-quality, in-network options and books them, from 24/7 chat-based care and same-day video visits to virtual mental-health therapy or in-person care. The memory engine is the thread through all three: it remembers what the doctor said and what the member shared, so the member does not repeat their story at every visit, and follow-ups and reminders support adherence after the visit. Transcarent describes WayFinding as the first practical use of agentic AI plus human support across those three jobs, with clinicians always a tap away, and its own site reports internal figures for inquiries resolved by the AI assistant, improved treatment plans through expert opinions, and reductions in avoidable emergency and urgent-care visits, all labeled as internal analysis where individual results may vary.

## Transcarent's Care Experiences: cancer, surgery, weight, pharmacy, and mental health

Beyond everyday navigation, Transcarent sells named Care Experiences for the expensive, complex cases where employers actually lose money. Cancer Care runs from prevention to survivorship with personalized, evidence-based guidance, dedicated ACS LION-certified Oncology Nurse Navigators, and a Centers of Excellence network across academic medical centers, NCI-designated cancer centers, and community sites; in 2026 it added a bundled payment model for BiTE and CAR T immunotherapies delivered through community providers, aimed at more predictable oncology costs. Surgery Care and Muscle and Joint Health run end-to-end musculoskeletal and surgery journeys — early intervention, orthopedic e-consults, virtual second opinions, a Centers of Excellence network, and coordinated recovery — and Transcarent reports a 27% surgery avoidance rate verified through 12 months of claims follow-up. Weight Health pairs a connected, on-demand care team with clinical, lifestyle, and behavior-change support. Pharmacy Care lets members manage and shop prescriptions in the app, with the company claiming members save an average of $85, more for specialty drugs. Mental Health offers confidential therapy and psychiatry from home. Everyday Care — primary care, mental health, and urgent care — sits underneath all of them, with Transcarent claiming connection to care in 60 seconds from its on-demand clinic.

## The Accolade merger and what Transcarent bought

Transcarent's scale jump did not come from organic growth alone. It acquired 98point6 in 2023 for virtual primary care capacity and BridgeHealth earlier for surgery navigation, then in January 2025 agreed to buy Accolade, the health advocacy and virtual primary-care company, for about $621 million, closing in April 2025. What Accolade brought was advocacy — human health assistants who know the member — plus expert medical opinions through 2nd.MD, virtual primary care through PlushCare, and 16 years of healthcare data. Combined with Transcarent's WayFinding and its Cancer, Surgery, and Weight Health experiences plus its Pharmacy Benefit offering, the merged company pitches itself as the most complete health-and-care platform for employers and plans. The risk in that pitch is integration: merging two large navigation and virtual-care stacks, two workforces, and two client bases is the kind of work that routinely slips, and the company's own growth story now depends on the combined product feeling like one place rather than two companies stapled together. Its next test is visible in partnerships like the October 2026 Angle Health deal, which extends Transcarent's musculoskeletal and surgery Centers of Excellence to small and midsize employers from January 1, 2027 — a segment the old large-employer model did not reach.

## Who Transcarent competes with, and who it does not replace

Transcarent's direct competitors in navigation and advocacy are Accolade's old rivals — Included Health, Lyra Health for behavioral health, and the advocacy arms of large insurers — and, in virtual care, the telehealth platforms employers already buy. Its difference is the combination: navigation plus clinical guidance plus care delivery plus bundled complex-care pricing in one contract, rather than navigation alone. What Transcarent does not do is replace the health plan or the insurer. It sits in front of the plan, steering members within the plan's network and benefits; it does not underwrite risk, set premiums, or pay claims as an insurer would. A member whose employer does not offer Transcarent cannot sign up individually, and a member who wants a specific doctor outside the guided network is still bound by their plan's rules. The company's reported utilization near 70% in third-party coverage, if accurate, is the number that separates it from navigation tools members ignore; Transcarent's own releases do not publish a single audited utilization figure, so that figure should be treated as reported, not confirmed.

## Transcarent's open questions: price, proof, and the AI answer

Three things are not public and matter for any buyer. First, price: no per-member-per-month rate or contract structure is published, so an employer cannot benchmark Transcarent against a rival without a sales process. Second, proof: the savings figures — surgery avoidance, emergency-visit reduction, pharmacy savings — come from Transcarent's internal analyses and partner announcements, not from independent published trials, and results are stated to vary by member. Third, the AI answer itself: WayFinding's assistant gives clinical guidance and books care, which puts accuracy and escalation to a human clinician at the center of the product; a wrong triage answer is a safety event, not a software bug. Transcarent's answer is that clinicians are always a tap away and that the memory engine and evidence-based guidelines constrain the assistant. No public safety controversy specific to WayFinding was found in this crawl. The company's position is that of the largest independent navigation platform after the Accolade merger, betting that one AI-guided front door beats a shelf of point solutions — a bet that will be judged on whether members keep opening the app and whether employers renew at the contract price they will not publish.

Sources: transcarent.com/care-experiences, accolade.com/connect (WayFinding), nasdaq.com Transcarent completes merger with Accolade 2025-04-08, businesswire.com Angle Health partnership 2026-10-15; accessed 2026-10-30.

desc: Dandy — LinkedIn Top Startups 2025 US #44. Fully digital dental lab and scanner platform. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Dandy, founded in 2020, in New York, is a fully digital dental lab that sells to dentists, group practices, and dental service organizations (DSOs) across the United States. Its pitch is a bundle no traditional lab offers: a free intraoral scanner, live chairside help from lab technicians while the patient is still in the chair, and the lab work itself, all run through one software workflow. A dentist scans a patient instead of taking a physical mold, Dandy's Chairside software guides the scan and its AI review checks it, a lab technician can be reached in 60 seconds or less to review the scan live, the dentist approves a 3D design, and the finished crown, denture, aligner, or implant restoration ships back with tracked delivery. Fixed restorations are made in Dandy's Utah lab; removable products are made in its Texas lab, with free shipping nationwide.

Dandy makes money two ways: a monthly lab-spend minimum plus per-case lab fees. Its published pricing page lists three tiers. The Dandy Vision tier carries a $1,000-a-month lab minimum and includes a Dandy Vision scanner the company values at $30,000, Chairside AI Scan Review, and AI-powered smile simulation. The TRIOS 5 tier carries a $2,500-a-month minimum and includes a 3Shape TRIOS 5 wireless scanner valued at $39,000. The DSO tier is customized, with a free Dandy Vision scanner per location, volume-based pricing, group contracts, and centralized billing. All three are month-to-month with no long-term contract; if a practice misses its minimum in a month, it pays the difference, unless it tells support in advance, for example for a vacation closure. Per-case fees are not listed in full on the pricing page — the company says it will provide a full turnaround and fee schedule on a sales call — though its lab pages advertise 5-day zirconia crowns at $99 per unit and 2-appointment dentures. Third-party reviews report more than $172 million in venture capital raised and more than 6,000 dental practices signed up; those figures are reported, not stated on Dandy's pricing page. Dandy ranks #44 on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2025 US list.

That matters because the traditional dental lab workflow is slow and remake-prone: physical impressions, two-plus weeks for a zirconia crown, and a remake when the impression is off. Dandy's bet is that giving the scanner away, then making the scan right while the patient is still seated, cuts remakes and chair time enough that practices will route all their lab work to one lab. Dandy claims up to a 50% reduction in remakes on its workflow, 36+ fewer rescan appointments a year, and that 99% of practices stay once onboarded. If those claims hold for a given practice, the scanner bundle pays for itself in saved appointments; if the practice is low-volume, the monthly minimum becomes a tax it pays whether it orders or not.


In September 2026 Dandy launched Fusion, a denture line combining digital precision with hand-finished craftsmanship, and third-party reviews report its acquisition of Neem, a dental practice-management software company. Dandy says its dentists are located in all 50 states, with free, fast shipping nationwide and a case tracker that keeps the practice on schedule.
## Dandy Vision, TRIOS, and the Chairside scan workflow

The scanner is the entry point, and Dandy offers two. Dandy Vision is its own scanner, built for speed — a full arch in under 45 seconds by the company's claim — with AI insights and live clinical support built in. The TRIOS 5 is 3Shape's wireless scanner, supplied on the higher tier. Dandy also supplies a laptop and scanner cart, and unlimited scanning training. The workflow runs in Dandy Chairside, proprietary software that guides the scan step by step, asks multiple-choice questions to submit the case, and lets the dentist chat with the lab team in real time, even video-calling, while the patient is still in the chair. The Dandy Portal then tracks the case through production, gives delivery estimates, and lets the practice review and approve designs and modify orders without calling the lab. Practices that already own a scanner are not excluded — Dandy says it works with practices that have a TRIOS scanner — but the free-scanner bundle is the offer that defines the deal, and the scanner is leased for as long as the practice stays subscribed, not owned outright.

## Dandy's lab products: crowns, dentures, implants, aligners, and guards

Dandy is a full-service lab, not a single-product shop. Its restorative line covers zirconia, e.max, PFM, and metal crowns, bridges, inlays, onlays, and veneers, with 5-day turnaround advertised for zirconia crowns and a lifetime warranty against breakage from defects in materials or workmanship on fixed products. Its removable line covers full and partial dentures — 2-appointment dentures ready in under 10 days — plus splints, night guards, sleep apnea devices, and bleaching trays, with a six-month wear-and-tear warranty and a ten-year breakage warranty. Implants are supported across approved systems with FDA-approved parts, custom abutments milled in-house in titanium, zirconia, and Ti-base, free scan bodies, and surgical guides at $109 per site on its lab pages. Clear aligners are doctor-directed, with 3D treatment simulations and three pricing plans, plus clear and wire retainers. In 2026 Dandy also launched Fusion, a denture line combining digital precision with hand-finished work. The breadth is the point: a practice can send everything to one lab and track it in one portal, instead of splitting crowns, dentures, and aligners across three vendors.

## Dandy's pricing in practice: minimums, remakes, and warranties

The economics turn on three details. First, the minimum is a spend commitment, not a subscription fee on top of lab fees — the practice's lab orders count toward it, and only the shortfall is charged. Second, remakes are free and, in Dandy's words, without hassle, which matters because a remake costs the practice a second appointment and the patient a second visit. Third, warranties are long: lifetime on fixed products, ten years on denture and guard breakage, which shifts the risk of a failed restoration from the practice to the lab. Dandy also claims 9 out of 10 dentists rate its lab support the best they have experienced, a company claim, not an independent survey result. The gaps in the public pricing are the per-case fee schedule itself, which requires a sales conversation, and the cost of leaving: month-to-month means no contract penalty, but a practice that leaves returns the scanner and loses the Chairside and Portal workflow it built its ordering around.

## Dandy against Glidewell, local labs, and the scanner makers

Dandy's competitors split three ways. Glidewell, one of the largest US labs, competes on raw speed and price for routine work — next-day BruxZir crowns on digital submissions, per-case pricing with no subscription or minimum — and beats Dandy's 5-day zirconia turnaround for a practice that only needs crowns fast. Local labs compete on relationships and complex esthetics, where a dentist who knows the technician by name will not trade that for a portal. Scanner makers 3Shape, iTero, and Medit compete indirectly: a practice that buys its own scanner can use any lab, while Dandy's bundle ties the scanner to Dandy's lab. Dandy's difference is the integration — scanner plus live technician plus manufacturing plus tracking in one system, which it describes as the first and only full-service lab to unite those pieces. Its recent acquisition of Neem, a dental practice-management software company reported by third-party reviews, signals an intent to expand beyond lab work into the wider dental software stack, which would put it in competition with practice-management vendors as well as labs.

## Dandy's risks: volume, dependence, and the low-volume practice

Dandy's risk is the mirror of its bundle. A high-volume restorative practice that scans daily will likely clear the $1,000 or $2,500 minimum easily and gain from the scanner, the live review, and the free remakes. A low-volume practice, a new practice, or one that does mostly hygiene and checkups will pay the minimum in slow months and may be better served by a per-case lab like Glidewell or a local lab with no commitment. A practice that already owns a premium scanner gains less from the bundle's headline offer. And a practice that routes everything to Dandy becomes dependent on one vendor's turnaround, pricing, and portal; if Dandy raises per-case fees — which are not published — the practice discovers it at renewal, not at signup. No public safety or quality controversy specific to Dandy was found in this crawl. Its position is that of the digital challenger to the national lab incumbents, winning where scanning, live support, and one-portal tracking save more chair time than the monthly minimum costs.

Sources: meetdandy.com/pricing, meetdandy.com/digital, meetdandy.com lab services pages, peakdentalstudio.com Dandy review 2026; accessed 2026-10-30.

name: Merge
desc: Merge — LinkedIn Top Startups 2025 US #48. Unified API for HR, ATS, CRM, and accounting. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Merge, founded in June 2020, in San Francisco by Shensi Ding and Gil Feig, sells integration infrastructure to B2B software companies. Its problem is concrete: a SaaS product that wants to connect to its customers' HR, recruiting, CRM, accounting, and ticketing tools would otherwise have to build and maintain a separate integration for each vendor — Workday and BambooHR for HR, Greenhouse and Lever for recruiting, Salesforce and HubSpot for CRM, QuickBooks and NetSuite for accounting — each with its own authentication, schema, pagination, and rate limits. Merge replaces that work with one API. A product team integrates Merge once, its customers connect their own tools through Merge Link, an embedded widget that handles OAuth and credential collection, and Merge syncs the data into Common Models, a normalized schema the product queries as if Workday and BambooHR were the same system. Merge reports more than 250 integrations and names OpenAI, Ramp, Lattice, Dropbox, Perplexity, and Netflix among its customers.

Merge makes money per linked account for its Unified API, and per tool call for its agent product. A linked account is one customer's connection to one integration: a customer connecting Salesforce and Workday counts as two. The Launch plan, self-serve, gives the first 3 production linked accounts free, then charges $650 a month for up to 10 production linked accounts, with $65 a month for each additional account. Professional and Enterprise plans are contract-priced; Professional adds custom fields, field-level scopes, and custom sync frequencies, while Enterprise adds audit trails, unlimited sandboxes, and uptime SLAs. Agent Handler, the separate product that gives AI agents authenticated access to those same connected tools, is priced by credits: Free at $0 a month with 2,000 monthly credits, Pro at $1,000 a month with 25,000 credits and overages billed at month-end, and Enterprise at custom pricing with custom connectors and on-prem deployment. Merge has raised more than $75 million reported, and it ranks #48 on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2025 US list.

That matters because integrations are where B2B deals are won and lost: a product that cannot sync with a prospect's HR system does not get bought, and a product that builds each integration by hand spends its engineering budget on plumbing instead of its core product. Merge's bet is that a normalized, synced copy of customer data, maintained by Merge as vendors change their APIs, is worth a per-account fee that grows linearly with the customer base. If that bet holds, a small team can ship an integration catalog that would otherwise take a dedicated integrations team. If the fee grows faster than the revenue per customer, the same pricing becomes the reason to build in-house or switch to a usage-priced rival.


Merge's newer products extend the same connectivity idea to agents and internal tools. Gateway routes large-language-model requests with cost and performance controls, and Merge for Workforce governs internal AI usage. Agent Handler's tool-call logs are kept for 90 days by default on the tiers third-party guides describe, and Enterprise adds SIEM streaming, custom deployments including on-premises, and a dedicated Slack channel.
## Merge Unified: Common Models, Merge Link, and the eight categories

Merge Unified covers HRIS, ATS, CRM, accounting, ticketing, file storage, marketing automation, and adjacent categories through one normalized interface per category. The architecture has three layers a buyer should understand. Merge Link is the embedded UI the end customer sees when connecting a tool. The Unified API is the normalized REST API the product queries, with Common Models that map provider-specific fields into one schema — a Workday employee and a BambooHR employee arrive in the same shape. The sync layer polls providers, stores a synced copy, and detects changes; on Launch, records refresh on a daily sync, while faster syncs and source webhooks start at Professional. That sync-and-store design is Merge's core tradeoff: it makes queries fast and consistent, but it means a third party holds a copy of the customer's HR and payroll data, with subprocessor and compliance obligations that a passthrough rival avoids. Custom fields, field mapping, and passthrough to provider-specific objects that fall outside the Common Model are gated to Professional and Enterprise, so a team whose enterprise customer relies on custom Workday objects cannot serve that customer on Launch.

## Merge Agent Handler, Gateway, and Merge for Workforce

Merge's second act is agents. Agent Handler, launched in 2025, gives AI agents managed connectors, credential and permission management, and a full audit trail of every tool call, so an agent can read and act across a customer's connected apps under a registered user's credentials rather than a shared service key. It is priced separately from Unified, by credits spent per tool call, with custom rules, an evaluation suite, and SIEM log streaming on higher tiers. Merge Gateway, launched in March 2026, routes LLM requests with cost and performance controls, and Merge for Workforce, launched in August 2026, governs internal AI usage and spend. Together the three products reposition Merge from a data-integration vendor to the connectivity layer for AI products and agents, and its June 2026 arrival on the Microsoft Agent Store puts Agent Handler in front of Microsoft 365 Copilot customers. The risk in that expansion is coherence: three products with separate pricing — per linked account, per credit, per workforce seat — are harder to buy than one API, and Agent Handler is limited to the normalized schema, so an agent cannot reach a custom object that Unified itself cannot model.

## Who buys Merge, and where Knit, Nango, Apideck, and Unified.to win instead

Merge's buyer is a B2B SaaS product team, typically HR-tech, recruiting-tech, or sales-tech, that needs customer-facing integrations fast and does not want to maintain them. Its named competitors are Knit, Nango, Apideck, Kombo, and Unified.to, plus the general iPaaS tools Zapier and Workato, which Merge is not: it does not build arbitrary workflows between any two apps, it normalizes a fixed set of categories. The competitive split is architectural. Knit offers a webhook-first, zero-storage design with tiered pricing that declines per account at scale, and wins where a buyer cannot let a third party cache HR data. Apideck offers real-time passthrough with flat monthly pricing from $599 and wins where freshness matters more than a synced copy. Nango offers a proxy-based, self-hosted option with usage pricing and wins where a team wants to own its integration code. Unified.to offers per-API-call pricing with unlimited connections and live reads and writes, and wins where per-account pricing would explode with customer count. Merge wins where breadth of catalog, documentation, and onboarding speed matter most, and where the buyer accepts the synced-copy model and linear pricing. At 200 linked accounts, third-party math puts Merge at $156,000 a year on the per-account model — a figure a buyer should compute for their own customer count before signing.

## Merge's pricing trap, data custody, and the scale question

Merge's standing risks are pricing scale, data custody, and category depth. Pricing scale: $65 per linked account per month is cheap at 10 accounts and punishing at 1,000, because the fee multiplies by customers times integrations, not by usage. Data custody: Merge stores synced data and credentials until deleted by its own documentation, which makes it a subprocessor for HR and payroll data and a diligence item for any enterprise customer's security review. Category depth: Merge's normalized schema covers standard objects well and custom objects only on higher tiers, so a team whose roadmap includes file storage or knowledge-base tools, or a customer-specific HR object, must check depth category by category rather than trusting the 250+ headline count. No public security breach specific to Merge was found in this crawl. Its position is that of the broadest, most mature unified-API vendor, with the clearest agent story, charging the most predictable and, at scale, the most expensive price in its category.

Sources: merge.dev/pricing/agent-handler, getknit.dev Merge pricing and evaluation guides 2026, unified.to best unified API platforms 2026, shownmedia.com Merge case study; accessed 2026-10-30.

name: Truveta
desc: Truveta — LinkedIn Top Startups 2025 US #42. Health system-led de-identified health data. Distilled agent held in custody by CopyCat.
distilled:
Truveta, founded in September 2020, and headquartered in Bellevue, Washington, is a health data company owned and governed by 30 U.S. health systems. Its product is de-identified electronic health record data at national scale, cleaned and harmonized so researchers can ask questions of it in days rather than years. Member health systems — Providence, Advocate Health, Trinity Health, Tenet Healthcare, Northwell Health, AdventHealth, CommonSpirit Health, Henry Ford Health System, and 22 others — send Truveta daily feeds of structured and unstructured EHR data: diagnoses, labs, medications, procedures, clinical notes, imaging reports, and pathology narratives, linked with closed claims, mortality data, and social drivers of health. Truveta normalizes that data to its Truveta Data Model, de-identifies it under HIPAA expert determination, and makes it queryable. A peer-reviewed paper in JAMIA Open reports data for 130 million patients, about 1 in 3 Americans; a Truveta whitepaper from August 2026 puts the figure above 140 million patients, with 8 billion clinical events and 190 million imaging studies.

Truveta makes money by licensing that data and the tools to query it to life-sciences companies, health systems, and public-health users, not by selling to patients or doctors. Pricing is not published as a list price; enterprise licensing and usage-based access through its platform are the model, with third-party job postings describing researchers paying only for the data and analytics they use. Funding is reported, not stated on Truveta's product pages: a $320 million Series C in January 2025, with Regeneron and Illumina investing alongside the round, bringing reported total funding to $515 million. Truveta ranks #42 on LinkedIn's Top Startups 2025 US list. Its first life-sciences customer was Pfizer in 2022, followed by Boston Scientific, and its named users include Bayer, Boehringer Ingelheim, the CDC, Stanford, and Johns Hopkins, with more than 100 scientific publications supported by Truveta Data reported in the peer-reviewed paper.

That matters because drug development and public-health research have historically run on fragmented, months-old data: a question about a new therapy's safety or a treatment's real-world effectiveness could take years of chart review across hospitals that do not share a schema. Truveta's bet is that a health-system-owned, daily-refreshed, nationally representative dataset, structured by AI from free text, lets researchers test hypotheses on the full patient journey — including the notes and images where the clinical story actually lives — and produce evidence regulators will accept. If that bet holds, real-world evidence stops being a retrospective report and becomes a living input to trials, safety monitoring, and care guidelines. If member systems withdraw, or if de-identification is ever shown to fail, the dataset's breadth and its trust collapse together.


Truveta says its member systems provide over 18% of the daily clinical care delivered across the United States, which is why it describes its dataset as representative rather than sampled. It has also launched Truveta Intelligence for real-time insights from continuously refreshed data, alongside Studio, its core research platform.
## Truveta Studio, Prose, and the Truveta Data Model

Truveta Studio is the platform researchers actually use. It lets a researcher define a cohort with Prose, Truveta's cohort-definition language, query the de-identified dataset iteratively, and generate full datasets for analysis inside or outside Truveta. The underlying schema is the Truveta Data Model, built on the HL7 FHIR standard and inspired by the OMOP common data model, developed with health systems and research users to capture the clinical nuance of real cases rather than just billing codes. Daily ingestion normalizes incoming data to standard ontologies, and AI — including natural-language processing — extracts concepts from free-text notes, imaging reports, and pathology narratives into standardized variables. Truveta's own account of its advantage is data gravity: because the dataset is large and representative, more researchers use it, which gives more health systems a reason to join, which makes the dataset larger. The platform's limits are the same as any de-identified dataset's: it cannot identify or contact an individual patient, it cannot support direct clinical care for a named person, and its representativeness depends on which systems are members and which patients receive care there.

## The Truveta Language Model and how notes become variables

The Truveta Language Model, introduced in 2023, is a multimodal large-language model that structures clinical data from EHRs. Its job is the unglamorous core of the company: turning a physician's note that says a patient had a heart attack into a coded, queryable event consistent across hundreds of hospitals that record the same event differently. Truveta describes the pipeline as generative-AI-driven transformation plus semantic and syntactic normalization, protected-health-information detection, tokenization, and patient matching, with AI-driven redaction and de-identification applied across tabular data, notes, and images. In 2025 Truveta won the SXSW Innovation Award for artificial intelligence for this work. The risk in the pipeline is silent error: an NLP extraction that misreads a negation, a dose, or a diagnosis propagates into every study built on it, which is why Truveta publishes a data-quality whitepaper and emphasizes provenance, quality controls, and audit-ready lineage for regulatory-grade use. Researchers who treat Truveta Data as ground truth without checking extraction quality for their specific question are using it wrong.

## The Truveta Genome Project: 10 million exomes linked to records

The Truveta Genome Project, announced in January 2025, is Truveta's largest bet. With its member health systems, the Regeneron Genetics Center, Illumina, and Microsoft Azure as exclusive cloud provider, it aims to sequence the exomes of the first 10 million consenting volunteers, building what it describes as the largest and most diverse database of genotypic and phenotypic information ever assembled, at more than ten times the scale of previous efforts. The mechanics are consent-based and narrow: a patient receiving care at a member system consents to the use of leftover biospecimens from routine lab tests, those specimens are sequenced while preserving anonymity, leftover material is stored for future multi-omics sequencing, and the de-identified genetic data is linked to de-identified medical records and added to Truveta Data. Regeneron and Illumina invested in Truveta to support the project with, by Truveta's own statement, no board seats, no governance over Truveta, and no access to customer confidential information. The project's value is causal: linking genotypes to longitudinal phenotypes lets researchers test whether a gene variant causes a disease pattern, not merely correlates with it. Its risk is consent and trust at scale — a single mishandled biospecimen or re-identification claim would damage the member systems whose patients supplied the data, not just Truveta.

## Who uses Truveta, and what its rivals offer instead

Truveta's buyers are life-sciences companies running real-world evidence studies, regulatory submissions, and trial optimization; member health systems' own research teams; and public-health agencies. Its named rivals are the established real-world-data vendors — Flatiron Health for oncology, TriNetX for federated hospital networks, IQVIA and Optum for claims-heavy datasets — and the cloud data platforms that sell de-identified data as a commodity. Truveta's difference is ownership and governance: it is owned by the health systems that supply the data, rather than buying data from them, which it argues aligns incentives toward completeness and quality rather than extraction. Its difference in data is the daily refresh and the unstructured content — notes and images, not just structured codes and claims. Its weakness against rivals is the same ownership: it depends on 30 member systems staying members, and a defection by a large system would narrow geographic and demographic coverage in a way a claims vendor, buying from many sources, would not feel. Pricing opacity is a second weakness: a research team cannot budget a Truveta study from a public price list, and must negotiate licensing and platform access.

## Truveta's risks: member dependence, privacy, and the evidence bar

Truveta's standing risks are member dependence, privacy proof, and the regulatory evidence bar. Member dependence: the dataset exists only as long as health systems keep sending daily feeds, and each member's governance, IT priorities, and competitive position can change. Privacy: de-identification at 130-million-patient scale, across notes and images, is a technical claim that must hold against re-identification attempts, and Truveta's HIPAA compliance and SOC 2 and HITRUST audits, reported by third-party guides, are the public evidence for it. Evidence bar: regulatory-grade real-world evidence requires provenance and quality documentation for every study, and a dataset that is complete for billing may still be incomplete for a specific clinical question — missing labs, missing social drivers, or uneven imaging coverage. No public privacy breach or re-identification finding specific to Truveta was found in this crawl. Its position is that of the only health-system-owned national EHR dataset, betting that ownership, daily refresh, and genomic linkage will make it the default source for real-world evidence — a bet that will be judged on whether researchers keep publishing from it and whether members keep feeding it.
